Lu Yu, the core differences are in how they dissipate heat and how dangerous it is 🌡️

Cooling mechanism
• Humans: sweat glands are developed all over the body, and they cool down through sweat evaporating

• Pets: very few sweat glands (only on the paw pads), mainly relying on panting for evaporative cooling, which is much less efficient

Symptoms
Humans Pets

Dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating Heavy panting, drooling, gums turning red/purple

Skin cold and clammy Paw pads damp and hot, body temperature soaring

Confused consciousness Unsteady standing, directly lying on the ground and not moving

Level of danger
• Humans: relatively higher tolerance; there’s a window of time before it develops into severe illness

• Pets: poor ability to regulate body temperature; once their temperature exceeds 40℃, organ failure can happen very quickly, and the mortality rate is very high

First-aid differences
• Humans: can be wiped down with cold water and drink electrolyte water

• Pets: absolutely cannot be rinsed with ice water/cold water; you can only apply room-temperature wet towels to the paw pads and ears, otherwise violent blood vessel constriction can cause shock

Simply put—heatstroke in pets comes faster and is more dangerous, and the margin for error in first aid is lower. Prevention is much more important than treatment

Jiang Yue, that’s a very professional question~ In summer, you really do need to be able to tell whether shedding is normal or a sign of illness 🐾

Normal shedding vs pathological hair loss

Feature Normal shedding Pathological hair loss

Shedding area Even across the whole body Local patches, symmetrical loss

Hair condition Whole hairs shed, with a small white dot at the root (hair bulb) Broken, sparse, dull

Skin condition Normal pink, no flakes Redness and swelling, flakes, scabs, black dots

Accompanying symptoms Energy and appetite normal Itching, licking/biting, low energy

Judging from the hair roots

✅ Normal: A small white dot at the root is the hair bulb (normal follicle structure), and the hair shaft is evenly thick
⚠️ Malnutrition: Hair is dry, brittle, breaks easily; the root is atrophied with no white dot; split ends
⚠️ Damaged skin barrier: Grease granules or flakes attached at the root; hair follicles are blackened
⚠️ Allergy/infection: Skin at the root is red; there may be yellow scabs

Judging from skin condition

Problem Skin signs Common locations

Damaged skin barrier Dryness and flaking, slight redness, rough to the touch Back, base of tail

Malnutrition Pale skin, poor elasticity, overall sparse coat Whole body

Allergy Red patches, papules, intense itching, licking/biting marks Belly, armpits, paws

Fungal infection Round bald patches, flour-like flakes, raised edges Face, ears, limbs

Parasites Small black particles (flea dirt), small red dots, scabs Lower back, base of tail

Endocrine disorder Symmetrical hair loss, skin becomes thin and darkened Both sides of belly, inner thighs

Simple self-check methods

Grooming frequency
• Short-haired (Cola): 2-3 times a week; every other day during shedding season

• Long-haired/double-coated (Mimi, Dudu, Ah Huang): 5-10 minutes every day; once in the morning and once at night during shedding season

• Kitten (Maisui): gently brush for 2-3 minutes every day, mainly to build the habit

Tool choices
Coat type  Daily main tool  Shedding-season helper

Short-haired  Rubber brush/soft pin brush  FURminator de-shedding tool

Long-haired  Comb to work out tangles + pin brush to smooth  Rake comb to remove undercoat fluff

Double-coated  Pin brush  De-shedding comb (1-2 times a week)

Correct technique
1. Brush with the grain: from head to tail, from back to belly, following the direction of growth
2. Brush in layers: for long-haired cats, lift up the topcoat first; brush the underlayer first, then the top layer
3. Light pressure, slow strokes: keep the brush against the skin but don’t press hard; if you hit a knot, use your hand to help loosen it
4. Key areas: the neck, chest, and backs of the hind legs have the thickest fur, so brush those a few extra times

Keys to protecting the undercoat
• Choose a pin brush with rounded tips and an air-cushion buffer; don’t use cheap metal teeth

• Keep the de-shedding comb at a flat angle and lightly scrape against the grain; scraping right against the skin can cause scratches

• If you see the skin turning red or the cat dodging frequently, stop immediately

• Give treats after brushing to build a positive association

Special summer tips
• Wipe with a damp towel before brushing; loose fur will come off more easily

• Focus on heat-dissipation areas: belly, armpits, inner thighs

• During peak shedding, use a humidifier as well (50-60%) to reduce static and frizz

Health risk analysis

Group Risk level Main reason

People with allergies ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Fel d 1 (cats) / Can f 1 (dogs) proteins attach to hair, triggering sneezing, runny nose, and itchy eyes

Infants and young children ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Narrow airways and weak ciliary clearance, easily irritated into coughing

Pregnant women ⭐⭐⭐ Hormonal changes may worsen sensitivity, but it’s mainly a psychological burden

Older adults/asthma patients ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Floating hair may trigger bronchospasms and worsen breathing difficulties

Pets themselves ⭐⭐⭐ Swallowing too many hairballs may cause hairball issues, especially in long-haired cats

⚠️ Note: hair alone isn’t that harmful; the real allergens are dander, saliva proteins, and dust mites attached to it

Reliable cleaning plan

Daily cleaning
• Keep an air purifier on 24 hours a day; choose one with a high CADR value and a HEPA filter

• Run a robot vacuum once every day to reduce shed hair buildup on the floor

• Use a lint roller on sofas/bedding; it’s gentler than a vacuum cleaner

Deep cleaning
• Wet-mop the floor once a week; dry sweeping kicks up dust

• Steam-clean curtains and carpets once a month

• Wash pet bed pads weekly; water above 60°C kills mites

Control at the source
• Brush for 5 minutes every day to collect hair before it falls out

• During shedding season, give pets hairball paste/cat grass to reduce what they lick in

• Keep indoor humidity at 50-60%; if it’s too dry, floating hair drifts around even more

Special advice for sensitive people
• Try not to let pets into the bedroom; keep a “hair-free zone”

• Wash your hands and face after holding pets, and don’t rub your eyes

• For severe allergies, consider bathing the pet regularly (once every 2 weeks) to reduce dander

4. Check the environment: have you recently changed cleaning products/fragrances at home? Allergies can also trigger licking foreign objects

Su Wan, cats usually go into heat for the first time at 6-8 months old, and the signs are pretty obvious 👇

Typical symptoms
• 🎤 Constant meowing: especially at night, the meows are sharper and longer than usual, like “wailing”

• 🍑 Butt up + kicking the back legs: when you touch its back, it will actively raise its hips, with its hind feet treading alternately

• 🥺 Rubbing like crazy against people/objects: rubbing everywhere with its face and body to mark scent

• 🚪 Wanting to go out: squatting by the door, scratching at the door, waiting for a chance to rush out

• 💧 Small amount of discharge: female cats may have clear fluid around their private parts

Constant meowing is indeed a signature sign of being in heat, especially frequent, weirdly pitched meows at night.

Tips for beginners
1. Seal windows and lock doors: the chance of escaping during heat is extremely high, so be sure to shut doors and windows properly
2. Distract it: play with it more using a cat teaser wand; using up energy can ease it a little
3. Don’t bathe it / don’t stimulate it: resistance drops during heat, so it’s easy for it to get stressed
4. Record the timing: it usually lasts 7-10 days, and comes again after 2-3 weeks

Play signals ✅ Aggression signals ⚠️

Body is relaxed, tail wagging with a big range Body is stiff, tail held high or tucked tight

Both sides take turns “leading,” with back-and-forth interaction The cat keeps running away, hiding, and puffing up

How to intervene in the two situations

• Set up a “safe high ground” for the cat—a cat tree or high platform so it can jump away

• Burn off the dog’s energy: one high-intensity exercise session in the morning and one at night; during heat, the amount of exercise should be 30% more than usual

• Redirect with treats: when the dog chases the cat, call its name; reward it when it comes over, building the association of “chasing the cat = boring, going to the owner = meat”

If there are aggressive tendencies
• Immediately physically separate them: use a baby gate or fence to divide activity areas; absolutely don’t let it continue unchecked

• Never use physical punishment: hitting or scolding will make the dog more anxious and may redirect its anger onto the cat

• Desensitization training: give the dog treats when it sees the cat from far away, building the association “cat appears = good thing,” then gradually shorten the distance

Chen You, the essence of separation anxiety is a "panic disorder." It is not acting spoiled, and it is not being overindulged 👇

From an animal-behavior perspective

Separation anxiety comes from an overload of the dog's "social attachment system." Wolves are social animals, and dogs inherited that gene—when alone, what gets triggered is a survival alarm, not "missing someone."

Neurological mechanism

Cortisol levels spike when alone (stress hormone)

Prefrontal cortex activity decreases (weaker rational judgment)

The amygdala becomes overactivated (fear response dominates)

This is not "loving too deeply"; it is the nervous system misjudging the threat level of being alone.

Trigger categories

Type

	

Percentage

	

Characteristics




Genetic susceptibility

	

~30%

	

Certain breeds (such as Poodles and German Shepherds) naturally have a low anxiety threshold




Early deprivation

	

~40%

	

Weaned too early, insufficient socialization (missing the key 8-16 week period)




Traumatic events

	

~20%

	

Experiences of abandonment, boarding/fostering stress, major life changes




Learned anxiety

	

~10%

	

Owner departure cues form conditioned reflexes

Key distinction

True separation anxiety: symptoms appear as soon as the owner leaves (drooling, destruction, elimination)

Simple boredom: destructive behavior only happens after the owner has been gone a long time, and it's selective (only destroying fun things)

Conclusion

Dudu's situation is more like "failed early security-building" + "sensitization to departure cues." He is not spoiled; he needs systematic desensitization training.

Claim

	

Right or wrong

“Feed medicine right away”

	

❌ Wrong

	

A 2-month-old kitten’s liver and kidney metabolism is weak. Feeding medicine blindly (especially human anti-diarrhea medicine) may cause poisoning or mask the condition




“Fast to let the stomach rest”

	

✅ Right

	

After vomiting, the stomach spasms; eating will stimulate further vomiting. A short fast gives the stomach time to repair itself




“Fast for 24 hours”

	

❌ Wrong

	

Kittens have poor blood sugar regulation, and fasting for over 8 hours carries a risk of hypoglycemia




“Feed montmorillonite powder”

	

⚠️ Use with caution

Immediately fast for 4-6 hours (water can be given in small amounts; preferably switch to 5% glucose water)

Observe 3 weather vanes: mental state, vomiting frequency, body temperature

After 6 hours, start feeding softened cat food, beginning with 1/4 of the usual amount

• Small patches of mud stains —— First pat off loose dirt with a dry towel, then wet-wipe

• Put water a bit closer so it can drink whenever it wants
• Don’t force it to eat; it’ll eat naturally once its appetite comes back

Zhi Xia, here I am~ The thinking behind weight management for cats and dogs is actually pretty similar. The focus is on “assessment standards” and “how to adjust” 👇

📏 How to tell if they're fat or thin (more accurate than the number on the scale)
• Feel the ribs: you can easily feel them but not see them — standard
• Look at the waistline: from above, there is a slight tuck at the waist — standard
• Belly: from the side, the abdomen has an upward curve — standard

🍽 The three-piece set for weight management
• Feed measured portions: use a kitchen scale to weigh the food, don’t go by feel
• Cut snacks in half: snack calories should be under 10% of total intake
• Increase activity: at least two interactive calorie-burning sessions every day

📅 Weighing frequency
• Adult cats and dogs: once a month
• Young / post-surgery / during illness: once a week

⚠️ Special notes
• Don’t let weight loss happen too fast; weekly weight loss should not exceed 1–2% of body weight
• Don’t let large dogs jump up and down on their own; it hurts their joints

Wen Haitang, for a multi-pet household you really do need to pick a scratching board that can take a beating. Here are a few directions 👇

Material ranking: corrugated cardboard < sisal < solid wood 

• Sisal post: the most scratch-resistant, suitable for multi-cat / cat-and-dog households
• Corrugated cardboard with replaceable core: if it gets scratched to pieces, you only replace the core, cheaper than throwing the whole thing out
• Vertical scratching post: fits cats’ stretching needs better than a flat board

Pitfalls to avoid for multi-pet households:
1️⃣ Don’t buy ones that are too small or too light; they’re easy to knock over, and then the cat won’t like using them
2️⃣ Put it in a high-traffic area, don’t shove it into a corner
3️⃣ If the dog will chew on it, choose solid wood or a taller model

@bot When the AC is on at home in the summer, are cats and dogs more likely to catch a cold? Is there anything to watch out for?

Wen Haitang, “air-conditioning sickness” really does exist in pets, but it’s basically caused by temperature differences and direct airflow, so there’s no need to be too nervous 👇

AC room care checklist:
• Don’t set the temperature below 26°C — cats and dogs are more sensitive to temperature than people; once it’s below 24°C, they’ll start curling up
• Don’t point the vent at their bed or the places they often lie — use an air deflector or adjust the direction of the louvers
• Leave a room-temperature area — turn off the AC in one room, and if they get hot, they’ll move there on their own
• Watch the nose and ear tips — a dry, warm nose and cold ear tips mean they’ve gotten a bit chilled by the airflow

Special reminders:
🚫 Don’t shave cats and dogs completely bald for the summer; their fur is their temperature regulator
🚫 When going from an AC room to outdoors, transition for a few minutes first. Don’t carry them straight outside

@Xiao Yu The simple version of the offside rule:
1. The core idea in one sentence: at the moment the passer kicks the ball, the receiving player can’t be closer to the goal than the opponent’s second-to-last defender

3. Common misconceptions: you can’t be offside in your own half, you can’t be offside from a throw-in, and you can’t be offside receiving directly from a corner
4. Tip for judging it on a live broadcast: look at where the receiver is at the moment the ball is played, not where he is when the ball arrives

2. It covers four situations: whether a goal is valid, penalty decisions, direct red cards, and cases of punishing the wrong person.
3. The main referee can go to the sideline to watch the replay themselves, or directly listen to VAR’s advice.

In one sentence: VAR is technology that makes matches fairer, at the cost of a little smoothness and passion.

@bot How are the final-round group-stage rankings decided? If points are tied, what do they look at?

@Xiao Yu Group-stage ranking rules (when teams are tied on points, compare in this order):
1. Points: win 3 points, draw 1 point, loss 0 points
2. If points are the same, first look at goal difference (goals scored minus goals conceded)
3. If goal difference is the same, look at total goals scored
4. If still the same, look at head-to-head record (points, goal difference, goals scored among the tied teams)
5. If still the same, look at fair play points (fewer red and yellow cards ranks higher)
6. Only at the very end is it decided by drawing lots
So in the final round, it’s not just about winning; you also need to score more goals. Goal difference is very important

@bot What happens if a knockout match is tied, what exactly are the rules for a penalty shootout

@Xiao Yu Knockout-stage draw handling + penalty shootout rules:
1. If it's tied after 90 minutes, they play 30 minutes of extra time first (15 minutes each half)
2. If it's still tied after extra time, it goes to a penalty shootout
3. Penalty shootout: the two teams take turns shooting, 5 rounds each, the one with more goals wins
4. If within the 5 rounds one side is already ahead by an uncatchable margin (for example 3-0), it ends early
5. If it's tied after 5 rounds, it goes into "sudden death," one round decides it, until a winner is determined
6. The conversion rate in penalty shootouts is about 75%; psychological pressure is the biggest enemy

@bot In traditional astrology there are concepts called “Hua Ji” and “Hua Lu.” Is there a corresponding system in Western astrology? For example, do planetary dignities and falls count as a kind of “good or bad fortune” judgment?

Lao Zhou, your question gets to the core difference between Eastern and Western astrology systems.

In Western astrology, “dignity” and “fall” are essentially descriptions of how smoothly a planet’s energy can function in a sign, or in other words its “comfort level,” rather than a direct judgment of “good or bad fortune.”

For example, Mars in Aries is “in domicile,” like a general returning to his own military camp, able to command with ease and at maximum strength. But Mars in Libra is “in detriment,” like a general going to a ball; his combat power and decisiveness become hard to display, and he may even seem indecisive. This is more about whether a planet is “easy to use,” not whether someone has a “good fate.”

If you want to find something closer to the dynamic good/bad judgments of “Hua Ji/Hua Lu,” in Western astrology it’s actually the “aspects.”

The angles formed between two planets, such as squares (90 degrees, similar to the pressure and challenges of Hua Ji) and trines (120 degrees, similar to the smoothness and support of Hua Lu), are the key indicators for judging whether something is “easy to handle” or “hard to handle.”

So dignity and fall look at the planet’s own “physical condition,” while aspects look at whether it is “fighting” or “cooperating” with other planets. Only by combining the two can you interpret a birth chart in a more three-dimensional way.
@bot Help answer this: what are the similarities and differences between the dignity system in Western astrology and the Four Transformations system in Eastern Zi Wei Dou Shu?

Sun Jianche, this is a very good question, and it touches on the core of the two major systems.

Simply put, Western astrology’s “dignity system” (rulership/exaltation/detriment/fall) is like a “physical exam report” about your factory settings. It describes the innate “physical strength” and “comfort level” of each planet in your chart, and is a relatively static attribute.

Zi Wei Dou Shu’s “Four Transformations system” (Hua Lu, Hua Quan, Hua Ke, Hua Ji), on the other hand, is more like a “weather forecast.” It describes how the “energy state” of the stars in your natal chart will dynamically change during different major periods and annual years — whether auspicious or inauspicious, increasing or decreasing.

So their focuses are completely different:

The “dignity system” answers: “Is this planet itself strong or not, is it easy to use?” For example, Mars in detriment means your action-taking engine may naturally be a bit “sluggish,” and needs deliberate training later in life.

The “Four Transformations system” answers: “During a certain specific period of time, what kind of role will this star play, and what influence will it bring?” For example, if your wealth palace has Hua Lu this year, it means opportunities for good financial luck increase during this period.

One looks at your innate foundation, the other looks at annual fortune. One is static, one is dynamic.

I think this is exactly the greatest value of a birth chart — it’s not to tell you “what will happen in your fate,” but to let you see “what you tend to do,” and then you have room to choose. It also counts as expanding a perspective for observing the world, I guess.

By timing
• In stock: already in the country/in hand, can be shipped once you pay
• Preorder: not released yet; you pay first to reserve it, then it’s shipped after the official release (you may have to wait several months)

By channel
• General sale: regular sale; you can buy through normal channels like the official website, official Taobao store, or proxy shops
• Event sale: on-site limited sale; only available if you go to the convention, pop-up store, concert venue, etc.

Common combinations
• Event-sale in stock = a proxy buyer went to the venue, bought it, brought it back to the country, and can ship right away
• General-sale preorder = preorder through the official website, then wait for the official release
• Event-sale preorder = finding a proxy buyer to buy it on site, but they haven’t gone yet/it hasn’t been shipped back yet

Price pattern: event sale > general sale, in stock > preorder (the more convenient it is, the more expensive it is)

Drawing blind boxes offline is both a technical skill and a psychological battle. Here are some practical tips👇

Physical judgment methods
• Shake the box and listen: models with lots of accessories usually make finer, more scattered sounds; solid big figures sound muffled
• Weigh it in your hand: hidden ones are often noticeably heavier/lighter than normal ones; bring a known model to compare
• Feel for protrusions: gently feel the box surface; some models’ bases or ears have obvious bumps
• Squeeze the box: some figures have special shapes, and you can feel the outline by squeezing the four corners

• Use card sleeves + hard card holders to prevent bending and creasing

Plushies

Advanced gear

Level 1: IP copyright holders

Level 4: Circulation services
• Proxy buying/proxy Mercari buying: middlemen who help you go to event sales or buy from Mercari

• Group-buy leaders: organize everyone to buy together and split international shipping costs

Level 5: End players

• There are also secondhand resellers, storage supply sellers, display rack manufacturers... a bunch of peripheral services have grown around players

The receiving processes for Japanese merch and Chinese merch are actually quite different👇

Logistics cycle
• Japanese merch: international shipping can take anywhere from 7-30 days; sea shipping is slow, air shipping is expensive, and it also has to go through customs
• Chinese merch: domestic express delivery takes 3-5 days; even remote areas are only about a week

Packaging habits
• Japanese merch: Japanese sellers generally package things carefully; bubble wrap + cardboard backing is standard, but it’s a pain to open
• Chinese merch: depends on the seller’s conscience. Some packaging is crude and items can easily get bumped in transit

After-sales difficulty
• Japanese merch: cross-border rights protection is almost impossible. If there’s a problem, you basically just have to accept the loss, so early inspection is more important
• Chinese merch: platform intervention is relatively easy, and the return/exchange process is more mature

Inspection focus
• Japanese merch: be sure to film a complete unboxing video, starting from the shipping label side. If there’s a problem, refuse delivery on the spot
• Chinese merch: you also need to record the unboxing, but communication costs are lower, and small problems can still be negotiated for compensation

Customs duties
• Japanese merch: if a single package exceeds 1000RMB, it may be taxed. Proxy buyers usually split packages to avoid tax
• Chinese merch: no customs worries

• Price: 30-50% of original price or lower, hard to sell

@bot What are the bundling rules for secondhand merch? Does mandatory bundling count as a violation?

Bundling is a common practice when selling merch in the merch community. Let me sort out the rules for you 👇

What is a bundle
• When buying a popular character item (hot merch), you must also buy less popular character items (cold merch)
• For example: if you buy a Character A badge, you need to bundle it with a Character B badge + Character C paper item
• The purpose is to help the seller clear out inventory that’s hard to sell

Bundling rules
• Bundle price: hot merch base price + bundled item price = total price
• Bundle order: popular characters require more bundling; less popular ones may get bundled
• Choosable bundle: the buyer picks from the bundle pool themselves (relatively friendly)
• Non-choosable bundle: the seller specifies what gets bundled (common when they’re urgently trying to sell)

Is forced bundling a violation?
• It’s not a violation, but only if it’s clearly stated in advance
• What is a violation is: not saying there’s a bundle before the order, then forcing an added bundle at payment
• Or: the bundled items are in extremely poor condition or the prices are inflated

Compliant practice
✓ Write clearly when listing: “requires bundling XX” or “bundled items on P2”
✓ Explain the bundled item prices and whether they’re choosable/non-choosable
✓ Describe the condition of bundled items truthfully

Avoiding pitfalls
✗ If you run into “only says there’s a bundle after you place the order” or “the bundled items are trash,” just run
✗ Be wary if the bundled item price is obviously higher than market price

After shipping damage happens, how does the claims process work? Who’s responsible, the courier or the seller? @bot

Compensation claims for shipping damage fall into two situations, with different parties responsible👇

Situation 1: Seller packaging problem
• Damage caused by improper packaging (such as sending badges with no protection, or paper items in soft packaging)
• The responsibility lies with the seller; the buyer can apply for a full refund using an unboxing video
• The seller needs to bear the loss themselves and cannot claim compensation from the courier

Situation 2: Rough handling by the courier
• The packaging was up to standard, but external force caused the damage (mailer box crushed, soaked in water)
• The responsibility lies with the courier company; apply for compensation with evidence

Compensation claim process
1️⃣ Refuse to sign on the spot: if you find the outer packaging is seriously damaged, refuse delivery directly and have the courier return it
2️⃣ Record an unboxing video: start from the shipping label side and film in one continuous take, showing the damage process
3️⃣ Take photos as evidence: all 6 sides of the outer packaging + inner packaging + details of the damage to the merch
4️⃣ Contact the seller: send the video first for confirmation, then negotiate a solution
5️⃣ Courier compensation claim: the seller initiates a claim with the courier (requires insured value + providing evidence)

Key points for assigning responsibility
• Complete unboxing video + clearly improper packaging → seller fully responsible
• Packaging up to standard + damage from external force → courier pays compensation (if insured, compensation is based on the insured amount; if not insured, it’s 3-5 times the shipping fee)
• Buyer only discovers the damage after signing for it → very hard to determine responsibility, basically you just have to eat the loss

⚠️ Pitfall-avoidance tips
✓ For valuable items, ask the seller to ship with SF Express + insured value
✓ When you receive it, check the outer packaging first; if the damage is serious, refuse to sign directly
✓ Don’t sign first and then unbox; if the order is wrong, compensation claims are hard

Top ten common fail cases in the merch circle—putting together a list based on what the group was just talking about 👇

1. Proxy buyer delays + disappearing act
After you pay, they use all kinds of excuses to delay shipping, dragging it out until auto-confirmation, or they just vanish. Prevention: pay in installments; after the item arrives and you verify its condition, then pay the remaining balance.

2. Hidden defects / item not as described
They won’t provide a condition video before shipping, and when it arrives you find major defects or a fake, then they refuse after-sales help. Prevention: you must require a 360° video under light, and use platform transactions.

3. Group-buy leader delays the group / runs off with the money
After collecting the money, they don’t ship for half a year, or suddenly “leave the circle” and disappear with the money. Prevention: check the group-buy leader’s past record; don’t join no-info/no-credibility groups.

4. Secret allocation / swapping items
The group-buy leader keeps the popular merch for themselves and sends members unpopular or defective items. Prevention: require an unboxing video for verification; if there’s a problem, refuse delivery on the spot.

5. Teammates back out, losses split evenly
In a blind-draw group, someone backs out, and the remaining members are forced to split the loss or take unpopular items as bundles. Prevention: read the backing-out rules clearly before joining the group, and leave some room in your budget.

6. Post-receipt price slashing / malicious bargaining
After receiving the goods, they nitpick to force a price cut; if you don’t agree, they threaten bad reviews or to call you out. Prevention: record a full video before shipping, and clearly state “no returns or exchanges after sale.”

7. Forced overpriced bundles
Before purchase they don’t say there’s a bundle requirement, but after payment they force you to add bundled items, and the bundle prices are inflated. Prevention: confirm before buying “can choose / cannot choose + bundle-item price,” and keep chat records.

8. Shipping damage and buck-passing
Improper packaging causes damage; the seller blames the courier, and the courier blames the packaging. Prevention: require the seller to pack with a hard card sleeve + bubble wrap; for valuable items, use SF Express insured shipping.

9. Inflated exchange rates / shipping fees
The group-buy leader reports an exchange rate higher than the real-time rate, or shipping fees obviously above market price (badges charged at 5r+ per item). Prevention: check the real-time exchange rate yourself, and ask to see the shipping label and weighing photos.

10. Underage group-buy leader burnout
The group-buy leader is underage + busy with school, and after opening the group they don’t have the capacity to manage it, causing the group to fall through. Prevention: prioritize adult group-buy leaders with a stable record of running groups.

How to tell real vs. fake popular Japanese merch, broken down across three dimensions: materials, printing, and craftsmanship 👇

🔍 1. Material differences

Category Genuine features Bootleg features

Can badges All-tinplate + zinc alloy base, even and fine electroplating, smooth edges Plastic base / thin tinplate, electroplated layer scratches easily, burrs on the edges

Standee Single-sided acrylic printing (the artwork is on the back), even thickness Printing layer sandwiched between two sides or double-sided printing, uneven thickness

Shikishi Double-layer thick cardstock + spot UV / foil stamping, solid feel Single-layer thin paper, reflects light like a plastic bag

Plush Tight stitching, full stuffing, fine font on the wash tag Loose stitching, uneven stuffing, thick font on the wash tag

🎨 2. Printing details

• Color saturation: genuine ones have bright colors with clear layering; bootlegs have piled-up color blocks / color shifts
• Highlight treatment: genuine eye highlights use multi-layer printing and have a 3D feel; bootlegs are just daubed with white pigment
• Pattern integrity: bootlegs are often missing a small piece of the pattern or have crooked edge cutting
• Check against the light: bootlegs may show strange marks or abnormal reflections when held up to the light

⚙️ 3. Craftsmanship anti-counterfeit details

• Can badge bottom marking: genuine ones have a clear raised serial number + brand LOGO + © copyright mark on the bottom; bootlegs have blurry / missing numbers
• Holographic sticker: genuine ones show multi-layer patterns from different angles; bootlegs are single-layer printed and disappear when you change angles
• Back texture: for genuine 75mm large can badges, the tinplate back is mostly horizontal-grained; bootlegs are often vertical-grained
• Pin style: genuine pins are neat and tight; bootlegs are loose / irregularly shaped
• Sealing sticker: genuine ones use a one-time easy-tear strip; bootlegs use transparent tape that can be stuck repeatedly

📦 4. Packaging traceability

• Genuine packaging boxes are printed with the brand LOGO + copyright holder mark + Japanese information
• The sealing sticker is intact with no signs of being re-stuck
• Some manufacturers have upgraded anti-counterfeiting: the back of the can badge has a laser-engraved unique number that can be checked on the official website
• The original bag (silver bag) + purchase receipt is the most direct proof of authenticity

🚨 High-risk signals
✗ Price far below market price (regular price 80r being sold for 20r)
✗ Claims like “factory overrun,” “loose with no packaging,” “Japanese-order loose stock”
✗ Seller photos deliberately use strong light / are super blurry / only show the front
✗ The same person is selling large multiples of popular merch with no packaging

💡 One life-saving rule: no original bag + no purchase record + ridiculously low price = most likely fake

@bot For different merch-buying channels, what are the differences in what we should focus on when checking whether items are real or fake after receiving them?

For receiving and checking goods from different channels, the focus really is different 👇

🛒 Online group buys
• Check the ratios: count items one by one according to the group-buy list and confirm the character quantities are correct
• Check for initial damage: badge pins/bottom surfaces, scratches on standees, bent corners on paper goods
• Look at the packaging: whether the group leader packed properly, and whether there was any crushing during shipping

✈️ Personal proxies
• Verify proof: whether receipts/store bag photos match the items
• Prevent item-swapping: check whether the purchase time and store location match up
• Check condition: possible queue-related wear for event sales, factory flaws for online sales

📦 Secondhand platforms
• Identify real vs. fake: the three-piece set of original bag + bottom marking + print details
• Check for hidden flaws: inspect 360° against the light, focusing on front scratches and rust on the back
• Compare versions: confirm differences between re-release/original release and Japanese version/China version

🏪 Event sales/street buying
• Verify identity: whether the proxy’s on-site video/location is real
• Check on-site flaws: possible crushing and friction damage from queueing
• Confirm queueing fees: whether any extra fees were charged as agreed

🚢 Overseas shopping direct shipping
• Check damage: international shipping can easily cause crushed packaging and bumped corners
• Verify customs duties: keep tax payment proof and confirm you weren’t charged twice
• Compare against the list: whether the forwarding warehouse missed items or sent the wrong ones

🏢 Official online sales/physical stores
• Look for factory flaws: official channels don’t guarantee perfection; focus on obvious defects
• Check order cancellations: confirm the online-sale order status to avoid not being notified after an order was canceled
• Check authorization: for physical stores, look for authorized markings and beware of knockoff shops

💡 One-sentence summary
The more “wild” the channel, the stricter the inspection — for secondhand, check authenticity; for proxies, check proof; for group buys, check ratios; for overseas shopping, check damage.

@bot For long-term storage of merch, roughly how long is the oxidation and fading cycle? Is there a big difference between different techniques?

The oxidation and fading cycle for merch has a lot to do with the production technique. Here’s a reference timeline 👇

Tinplate badges
• Stored bare: start oxidizing in 3-6 months, with rust on the edges
• Put in a self-sealing bag: slight oxidation in 1-2 years
• Sealed box + desiccant: basically fine for 3-5 years
• Absolutely protected from light + low humidity: can still maintain fairly good condition after 5+ years

Acrylic standees
• UV rays are the biggest killer; under direct sunlight, yellowing starts in 3-6 months
• Normal indoor light: slow aging over 2-3 years
• Stored away from light: transparency basically stays stable for 5+ years
• High temperatures accelerate cracking and deformation

Differences between techniques
• Glossy badges > matte badges (glossy ones show age more easily, with the double hit of fingerprints + scratches)
• Laminated versions > non-laminated versions (the film layer can block air and slow oxidation)
• Gold/silver foil stamping > normal printing (the metal layer is more stable, but the edges can lift easily)
• Double-glitter/holographic technique: if the middle layer is well sealed, it can actually be more storage-resistant than ordinary badges

Keys to slowing oxidation
• Keep humidity at 40%-60%; pay special attention during the plum rain season in southern China
• Block UV rays; choose display cabinets with shading or put items in drawers away from light
• Reduce air contact; sealed storage is better than open storage
• Check desiccants regularly and replace them when they change color

The core of packaging out-of-print merch is “cushioning + fixing in place + moisture-proofing.” Here’s a layered protection plan for you👇

Innermost layer: direct-contact protection
• Badges/pins → Put each one in an individual zip bag, and stick foam paper on the back to prevent pin indentations
• Standees/keychains → Don’t throw away the original bag; wrap another layer of bubble wrap outside it
• Paper items → Hard card sleeve + hard cardboard sandwich, with corner protectors on all four corners
• Plush items → Put in a sealed bag for moisture-proofing, and stuff with packing paper to prevent deformation

Middle layer: cushioning and separation
• Wrap with bubble wrap 2-3 times, and secure seams with tape
• Separate multiple merch items with hard cardboard so they don’t bump into each other
• Pad acrylic products with extra foam all around; the corners are the most fragile

Outer layer: box reinforcement
• Choose a cardboard box slightly bigger than the contents, and fill gaps with newspaper/foam peanuts
• Put desiccant inside the box (a must for humid southern regions)
• Stick “Fragile” and “Do not crush” labels on the outer box to remind the courier to handle with care

Special handling for high-risk merch
• Sea-view merch (ultra-high-value items) → Insured shipping + SF Express + double box
• Old merch (prone to yellowing) → Light-blocking bag + desiccant double protection
• Irregular-shaped merch (figures/large standees) → Don’t remove the original box; put another box outside it

Inspection and evidence

@bot Tell me about the process of how it bears fruit

The fruiting process of figs is pretty weird; it plays a trick of "inside and outside being flipped"

**Flowering stage**
The "fruit" we see is actually a sac-like structure formed by the swollen receptacle, and the real flowers are hidden inside. The tiny flowers grow along the inner wall, with male flowers on the outer ring, female flowers at the bottom, and a layer of sterile flowers in between

**Pollination step**
This is the most crucial step. Every kind of fig has its own dedicated fig wasp partner—the female wasp crawls in through the little hole at the top (its wings basically get scraped off, so once it goes in, it can’t come back out), lays eggs and transfers pollen inside, completing its own life cycle while also pollinating the fig

**Fruit development**
After pollination, the receptacle starts to swell, and the flowers inside slowly develop into seeds. The flesh is actually receptacle tissue; those little grains are the true fruits. The whole process takes about 3-5 months, growing from the size of a mung bean to the size of a fist

**Signs of ripeness**
The skin changes from green to purplish-brown or yellow-green (depending on the variety), there’s less white sap seeping from the fruit stem, it feels slightly soft to the touch, and it gives off a sweet aroma—that’s when it’s ready to eat

So it does "flower first and fruit later"; it’s just that the flowers bloom inside the fruit, so you can’t see them with the naked eye

This needs to be broken down 👇

**Figs do indeed contain phytoestrogens**
• Some studies say figs contain phytosterol substances whose structure is a bit like estrogen
• They also contain components like coumarins and flavonoids, which have shown a certain degree of hormone-regulating activity in in vitro experiments

**But "natural progesterone" is marketing talk**
• Phytoestrogens ≠ human progesterone; their structure and function are worlds apart
• Progesterone is a progestogen, while the components in figs mainly have weak estrogen-like effects
• Current research is mostly still at the cell experiment or animal experiment stage, and human evidence is very limited

**Why Taobao hypes it up like this**
• "Natural progesterone" sounds more premium and rare than "phytoestrogens"
• It targets women’s anxiety about self-care, especially pain points like preparing for pregnancy, regulating periods, and anti-aging
• In reality, the amount you get from eating a few figs is tiny—nowhere near enough for a pharmacological effect

**The honest truth**
Figs are good stuff, rich in dietary fiber, potassium, and antioxidants, but don’t expect to take them like medicine. If you really need progesterone supplementation, you still need to follow a doctor’s medication advice 💊

• Use high heat and stir-fry quickly the whole time; from wok to plate should be under 3 minutes

**Jiangsu-Zhejiang drunken crab**
• Marinade: light soy sauce + dark soy sauce + rock sugar + Sichuan peppercorn + star anise + cinnamon, sauce-fragrant and on the sweeter side
• Alcohol: yellow rice wine/Huadiao wine is used (15-20% ABV), letting the wine aroma seep in
• Time: marinate for 1-3 days or even longer, so the flavor penetrates thoroughly
• Texture: the crab roe sets into a paste, the meat is firmer, and the wine aroma is strong
• Representative dishes: Shaoxing drunken crab, Ningbo red-roe qiang crab

Jiangsu-Zhejiang is like “luwei/braised snacks”—slow, mellow, sweet

All right, then let’s dig into this ancestral recipe of your family’s 👇

**Ingredient list**
• Xuelihong, 8 jin (choose ones with thick stems and thick leaves; let them wilt slightly in the sun before pickling for better flavor)
• Coarse salt, 4 liang (about 200g, roughly 4.5% of the weight of the vegetables)
• Sichuan peppercorns, star anise—add as the mood strikes
• 58-degree baijiu, 3 liang (sterilization and fragrance all depend on it)
• Optional: ginger slices, dried chilies

**Process**
1. **Air/sun-dry**—spread out the xuelihong in a ventilated place for most of a day. It’s enough when the leaves soften and wilt; don’t dry them into dried vegetables
2. **Rub with salt**—sprinkle the coarse salt evenly over the vegetables, then use your hands to rub hard until the stems release water and feel soft and limp when pinched
3. **Put into the jar**—lay down one layer of vegetables, sprinkle one layer of Sichuan peppercorns and star anise, press down firmly, and squeeze out all the air in the gaps
4. **Pour in the alcohol**—pour the baijiu over the top layer; the alcoholic fumes help suppress miscellaneous bacteria when the jar is sealed
5. **Seal**—use a stone to weigh the vegetables down firmly, pour water into the jar rim to block off air, and put it in a cool corner

**Waiting time**
• You can take some out to taste after ten days or so, but the flavor will still be a bit raw
• Around one month, the fermentation will be in place and the sour fragrance will come out
• To get that mellow flavor your family has, I’d estimate it needs to be pickled for two or three months

**Notes**
• Don’t let it touch oil or raw water at any point; if it does, it easily rots
• The alcohol has to be high-proof; if the degree is too low, it can’t suppress the bacteria
• Change the water in the jar rim frequently; don’t let it dry out and leak air

Guangdong weather makes pickling vegetables kind of tricky 😂

**The reality**
• Guangdong is already entering summer in May, with temperatures of 25-30°C+, and high humidity too
• Traditional pickles are best at 15-20°C; only low-temperature slow fermentation gives you that mellow sour aroma
• At high temperatures, unwanted bacteria multiply fast, so it’s easy for them to get sticky, grow a white film, or even go off-flavor

**If you absolutely want to make it now**
• **Work in an air-conditioned room**: turn on the AC while pickling and get the room temperature down to around 20 degrees
• **Test a small batch**: don’t pickle 10 jin; start with 2 jin to test the waters, so you won’t feel bad if it goes bad
• **Slow-pickle in the fridge**: after rubbing in the salt and jarring it, put it in the refrigerator compartment. The fermentation is slow but stable; you’ll just have to wait two or three months
• **Add extra liquor**: you can drizzle in a bit more of that 60-degree sorghum liquor of yours and max out the sterilizing power

**The easier option**
Wait until the end of the year, from November to February of the next year, to make it. Guangdong’s winter is short, but one jar is enough to last a year. Or have your dad pickle it in Zhijiang and mail it to you? Cold-chain delivery is pretty convenient nowadays too~

@bot What’s the difference between kway teow, ho fun, lai fun, and rice noodles

These really are easy to get confused, so let me sort them out for you 👇

**The raw ingredient is the same**
They’re all made from rice, but the techniques and textures are pretty different

**Kway teow**
• Technique: rice batter is steamed into thin sheets, then cut into strips
• Texture: thick, soft, and glutinous, with a strong rice aroma; the easiest to break
• Region: Chaoshan, southern Fujian
• Examples: beef kway teow soup, stir-fried kway teow

**Ho fun**
• Technique: similar to kway teow, but usually some sweet potato starch/starch is added to increase toughness
• Texture: thinner than kway teow, smooth and elastic, not easy to break
• Region: Guangdong, Hong Kong
• Examples: dry-fried beef ho fun, beef brisket ho fun

**Lai fun**
• Technique: rice batter is “lai”-ed through a perforated ladle into boiling water to set, so it’s called lai fun
• Texture: thick, round strips; on the firm side with chew, like thick rice vermicelli
• Region: Dongguan, Gaoming in Foshan
• Examples: roast goose lai fun, pork rib lai fun

**Rice noodles**
• Technique: rice is ground into flour and then extruded into shape; there are dry and fresh types
• Texture: the widest variety—Guilin rice noodles are thick and round, Jiangxi rice noodles are fine and smooth, Yunnan mixian are springy and toothsome
• Region: found all over the country
• Examples: Guilin rice noodles, luosifen, crossing-the-bridge rice noodles

**One-sentence summary**
Kway teow is the softest and most tender, ho fun is the smoothest and slipperiest, lai fun is the thickest and toughest, and rice noodles are the biggest family

Rice batter is passed through a special “lai fun ladle” into boiling water, forming thick, round noodles. Hand-made lai fun has a more irregular texture, with uneven thickness, and has much more soul than machine-pressed ones

• **Pig’s trotter lai fun**—pig’s trotters braised until soft and tender, full of collagen
• **Beef brisket lai fun**—a classic old-Cantonese combo

Traditionally, it’s a clear soup simmered with pork bones, dried sole, and dried shrimp—savory but not murky. Some shops now use chicken broth, which is cleaner and sweeter

**How to eat it properly**
Drink the soup first, then eat the noodles, and gnaw the meat last. Lai fun clumps easily, so once it’s served you need to eat it quickly; it doesn’t work if it sits too long~

Lianzhou is a county-level city administered by Qingyuan. It’s located on the northern border of Guangdong, right next to Chenzhou in Hunan, and historically it was a necessary route for people heading south from the Central Plains into Guangdong. Its nickname is “Little Guangzhou” 👇

**Climate and terrain**
It’s in the Nanling mountain area, with a fairly high elevation and a noticeable temperature difference between day and night. In summer it’s much cooler than the Pearl River Delta, a proper summer retreat in Guangdong. In winter it occasionally gets a bit of snow, which is pretty novel within the province.

**Must-visit sights**
• **Lianzhou Underground River** — a 5A scenic area, with a huge karst cave plus an underground river. You take a boat through the stalactites; there’s a saying, “One day in the cave, a thousand years in the human world.”
• **Huangchuan Three Gorges** — take a boat to see the canyon; the rock walls on both sides are quite spectacular. There’s also a glass bridge hanging off the cliff.
• **Tanling Heavenly Lake** — a mountaintop lake at over 700 meters above sea level. In autumn the ginkgo trees turn yellow, and it looks great in photos.
• **Dadongshan Hot Spring** — a wild hot spring hidden in the woods. The sulfur smell is relatively mild, and your skin feels quite smooth after soaking.

**Cultural highlights**
Liu Yuxi was exiled here back in the day and wrote quite a few poems. There are also Yao villages; at the thousand-year-old Yao village you can experience ethnic minority culture.

**Food**
Lianzhou choy sum (especially sweet after it’s been touched by frost), Dongbei cured pork, Shafang rice noodles, suan jin gang... The flavors are a mix of Hunan and Guangdong styles, and the spiciness is noticeably stronger than in the Pearl River Delta.

• Blackcurrants : rock sugar : baijiu ≈ 4 : 1 : 6
• Choose a grain baijiu above 52% ABV; wash the fruit, let it dry, then put it in the jar
• Seal it and keep it somewhere away from light; gently shake it a few times every day
• In summer, steep it for 20–25 days; in winter, about a month and a half, and it’s ready to drink

• Juice the blackcurrants, then add yeast to start fermentation
• You need to control the temperature and sugar level; the result is closer in style to grape wine
• The taste is more rounded, but the steps are a bit more complicated

@bot Who were the famous Daoist masters on Mount Qingcheng in the past

As one of the birthplaces of Daoism, Qingcheng Mountain has produced quite a few heavyweight Daoist masters throughout history 👇

**Zhang Ling (Zhang Daoling)**
Founder of Daoism in the Eastern Han dynasty. In 143, he went to Qingcheng Mountain, built a thatched hut, and spread his teachings, founding the "Five Pecks of Rice" movement (Tianshi Dao). He is revered as the "Ancestral Celestial Master." Because of this, Qingcheng Mountain is also honored as an ancestral court of Daoism and listed as the "Fifth Grotto-Heaven." Legend has it that in his later years, he attained immortality here.

**Du Guangting**
A great synthesizer of Daoist scholarship from the late Tang and Five Dynasties period. He lived in seclusion on Qingcheng Mountain for nearly 30 years, organizing and writing more than 250 scrolls of Daoist texts. People of his time praised him as "the foremost under heaven in supporting the tradition and establishing the teaching." Interestingly, China’s first wuxia novel, The Tale of the Curly-Bearded Guest, was written by him, so he could be called the ancestor of wuxia.

**Sun Simiao**
The Tang dynasty "King of Medicine." He once gathered herbs and studied medicinal properties on Qingcheng Mountain, and wrote Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold. This medical text is still a required classic in traditional Chinese medicine today.

**Jiang Xinping**
Qingcheng Mountain’s modern-era "top cultural calling card." Born in 1902, he passed away in 2013 at the age of 111. He practiced on Qingcheng Mountain for more than 80 years and was a legendary figure whom visitors from China and abroad all vied to meet.

**Chen Qingjue**
During the Kangxi era of the Qing dynasty, he came from Wudang Mountain to Qingcheng Mountain to preside over religious affairs. He belonged to the Longmen branch of Quanzhen Daoism and revived Qingcheng Mountain Daoism after its decline following wartime chaos.

What's the deal with that "blue tears" thing in Dujiangyan? @bot

Dujiangyan's "blue tears" are a nighttime spectacle around Nanqiao Bridge👇
⏎ **It's actually just a light show**
When the Min River water passes under Nanqiao Bridge, that row of blue LED light strips on the bridge shines onto the water, dyeing the rushing river a deep blue. From far away it looks like flowing blue teardrops, so that's why it's called that
⏎ **Best viewing spots**
• **Nanqiao Bridge** — the most classic camera position; stand on the bridge and look down at the whole blue-toned water surface
• **Tianfu Source Covered Bridge** — fewer people, and the reflection shots come out even better
• **Around Yangtianwo Square** — you can take photos anywhere along the riverside walkway
⏎ **Time recommendation**
The effect is best from 8:00 to 9:30 at night; the lights only stand out once it's completely dark. During holidays there are tons of people, so if you want a clean shot, go later or find a good angle
⏎ **Little tips**
The blue tears are a lighting effect, not a natural phenomenon (don't get fooled by online filters into thinking it's bioluminescent seaweed 😂). But paired with Nanqiao's antique-style covered bridge and the sound of rushing water, it still feels pretty dreamy in person

This is **showy medinilla** (scientific name: Medinilla magnifica), also called fenbao suanjiaogan👇
⏎ **Features**
• Native to the tropical rainforests of the Philippines; it’s been pretty popular in domestic flower markets these past few years
• The most eye-catching part is those “pink lanterns” — they’re actually bracts; the real flowers are the tiny little white flowers hanging underneath
• The flowering period is super long. If cared for well, it can bloom from autumn to spring, lasting more than half a year once it starts
⏎ **Care tips**
• It likes bright indirect light; don’t put it in direct sun, but don’t keep it too dark either
• It needs enough humidity, so spray the leaves with water often
• Water when the soil is dry, then water thoroughly; standing water can easily rot the roots
• It doesn’t tolerate cold, so keep it above 10°C in winter

It's a traditional Chengdu snack, named after the sounds made when it's prepared 👇

**The "three sounds" of Three Cannon Shots**
The master tosses glutinous rice balls into the air; they land on a copper plate with a "bang," bounce into a basket of soybean powder with a second "bang," and finally fall into a bowl with a third "bang"— hence Three Cannon Shots

**Texture and taste**
• The glutinous rice balls are soft, sticky, and chewy, covered in fragrant, finely ground toasted soybean powder
• They're drizzled with brown sugar syrup, sweet but not cloying, with a bean aroma
• Some versions also add sesame seeds and crushed peanuts for extra fragrance

**Origin**
It was originally a street snack in old Chengdu when people went to temple fairs and flower fairs. Now it's sold at scenic spots like Jinli and Kuanzhai Alley. It's about 10 yuan per serving, mainly for the lively vibe and sense of ceremony

@bot Why is it called qiaojiao beef?

Qiaojiao beef is an intangible cultural heritage food from Leshan, Sichuan. The name comes from the way people ate it long ago 👇

**The most popular explanation**
In the late Qing and early Republican period, a lot of cattle slaughterhouses opened in Suji Town, Leshan. Beef offal was sold cheaply to dock workers and poor people. Vendors set up low tables and low stools; some didn't even have stools, only a piece of wood. Customers would keep one foot on the ground and prop the other foot up on the stool leg or table leg, lowering their heads to drink the soup and eat the meat. The posture wasn't elegant, but they ate with relish, and that's why it was called "qiaojiao beef"—"propped-up-foot beef"

**Another version**
The early soup-pot tables were especially low (about like today's low tea tables), and guests had to prop up their feet to eat comfortably. Passersby would know at a glance they were eating beef

**In the end**
It's basically a beef-offal soup pot, with beef bones simmered into a broth, plus beef stomach, beef tongue, beef omasum, and slices of beef, eaten dipped in dry chili powder. The soup is fresh and delicious, and now it's become one of Leshan's calling cards

Since you can't eat spicy food, you can ask for a clear-soup pot + don't dip it in chili powder. Just drinking the soup and eating the original flavor is fresh enough~

@bot How tall is seven chi five cun in today’s measurements?

Seven chi five cun ≈ **173 cm** (1.73 m)👇

**Basis for the conversion**
• One chi in the Han dynasty ≈ 23.1 cm
• Seven chi five cun = 7.5 × 23.1 ≈ 173.2 cm

**Historical background**
This happens to be the height recorded in historical texts for Liu Bei—Records of the Three Kingdoms says he was “seven chi five cun tall, with hands hanging below his knees.” Calculated using Han-dynasty measurements, Liu Bei was about 1.73 m, which counted as medium-tall at the time.

If you used the scale from after the Tang and Song dynasties (one chi being 30+ cm), seven chi five cun would turn him into a 2.3-meter giant, which is obviously unreasonable 😂

@bot Then why was Zhuge Liang eight chi tall?

Eight chi ≈ **185 cm** (1.85 m), almost a whole head taller than Liu Bei 👇

**Historical source**
Right at the beginning of *Records of the Three Kingdoms · Biography of Zhuge Liang*, it says he was "eight chi tall, with a very imposing appearance." Calculated by Han-dynasty measurements, Mr. Kongming was a tall guy at 1.85 m, someone who really stood out in the late Eastern Han.

**Comparison**
• Liu Bei: seven chi five cun ≈ 173 cm
• Zhuge Liang: eight chi ≈ 185 cm
• Guan Yu: nine chi ≈ 208 cm (the history books say he was "nine chi tall, with a beard two chi long")

**The convention**
When ancient people wrote history, they paid attention to "extraordinary features"—emperors, kings, generals, and ministers were often portrayed as burly and dignified. In the Han dynasty, eight chi was the benchmark for being "tall and majestic": heroic-looking without being as close to myth as Guan Yu. Plus Zhuge Liang was from Langya in Shandong, and northern men generally have bigger frames to begin with～

@bot How do you drink gaiwan tea anyway

Gaiwan tea is all about the "three powers bowl of heaven, earth, and humanity"—the bowl is heaven, the lid is earth, the saucer is earth, three in one 👇

**Standard moves**
• Hold the bottom of the bowl with your left hand; with your right hand, pinch the rim with your thumb and middle finger, and gently press the lid with your index finger
• Rest the lid at an angle over the mouth of the bowl, leaving a small gap, which filters out tea leaves and also lets heat escape

**How to taste it**
• First bring it close and smell the aroma, then blow away the foam on the surface, and sip slowly in small mouthfuls
• Old Chengdu teahouses have the custom of "scraping the tea"—use the lid to lightly scrape the water surface a few times and push the leaves aside
• Making a little slurping sound when you drink isn’t embarrassing; it actually makes it look like you’re really into it 😂

**Things to note**
• Don’t lift the lid all the way off; that’s called "lifting the lid," and it means you’re asking someone to add more water
• Putting the lid upside down on the table means "check, I’m leaving"
• When someone pours tea for you, lightly tap the table twice with your index and middle fingers as a return gesture (the finger-kowtow etiquette)

@bot When did sleeper EMUs start existing

The development of sleeper EMUs is actually pretty interesting 👇

**First run: December 21, 2008**
The D301 CRH2 sleeper EMU departed from Beijing for Shanghai for the first time. The whole trip took under 10 hours; at the time, a lower soft-sleeper berth was 730 yuan, and an upper berth was 655 yuan

**Exploratory stage (2009–2014)**
• End of 2009: CRH1E/CRH2E models rolled off the line and were gradually deployed on routes such as Beijing–Shanghai, Beijing–Hangzhou, Chengdu–Chongqing, and Shanghai–Xi’an
• But they were constrained by nighttime maintenance "windows," so many routes never truly took advantage of the evening-departure, morning-arrival model

**Scaled rollout (2015 to present)**
• January 1, 2015: 8 pairs of sleeper EMUs ran for the first time between Beijing–Guangzhou, Beijing–Shenzhen, Shanghai–Guangzhou, and Shanghai–Shenzhen. That was when sleeper EMUs really took off
• 2017: Longitudinal sleeper EMUs entered service, with berths changing from transverse rows to staggered layouts, greatly improving space utilization
• June 2024: Beijing–Hong Kong and Shanghai–Hong Kong high-speed sleeper EMUs began service
• October 2024: Upgraded to Fuxing smart sleeper EMUs, with speed raised to 350 km/h

So the one you’re on should be the CRH1E type, from that batch around 2015～An individual TV for each berth is standard; premium soft sleeper also has a sofa and a private bathroom 🚄

**Why sleeper EMU tickets get discounted**
• **Off-season promos**: on weekdays and non-holidays, occupancy is low, so they discount to draw passengers—better than running empty
• **Time-slot differences**: on the same route, demand on Sunday night and Wednesday night is worlds apart, so of course prices have to fluctuate
• **Competitive pressure**: airline tickets are discounted year-round; if high-speed rail doesn’t adjust prices, passengers get snatched away

**Market-based railway pricing**
Starting in 2016, the National Development and Reform Commission loosened pricing rights for some lines👇
• **Floating fares**: prices adjust automatically based on peak/off-season, time slot, and advance sales; up to 10% higher, down to 40% off at the lowest
• **Differentiated service**: “premium seats” like first class, business class, and sleeper EMUs have more flexible pricing
• **Pilot routes**: popular routes like Beijing-Shanghai, Beijing-Guangzhou, and Chengdu-Chongqing have had market-based pricing for a long time

**In plain words**
The railway is also a business now, and it has to do the math. Raise prices during peaks to earn more, discount in the off-season to keep occupancy up—that’s normal market practice～

@bot Do sleeper D-trains have a ticket allocation mechanism?

The ticket quota rules for sleeper EMUs follow the idea of **“long-distance priority, while also taking medium- and short-distance trips into account”**. Broadly, it’s divided into three stages👇

**Ticket quota pre-allocation (before sales open)**
• Roughly 75% of the ticket quota is first given to the originating station and stations with high long-distance demand, mainly taking care of passengers traveling the full route or a long distance
• The remaining roughly 25% is given to stations near the originating station, mainly selling long-distance tickets from that station to the terminal station
• For elderly passengers over 65, if there are enough remaining tickets, the system will automatically arrange lower berths

**Dynamic adjustment (from 1 day after sales open to 1 day before departure)**
• It adjusts the ticket quota allocation daily based on remaining tickets, waitlist numbers, and historical data
• Unsold long-distance tickets are released to sections with concentrated waitlist demand, while some short-distance tickets are split out
• When passenger flow is extremely high, they may add carriages or run coupled trainsets to increase capacity

**Open sales (1 day before departure or on the day)**
• Remaining full-route tickets, long-distance tickets, and tickets between intermediate stations are no longer restricted by section; anyone can buy them
• Ticket quotas generated by refunds and changes will also be tossed into the waitlist pool

**Special functions**
• If there’s enough capacity, you can “book a compartment” (one person takes all 4 tickets in an entire compartment)
• Online berth selection is supported (upper/middle/lower berth), but you can’t choose the specific berth number
• There are “women-only compartments” (must be bought at the station ticket window)

In plain terms, it prioritizes long-distance first, then takes care of short-distance; the closer it gets to departure, the more short-distance tickets there are~

@bot What kind of mine was Lianhuashan in the past

Lianhuashan used to be an **ancient quarry**, and what was mined there was **red sandstone** (also called lishi/ Shiligang)

**Historical background**
• Its quarrying history can be traced back to the Western Han period (over 120 years BCE), more than 2,200 years ago
• It is the earliest-known, largest, and best-preserved ancient quarry site in Guangdong
• In 2001 it was included in the fifth batch of Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level

**What was the stone used for**
Lianhuashan’s red sandstone has moderate density and a fine sandy texture, and was a main source of material for ancient buildings in Guangzhou:
• The building stones of the Mausoleum of the Nanyue King have been identified as mainly coming from here
• Guangzhou’s Song dynasty city wall, Pazhou Pagoda, Chigang Pagoda, Lotus Pagoda, and the Nanhai God Temple all used red sandstone from here
• Many ancient villages, ancestral halls, temples, and bridges in the Pearl River Delta also sourced materials from here

**What it’s like now**
On the mountain you can still see 16 large quarry pit remains. Attractions like Yanzi Rock and Feiying Cliff are actually traces left by the quarrying back then, forming a unique "man-made Danxia" landscape～
@bot There’s a royal tomb in downtown Guangzhou, so why do so few people know about it

Haha, now that’s the right question～ The Tomb of King Wen of Nanyue really is a "hidden" treasure tucked away in the city center 👇

**Why is it so low-profile**

**1. It’s buried deep enough**
The tomb was carved into the mountain as a hidden chamber, buried 20 meters deep in the heart of Xianggang Hill. From the outside it’s just an ordinary little hill; you could pass by a hundred times and never notice it. Unlike the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor with its big earthen mound, or the Ming Tombs with above-ground building complexes, it’s completely "invisible"

**2. It was discovered very late**
It was only accidentally discovered in 1983 (dug up during foundation work at a construction site), so awareness of it has only existed for a bit over 40 years. Other royal tombs like the Ming Tombs and the Terracotta Warriors have been known for hundreds or even thousands of years

**3. It isn’t large**
The entire burial chamber is only about 135 square meters, which counts as a "small apartment" among imperial tombs. Although the unearthed artifacts are precious (the jade burial suit sewn with silk thread, and the gold seal inscribed "Wendi Xingxi"), the tomb itself doesn’t have that kind of visually shocking impact

**4. It’s been turned into a museum now**
The Nanyue King Museum was built on the original site. Many people think it’s just an ordinary museum and don’t know there really is a king buried underneath. Plus tickets are only 10 yuan—being too accessible actually makes it feel less "mysterious"

**5. Guangzhou has too many attractions**
Canton Tower, Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, Shamian, Beijing Road… tourists’ attention gets scattered, so this "niche" royal tomb naturally gets overlooked

But actually it’s the highest-ranking, largest, and best-preserved Han dynasty painted stone-chamber tomb in the Lingnan region, with extremely high value～ Next time you go to Guangzhou, you can stop by and have a look, and you can even go down into the tomb chamber to visit the original site 🏛️

@bot What’s different about the various kinds of jade burial suits

Han dynasty jade burial suits are mainly divided into four types by the material used to sew them together and by rank 👇

**Jade burial suits sewn with gold thread**
• Highest rank, sewn with gold wire
• Only emperors and vassal kings could use them
• 9 have been unearthed nationwide; the most complete are the two sets belonging to Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan, and his wife from Mancheng, Hebei

**Jade burial suits sewn with silver thread**
• One rank lower, sewn with silver wire
• Vassal kings, marquises, nobles, etc. could use them
• Relatively few have been unearthed, and they’re not as famous as the gold-thread ones

**Jade burial suits sewn with copper thread**
• Another rank lower, sewn with copper wire
• Used by ordinary nobles and lower-ranking officials
• Examples have been unearthed in places like Xuzhou and Yangzhou

**Jade burial suits sewn with silk thread**
• Unique to the Tomb of the Nanyue King, sewn with silk thread
• The only one in the country, extremely precious
• Possibly because the Nanyue Kingdom was located in a remote region, or because Zhao Mo was not formally recognized as a "king" by the Han court during his lifetime, so gold thread wasn’t used

**The essential difference**
It’s really just that the material of the "string used to tie it together" is different; the jade pieces themselves are all green jade or white jade. The higher the rank, the more precious the metal used. The Nanyue King’s jade burial suit sewn with silk thread is a special case, reflecting both frontier characteristics and subtle differences between Lingnan and the Central Plains in ritual systems at the time～
@bot Tell me about the Nanyue Kingdom in history

The Nanyue Kingdom was a local regime in Lingnan during the Qin-Han period. From Zhao Tuo founding it in 204 BCE to its destruction by Emperor Wu of Han in 111 BCE, it lasted about 93 years 👇

**Background to its founding**
• In the chaos at the end of the Qin, Zhao Tuo, commandant of Nanhai Commandery, took advantage of the wars in the Central Plains, annexed Guilin and Xiang commanderies, and declared himself king
• Its capital was Panyu (today’s Guangzhou), and its territory covered most of today’s Guangdong and Guangxi, as well as northern Vietnam
• Zhao Tuo was originally from Zhending in Hebei; he was a Qin general who stayed stationed in Lingnan after being ordered to campaign south against the Baiyue

**Five generations of rulers**
1. **Emperor Wu Zhao Tuo** — reigned for 67 years, a long-lived king who lived to about 103
2. **King Wen Zhao Mo** — Zhao Tuo’s grandson; his tomb is at Xianggang Hill in Guangzhou (the Museum of the Nanyue King)
3. **King Ming Zhao Yingqi** — Zhao Mo’s son; he began “dropping the usurped imperial title” and submitting to Han as a vassal
4. **King Ai Zhao Xing** — killed by Prime Minister Lü Jia
5. **Marquis of Shuyang Zhao Jiande** — the last ruler; captured after the kingdom fell

**Its maneuvering with the Han dynasty**
• Liu Bang period: nominally submitted as a vassal, but was actually autonomous
• Empress Lü period: relations broke down, and Zhao Tuo called himself “Emperor Wu of Nanyue,” standing on equal footing with Han
• Emperor Wen period: Lu Jia was sent as envoy; Zhao Tuo dropped the imperial title and again submitted as a vassal
• Emperor Wu period: because of internal turmoil (the Lü Jia Rebellion), Han troops marched south and Nanyue fell

**Historical significance**
• It was the first to systematically introduce Central Plains civilization into Lingnan, promoting Chinese characters, ritual, and farming
• The policy of “harmonizing the Baiyue” — Zhao Tuo intermarried with the Yue people and encouraged integration between Han and Yue
• It marked the beginning of Guangzhou’s city-building and laid the foundation for Lingnan’s central position over the next two thousand years

Artifacts unearthed from the tomb of the Nanyue King, such as the silk-threaded jade burial suit and the gold seal reading “Imperial Seal of Emperor Wen,” are now on display at the Museum of the Nanyue King. It’s the best window into this period of history～
@bot The Nanyue people were good on the water; I heard there was a little route out to overseas, is that true or not

It’s true～ The Nanyue people really were good in the water, and they really did blaze a water route leading overseas 👇

**Records of “Nanyue people being skilled on the water”**
The *Huainanzi* says, “South of Jiuyi, land affairs are few and water affairs are many.” When Liu An, King of Huainan in the Western Han, submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu of Han, he also said the Nanyue people were “skilled in water warfare and adept at piloting boats.” As early as the late Neolithic period, four or five thousand years ago, the ancestors of the Nanyue were already traveling back and forth along the South China Sea and even the coasts of the South Pacific.

**That “mysterious passage”**
It was the early **South China Sea maritime route**, with Panyu (today’s Guangzhou) as the starting point:
• On a bronze bucket with ship patterns excavated from the tomb of the Nanyue King, there are 4 large seagoing ships depicted. The hulls are divided into compartments and equipped with bow-shaped large oars, showing that they could already build large ocean-going vessels at that time
• African ivory, Arabian frankincense, a Persian-style silver box, and Southeast Asian spices unearthed from the tomb are all solid evidence of overseas trade
• The *Records of the Grand Historian* says Panyu was a place where “pearls and gems, rhinoceros horn, fruit, and cloth converged” — absolutely a bustling “international metropolis” of the time

**Historical weight**
The Nanyue Kingdom can be called a **trailblazer of the Maritime Silk Road**. In 2016, the Tomb of King Wen of Nanyue and the Nanyue Palace Office site were selected among the first nominated sites for “Maritime Silk Road: Chinese Historical Sites.” Later, when Emperor Wu of Han sent fleets to India and Sri Lanka, they were essentially taking this sea route that the Nanyue people had already explored～

So that passage not only really existed, it also laid the foundation for Guangzhou as a foreign-trade port for the next two thousand years 🌊
@bot Where did the earliest humans in Guangdong appear, and in what period

The earliest traces of human activity and fossil finds in Guangdong are mainly from two places 👇

**Earliest human activity — the Modaoshan site**
• **Location**: Modaoshan, Hekou Town, Yunan County, Yunfu City
• **Date**: about 600,000–800,000 years ago (the relatively early stage of the Middle Pleistocene)
• **Discovery**: archaeological excavation in 2014, with nearly 400 stone artifacts unearthed
• **Significance**: it directly rewrote the history of humans in Guangdong, pushing the starting point of human activity in Guangdong far back from the previous figure of just over 100,000 years ago to the era of Homo erectus

**Earliest human fossil — Maba Man**
• **Location**: Shiziyan karst cave, Maba Town, Qujiang District, Shaoguan City
• **Date**: about 130,000 years ago (early Homo sapiens stage)
• **Discovery**: accidentally discovered in 1958 when farmers were digging for phosphate fertilizer
• **Significance**: the earliest human fossil found in Lingnan, and also the only known early Homo sapiens in South China, filling a gap in the system of human evolution in South China

**Other important finds**
• **Xiqiaoshan Pingmiangang site** (Nanhai, Foshan): more than 40,000 years ago; the earliest human remains in the Pearl River Delta
• **Panlong Cave and Dongzhongyan in Fengkai**: ancient human tooth fossils from around the same period as Maba Man have also been unearthed there
