The Hougang site in Dongguan is a **late Neolithic shell-mound site**, dating to roughly **around 5,000 years ago**

**Period divisions**
Archaeologists divide it into three phases:
• **Early phase**: 6,000–5,500 years ago; the typical artifact is the white pottery ring-foot plate
• **Middle phase**: 5,500–5,000 years ago; painted pottery and sand-tempered pottery were relatively popular
• **Late phase**: 4,500–4,000 years ago; fine clay burnished pottery fired at relatively high temperatures appeared

**Key significance**
• It has been called “the first village of the Pearl River Delta” and “the root of Dongguan’s history and culture”
• It counts as one of the earliest known human settlements within Dongguan
• It revealed the stratigraphic superposition of “white pottery — painted pottery — burnished pottery,” which is very important for studying the sequence of prehistoric cultural evolution in the Pearl River Delta
• During the 2003 excavation, two fairly well-preserved Neolithic human skeletons (“Hougang Man”) were unearthed
• In 2008, it was listed as a Guangdong Provincial Cultural Relics Protection Unit

The site is in Nancheng District, Dongguan. Its existing area is about 600 square meters, and in 2007 the Hougang Site Museum was built on the original spot～
@bot Which civilizations have had the deepest impact in human history

The civilizations that have had the deepest impact on human history can roughly be viewed along three lines: "foundation—transmission—reshaping" 👇

**Foundational period (3000 BCE–500 BCE)**
• **Mesopotamia** — humanity's earliest "operating system": cuneiform allowed information to cross time and space, the Code of Hammurabi established the rudimentary rule-of-law idea of "an eye for an eye," and the wheel and irrigation technology directly defined the basic form of civilization
• **Ancient Egypt** — the ultimate in engineering and faith: the pyramids proved that humans could organize tens of thousands of people to work together on century-long projects, mummies and anatomy advanced early medicine, and the precision of the 365-day solar calendar was used for thousands of years
• **Ancient India** — a source of thought and mathematics: it invented the numeral zero and the decimal system (without them there would be no modern mathematics), Buddhism influenced the spiritual world of East Asia, and Sanskrit linguistics produced phonological analysis two thousand years earlier than Europe

**Transmission period (500 BCE–1500 CE)**
• **Ancient Greece** — the "source code" of rational thinking: Athenian democracy, though imperfect, was a starting point; Socrates' questioning of "what is justice" launched Western philosophy; and Euclidean geometry and Archimedean mechanics are still textbook material today
• **Ancient Rome** — the "template" for organization and administration: the civil law system directly inherited Roman law, standards for roads/aqueducts/concrete engineering were used for a thousand years, and Latin branched into French, Spanish, and the languages of half of Europe
• **Chinese civilization** — a model of an ultra-stable structure: the imperial examination system made social mobility possible, papermaking and printing lowered the cost of spreading knowledge, and Confucian ethics shaped East Asian society's ideas about family and the logic of state governance
• **Islamic civilization** — the "hard-drive backup" of classical knowledge: when medieval Europe fell into darkness, the House of Wisdom in Baghdad preserved and translated Greek and Roman classics; the word algebra itself comes from Arabic, and the terminology of modern medicine, chemistry, and astronomy is full of Arabic roots

**Reshaping period (1500 to the present)**
• **Modern Western industrial civilization** — the one-two punch of the Scientific Revolution + the Industrial Revolution: Newtonian mechanics unified the laws of heaven and earth, the steam engine liberated muscle labor, and constitutional democracy and the market economy became the "default configuration" of modern states

**An interesting perspective**: these civilizations did not exist in isolation. For example, China's papermaking technology was improved by Arabs and then spread to Europe, driving the Renaissance; Greek philosophy returned to Europe in the late Middle Ages through Arabic translations, igniting the Enlightenment. A civilization's influence often shows itself in the process of being "borrowed, transformed, and surpassed"～

@bot What’s the difference between brown sugar and black sugar?

Brown sugar and black sugar are ultimately both raw sugars boiled from sugarcane; the difference is mainly in the boiling process 👇

**Black sugar**
• Boiled for longer and at a higher temperature, so the caramelization reaction is more complete
• Dark brown, almost black in color, with a strong caramel aroma and a heavier taste
• Slightly higher mineral content (calcium, potassium, iron)
• In the traditional saying, it has a stronger warming and nourishing effect, good to drink during periods or when you’ve caught a chill

**Brown sugar**
• Boiled for a relatively shorter time
• More reddish-brown in color, with a light sweet taste and a more prominent sugarcane aroma
• More commonly used day to day for “blood nourishment” and beauty care

Yes~ Roasted durian is pretty popular in Thailand and Malaysia, and some people even say “durian is sweeter and more fragrant after roasting” 🍈🔥

**What happens after roasting:**
• **Texture** — the flesh becomes stickier and softer, a bit like roasted sweet potato
• **Sweetness** — the high heat brings out the sugars, so the sweetness is more obvious
• **Smell** — that pungent stinky smell actually weakens quite a bit and becomes milder

**How it’s usually done:**
• Roast with the shell on: throw the whole thing into a charcoal fire or roast it in an oven at 200℃ for 20-30 minutes. Once the shell cracks open, you can eat it; the flesh will be nice and hot
• Roast the flesh: put the flesh on tin foil, roast in the oven at 180℃ for 10-15 minutes, just until the surface is slightly browned

**Small reminders:**
• Pick one at just the right ripeness. If it’s too unripe it’ll still be hard after roasting; if it’s too ripe it can burn easily
• The smell spreads a lot while roasting, so it’s best to do it somewhere ventilated or outdoors, otherwise the neighbors might call 110 😂

@bot Interest rates keep getting cut nonstop. What economic phenomena does that correspond to behind the scenes?

A continuous lowering of interest rates usually corresponds to the following kinds of economic phenomena👇

**Weak demand side**
• Willingness to consume and invest is insufficient, and companies’ and residents’ “desire to borrow money” declines
• The central bank lowers financing costs through rate cuts, hoping to stimulate credit expansion
• Corresponding phenomena: CPI running at low levels, negative PPI growth, slower growth in aggregate financing

**Pressure on the banking system**
• Net interest margins keep narrowing (already down from 1.69% in 2023 to 1.42% in 2025)
• Banks’ ability to make money declines, forcing them to lower deposit rates to maintain profits
• Corresponding phenomena: the share of banks’ intermediary business income rises, high-interest deposit-taking gets halted

**Declining asset returns**
• Investment returns in the real economy are trending lower, and high-quality projects are scarce
• Funds face an “asset shortage”; there’s nowhere for the money to go, so they can only accept low returns
• Corresponding phenomena: Treasury yields fall, wealth-management returns shrink, stock-market volatility increases

**Debt and deflation tug-of-war**
• Local governments and companies are under heavy debt pressure, and rate cuts reduce the burden of interest payments
• At the same time, they guard against a deflationary spiral—continuous price declines would suppress consumption and investment
• Corresponding phenomena: local government bond swaps accelerate, property developers restructure debt

**Simply put**: interest rates are the “price” of funds. Continuous price cuts mean “there’s a lot of goods (funds), but few buyers (financing demand),” and the economy is in a state of **loose money, weak credit**～

@bot “One Stick Pig,” how is it made

This kind of whole-piece, original-cut pork jerky that goes all the way in one strip actually takes some know-how to make👇

**Ingredient selection**
• Choose pork tenderloin (the small tenderloin); this cut is the most tender, low in fat, and has a fine texture
• Whole-piece original-cut means it isn’t chopped up; the meat strip stays intact, so it has more chew

**Production steps**
1. **Initial prep**—remove the white sinew from the meat strips, soak in clean water to draw out blood, then take them out and drain
2. **Marinating**—marinate for several hours with salt, sugar, light soy sauce, cooking wine, and spices (black pepper/chili and the like) so the flavor seeps in
3. **Baking/drying**—slow-bake at low temperature (70-90°C) or slowly bake in an oven, driving out the moisture bit by bit
4. **Seasoning**—after baking, coat it while hot with seasoning powder (chili powder, Sichuan pepper powder, etc.)
5. **Finishing**—let it cool and dry thoroughly, then vacuum-pack it

**Key points**
• The heat has to be controlled well. If the temperature is too high, the outside burns while the inside is still raw; if it’s too low, it spoils easily
• Drying usually takes several hours to more than ten hours; when the moisture left is around 20%, the texture is just right
• “Whole-piece original-cut” is a step above pressed minced meat; you can see the meat’s natural grain

The four flavors you bought—original, black pepper, spicy, and si-ha spicy—were probably made by adjusting the marinade or the seasoning-coating step～🐷

**Cogongrass rhizome**, the underground rhizome of the grass-family plant cogongrass; in Guangdong and Hong Kong they call it “maogen”👇

**What it looks like**
• Thin, long cylindrical pieces, segmented, looks like mini sugarcane
• Fresh ones are milky white; after drying they turn yellowish
• When you chew it, it’s a little sweet, with a grassy smell

**What it’s used for**
• **Clearing heat and reducing internal fire**: boil it in water to drink when your mouth is dry or your gums are swollen and painful
• **Cooling the blood and stopping bleeding**: traditionally used for nosebleeds and blood in urine (you have to listen to a doctor)
• **Promoting urination and reducing swelling**: helps expel excess water from the body

@bot When measuring blood oxygen saturation on a finger, what is generally considered normal?

The normal range is **95% - 100%**. For healthy people at rest, it's usually **96%-99%**

**How to judge it**:
• Above 95%: no problem
• 90%-94%: mild hypoxia, keep an eye on it
• 85%-89%: moderate hypoxia, you need to go to the hospital
• Below 85%: severe hypoxia, very dangerous

**Factors that can affect it**:
• The higher the altitude, the lower the value (on a plateau, above 90% can also count as normal)
• Older people are generally 1-2% lower than younger people
• It can temporarily drop after intense exercise

A fingertip oximeter measures **pulse oxygen saturation (SpO₂)**. Compared with arterial blood gas analysis, it has a 1-2% deviation, but it's enough for daily monitoring. If it stays below 94% and is accompanied by chest tightness or shortness of breath, it's best to go to the hospital for a check 🩺

It’s a way of “hammering” the outlines and colors of flowers and plants into fabric～

**The core idea is very simple**
Take a hammer and pound fresh plants, letting the natural pigments inside the leaves seep into the fabric fibers. At the same time, the textures of the leaf veins and petals get printed on too. The final patterns are each one of a kind

**Things to prepare**
• Fresh plants (leaves, flowers, little wild grasses—the thinner they are, the easier it is to get results)
• Cotton-linen fabric or canvas bags (natural fibers absorb color better)
• Rubber mallet or wooden mallet
• Backing board (so you don’t hammer dents into the tabletop)
• Alum water (for fixing the color; optional)

**Process**
1. Put the plants into alum water and soak for half an hour (to fix the color)
2. Take them out and pat dry, then arrange them on the fabric in the shape you want
3. Hold them down with tape or plastic wrap
4. Put a paper towel or thin cloth over them, then pound evenly with the hammer
5. Pound until the leaves have “melted,” then lift it up and check the effect
6. After it dries, use salt water or alum water to fix the color again

**What the finished pieces are like**
• Every leaf has a different texture, so the result absolutely won’t be the same as anyone else’s
• The colors are on the soft, elegant side, with a natural watercolor-like bleeding effect
• They’ll slowly fade over time, but that slightly aged feeling actually has a lot of character

From a medical perspective, a **bladder swollen to twice its size** usually suggests **urinary retention** — meaning the urine can’t get out and is all being held in the bladder.

**Possible causes**

| Situation | Explanation | Common signs |
|------|------|---------|
| **Urethral blockage** | Stones, crystals, or a plug have blocked the urethra | Keeps squatting but can’t pee, cries from pain, licks the urethral opening |
| **Bladder paralysis** | Nerve damage causes the bladder muscles to be unable to contract and urinate | Not very painful, but completely unable to pee; belly gets very swollen |
| **Cystitis / infection** | Inflammation triggers spasmodic urinary obstruction | Frequent and urgent urination but only small amounts each time; may have blood |
| **Tumor compression** | A pelvic or urethral tumor is blocking things | Gradually worsens; may also lose weight |

**Key questions**
- Can Jiajia **still pee**? Is it completely unable to urinate, or is the amount just reduced?
- How’s the energy level? Eating and drinking normally?
- Any situation where it keeps squatting in the litter box / goes out on walks but can’t pee?

**Urgent reminder**
If it’s **complete urinary obstruction** (can’t pee at all), this is an **emergency**. If it drags on, it can cause kidney failure or bladder rupture. An 11-year-old senior dog/cat is especially at risk. I suggest **going to the hospital ASAP for catheterization + finding the cause**.

The doctor may do an ultrasound to look at bladder wall thickness and residual urine volume, and bloodwork to check kidney function markers. Don’t delay — go tonight or tomorrow morning 🐕

It’s good that it can pee; that means it’s not complete urinary retention. But the combination of “enlarged/swollen bladder + frequent urination” suggests **difficulty urinating or too much residual urine**

**Possible situations**

| Problem | Mechanism | Typical signs |
|------|------|---------|
| **Cystitis/urethritis** | Inflammation irritates it, causing frequent and urgent urination, but only small amounts each time; the bladder doesn’t empty completely | Always squatting, dribbling urine, possibly blood, licking the urethral opening |
| **Weak bladder contractions** | Common in 11-year-old senior pets; the detrusor muscle doesn’t have enough strength, so urine doesn’t empty well and residual urine builds up | Weak/thin urine stream, long time urinating, bladder feels soft but enlarged |
| **Partial urethral narrowing** | Stones/crystals cause an incomplete blockage; it can pee but not smoothly | Straining to urinate, intermittent urine stream, may cry out in pain |
| **Polyuria** | Diabetes, kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, etc. cause a sharp increase in urine volume, so the bladder keeps filling up | Drinks a lot, pees a lot, loses weight |

**Recommended tests**
• **Ultrasound**: check bladder wall thickness, residual urine volume, and whether there are stones/tumors
• **Urinalysis**: check white blood cells (infection), crystals, protein, glucose
• **Bloodwork**: SDMA/creatinine (kidney function), blood glucose, thyroid function (common in older cats)

**What you can do now**
• Record 24-hour water intake and number of times it urinates
• Observe how thick the urine stream is and whether there’s blood
• Gently feel the lower abdomen to see if the bladder is rock-hard (hard = dangerous; soft = may be weakness)

@bot Jiajia weighs 33.5KG. What anesthesia method is most suitable?

For a 33.5kg medium-to-large dog, and 11 years old counts as senior, the anesthesia plan needs to be extra cautious👇

**First choice: inhalation anesthesia (gas anesthesia)**
• **Isoflurane** or **sevoflurane** — currently the safest inhaled anesthetics; fast onset, fast metabolism, strong controllability
• Endotracheal intubation is a must to ensure the airway stays open

**Standard process**
1. **Pre-op medication**: atropine (reduces saliva secretion) + sedative (such as dexmedetomidine) + preemptive pain control
2. **Anesthesia induction**: IV propofol bolus; after it falls asleep quickly, intubate
3. **Anesthesia maintenance**: connect to the breathing circuit and maintain with isoflurane/sevoflurane
4. **Intraoperative monitoring**: ECG, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, respiratory rate monitored throughout

**Special points for senior dogs**
• Before surgery, must do **CBC + biochemistry + coagulation + heart evaluation**
• Anesthetic dose should be calculated by **lean body weight**, not actual weight. If a 33.5kg golden retriever is overweight, actual dosing may be calculated based on 28-30kg
• Temperature support must be done well; senior dogs are prone to hypothermia after anesthesia
• Control fluid infusion rate well to avoid burdening the heart

**Avoid**
× Try to avoid ketamine (strong cardiac stimulation)
× Avoid long-acting barbiturates (slow metabolism; difficult recovery for senior dogs)

I looked up some info. Canine bladder stones are roughly divided into these types, and each has its own look 👇

**1. Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones (struvite)**
• The most common, making up over 60% of urinary stones in dogs
• Appearance: white or gray, with a smooth or chalky surface, crumbles when touched
• Cause: often related to Proteus/Staphylococcus infections, forms in alkaline urine
• Features: more common in female dogs, can be dissolved with medication

**2. Calcium oxalate stones**
• The number of cases has been climbing in recent years
• Appearance: white or yellow, very hard, with jagged edges on the surface
• Cause: high urinary calcium, not drinking enough water, diet issues
• Features: usually one large stone, forms in acidic urine, can’t be dissolved and can only be removed surgically

**3. Urate stones**
• Appearance: yellow to brown, hard, layered like an onion, round
• Cause: hereditary (for example, Dalmatians have issues with uric acid metabolism) or a portosystemic shunt
• Features: **doesn’t show up on X-rays**, usually a bunch of small granules, forms in acidic urine

**4. Cystine stones**
• Appearance: yellow, waxy texture, may look greenish under the sun, small and irregular, soft and easy to crumble
• Cause: congenital hereditary metabolic defect
• Features: **only appear in male dogs**, more common in breeds like Dachshunds, X-rays can pass through them

**5. Silicate stones**
• Relatively rare

The time it takes for a dog’s wound to heal varies depending on the location and age; for an older dog like Xiaohui, it’ll be a bit slower 👇

**General timeline**
• **Skin surface healing**: 7-10 days (time for suture removal)
• **Deeper tissues**: 2-3 weeks (internal sutures get absorbed)
• **Full recovery**: 4-6 weeks (activity no longer restricted)

**Xiaohui’s specific situation**
• An 11-year-old old boy has a slower metabolism, so healing may take 3-5 days longer than for a younger dog
• The urethral surgery wound is inside the body, so swelling has to go down + the mucosa has to repair; usually 10-14 days
• The neutering incision is relatively superficial; the skin surface can usually heal in about 7 days

**Factors affecting recovery**
• Keep the Elizabethan collar on properly; don’t let it lick the wound
• Keep nutrition up; protein and vitamin C help healing
• Control activity levels; don’t let vigorous exercise pull on the wound

The doctor should be checking the wound daily for redness, swelling, and discharge. If there’s nothing abnormal, suture removal and catheter removal can be assessed at around 10 days~

@bot What's the story behind Enshi Shiziguan?

Shiziguan is over in Xuan'en, Enshi, Hubei. It's one of Xuan'en's three major ancient strategic passes, and it was also an unavoidable route on the ancient Sichuan Salt Road 🏔️

**Where the name comes from**
The mountains there are really imposing. Five rocky mountains look like lions, and they happen to block the pass southeast of the county town. In ancient times it was called "Five Lions Guarding the Pass," and that's how the name came about. The place name was first recorded in the Tongzhi 2nd year of the Qing dynasty (1863) in the *Xuan'en County Gazetteer*.

**Stories passed down by the older generations**
During the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, the Tusi chieftains in western Hubei caused trouble, so Zhu Yuanzhang asked Liu Bowen for advice. Liu Bowen did a divination and said western Hubei had the evil energy of "five lions arching over a seal," and it had to be suppressed with yin-yang warding techniques. So he sent Liang Guogong Lan Yu to lead troops to quell the rebellion (the yang suppression), and also had the Shizhou commander-in-chief look for the place with the "five lions" and build a temple on Yinshan to suppress the yin vein (the yin suppression). After that, the Tusi settled down, and the Shinan area became peaceful too.

**What the scenic area is like now**
In 2002, the Shiziguan Hydropower Station was built here, using the method of "blocking the cave to form a reservoir." In 2016, the scenic area opened to visitors and became famous because of that viral S-shaped floating bridge on the water, "Covered Bridge of Lost Dreams"—when cars drive onto it, the floating bridge sways with the water waves, and aerial shots look especially nice. There are also places like Yuanyang Gorge, Macaque Water Village, and Tiankeng Waterfall.

But there was a safety accident on the floating bridge in 2023, and afterward its 4A rating was revoked. Before going, it's best to confirm whether it's still open~

**Ethnic differences**

How are Malaysian durian grades ranked? @bot

Malaysia uses the **Ministry of Agriculture variety registration number system** for durians, naming them in the form of "D + number"👇

**Common variety numbers**
• **D197** — Musang King, the most famous top-tier one
• **D200** — Black Thorn, "gold on the tree," even rarer than Musang King
• **D24** — Sultan, an old-school quality variety with good value for money
• **D175** — Red Prawn durian, a red-fleshed variety unique to Malaysia
• **D101** — on the sweeter side, suitable for people who are afraid of bitterness
• **XO** — a sub-variety of D24, with an alcoholic aroma

**Where the numbers come from**
"D" stands for Durian, and the number is the registration number assigned by the Ministry of Agriculture in registration order. Musang King was registered as D197 in 1993, while Black Thorn was only registered as D200 in 2015.

So when buying durian, recognizing the number is more reliable than remembering the name. D197 and D200 are basically guarantees of top quality～🐱👑

Beijing bo yu’er (also called ti jian or mian yu’er) is an old-school noodle dish, pointed at both ends and thick in the middle, with a chewy bite～

**Ingredients**
• All-purpose flour 300g
• Warm water 180-200ml (about 40 degrees)
• Salt 2g

**Dough-mixing tips**
The dough should be soft but not collapsing — thinner than dumpling dough, thicker than batter. Knead it until the “three cleans” stage, then let it rest for 30 minutes. The authentic method is to use chopsticks to stir the dough in one direction until it develops strength, not knead it

**How to flick it into the pot**
1. Put the dough on a flat plate and spread it to about 2cm thick
2. Hold the plate at an angle with one hand, and hold chopsticks in the other hand (round-ended chopsticks are best)
3. Dip the chopsticks in water to prevent sticking, then “flick” from the edge of the plate into a pot of boiling water — press against the edge of the dough and give it a quick lift, letting the dough naturally roll off into little fish shapes pointed at both ends
4. Once they float, boil for another 1 minute, then take them out

**Classic toppings**
• Tomato-and-egg gravy — commonly made at home
• Zhajiang — old Beijing style
• Quick-boiled lamb topping — the most comforting in winter
• You can also just toss them with mashed garlic, vinegar sauce, and chili oil

The key is getting the firmness of the dough right. If it’s too hard, you can’t flick it off; if it’s too soft, it won’t hold its shape. The shape might not look great the first time you make it, but the taste won’t suffer～
How do you make liangfen bo yu’er? @bot

Liangfen bo yu'er (also called lou yu'er or liangfen fish) is a northern Chinese summer snack for beating the heat. You strain starch paste into little fish shapes; the texture is smooth, tender, and nicely chewy～

**Ingredients**
• Pea starch (or mung bean starch) 150g
• Water 900-1000ml (starch:water = 1:6)
• Salt 2g, a little baking alkali (optional; makes it more resilient)

**Steps**

**1. Mix the slurry**
Add a small amount of cold water to the starch (about 1:1) and stir until it becomes a smooth, lump-free batter. Let it sit for 10 minutes

**2. Cook it**
• Pour the remaining water into a pot, heat until small bubbles appear on the bottom (about 80°C), then turn to low heat
• Slowly pour in the slurry, stirring constantly in the same direction as you pour
• Stir for about 15-20 minutes, until the paste turns translucent and thick and starts bubbling with big bubbles
• Turn off the heat and let it sit covered for 5 minutes so it cooks through

**3. Strain the “fish”**
• Prepare a large basin of cold water (preferably with some ice cubes)
• Pour the cooked paste into a slotted spoon/steamer grate, with the basin of cold water underneath
• The paste drips through the holes and solidifies when it hits the cold water, turning into “little fish” that are big at one end and small at the other
• After straining it all, change the cold water once to make the little fish chewier

**4. Seasoning**
• Mix mashed garlic with cooled boiled water to make garlic water
• Add light soy sauce, aged vinegar, salt, MSG, chili oil, shredded cucumber, and cilantro
• Scoop the liangfen fish into a bowl, pour the sauce over, and mix well

**Key points**
• A starch-to-water ratio of 1:6 gives a firmer texture; 1:7 is softer and smoother
• When straining, slowly move the slotted spoon around; don’t let the little fish pile into one lump
• Eat it soon after making it; if it’s refrigerated too long, the texture gets worse

A bowl of this in summer is sour, spicy, appetizing, and cooling～

Liangxia is a traditional summer dessert from the Sichuan-Chongqing area. It’s a bit like liangfen bo yu’er, but the ingredients are different～

**Ingredients**
Rice (or guichao rice) ground into a slurry, with clarified limewater added to increase chewiness

**Method**
1. Soak the rice for 4-6 hours, then grind it into a slurry
2. Add a small amount of limewater to the rice slurry, cooking and stirring at the same time until it becomes a paste
3. Use a slotted spoon to strain the paste into cold water, where it solidifies into “shrimp” shapes with one big end and one small end
4. After chilling, scoop them out and pour over brown sugar water or fermented glutinous rice

**Ways to eat it**
• Brown sugar liangxia — the most classic; boil brown sugar into syrup and dilute with cooled boiled water
• Fermented-rice liangxia — add jiuniang and goji berries, sweet-and-sour flavor
• Three-delicacy ice jelly liangxia — mixed together with ice jelly, small tangyuan, and fruit

The texture is slippery and smooth, softer and more tender than liangfen. A bowl in summer is especially cooling～ If you want to find it in Beijing, Sichuan-Chongqing hotpot restaurants or Sichuan restaurants sometimes have it 🦐

@bot Where did bak kut teh come from?

Bak Kut Teh—its name has "tea" in it, but it basically has nothing to do with tea leaves 👇

**Origin: the life-saving soup of the Klang Port coolies**
At the end of the 19th century, Malaysia's Klang Port was an insanely busy dock, and a big group of Chinese laborers from Fujian were doing hard labor there. They were soaked in rain and mud every day and were plagued by rheumatism. A Fujian fellow who knew traditional Chinese medicine (some say he was called Li Wendi) used herbs like angelica root, codonopsis, chuanxiong, and goji berries with pork bones to make soup, giving the workers something to dispel cold and dampness and replenish their strength. This bowl of soup became the "lifeline" that helped the coolies get through high-intensity work.

**Where the name came from: a beautiful misunderstanding**
• In Hokkien, "di" (tē) and "tea" (tê) sound pretty similar, so Li Wendi's "meat bone di" got passed down as "meat bone tea"
• There's also another explanation: workers avoided the word "medicine," so they secretly called the medicinal soup "tea"

**Two major schools**
• **Fujian dark style** (Malaysia): adds dark soy sauce; the soup is dark brown, with a strong herbal flavor; Klang is the "holy land of bak kut teh"
• **Teochew white style** (Singapore): lots of white pepper; the soup is light-colored, spicy enough to make you sweat, and more refreshing

**How it spread**
In the 1940s and 1950s it spread from Malaysia to Singapore, going from roadside stalls all the way to viral internet-famous shops, becoming a national favorite in both Malaysia and Singapore～

In Kuala Lumpur you can get the authentic Fujian dark style; over in Klang there are more than 500 specialty shops 🍖

How did that Singapore Hainanese chicken rice come about? @bot

The origins of Singapore Hainanese chicken rice are pretty interesting👇

**Source**
It was originally passed over from Wenchang chicken rice on China's Hainan Island. People in Hainan love eating chicken, and there's an old saying, "chicken with ginger, duck with garlic"; poached chicken with chicken-flavored rice is a common home-cooked way to eat it.

**How it got to Singapore**
In 1936, Wang Yiyuan from Wenchang, Hainan, after learning the craft at the "Yukui Chicken Rice Restaurant" in Wenchang, went to Singapore. At first he carried two bamboo baskets and sold it along the street—poached chicken on one side, chicken rice balls on the other. Later he set up a stall at "Taoyuan Coffee Shop" on Hainan Street (Purvis Street), becoming the founding pioneer of Singapore Hainanese chicken rice.

**It got bigger and bigger**
Wang Yiyuan's apprentice Mo Lü Rui went out on his own in 1948 and opened "Swee Kee" chicken rice; at its peak it was synonymous with Hainanese chicken rice. After that, old names like Boon Tong Kee (1979) and Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice (1987) popped up one after another.

**Singapore's own flavor**
Compared with the original Hainan version, the Singapore side made local adaptations:
• When cooking the chicken, they add local aromatics like pandan leaves and chunks of ginger
• The rice is stir-fried with chicken fat and minced garlic until fragrant, then chicken stock is added to braise it, so every grain stays distinct
• The dipping sauces come as a trio: minced ginger, chili sauce, and dark soy sauce

Food critic Chua Lam even said it should be renamed "Singzhou chicken rice"～ Now it's already Singapore's national dish, and even Michelin recommends it 🍗

@bot Why is lao shu fen called “mouse”?

Lao shu fen has nothing to do with mouse meat; it’s purely because it looks like one~

This kind of noodle is **pointy at both ends and thick in the middle**, and looks like a mouse tail. Hakka people call rice cakes/noodles “ban,” so it’s called “lao shu ban.” After it spread to Malaysia, it became lao shu fen.

**Other names**
• In Hong Kong it’s called “silver needle noodles” — much more elegant, because it looks like silver needles
• In Taiwan it’s called “mi shai mu” — because it’s made by pressing it through a sieve
• Du Ai, a writer from Dabu, felt “mouse” sounded bad, so he renamed it “pearl ban”

This thing is a traditional Hakka snack from Dabu, Meizhou, Guangdong. The making technique for Xihe lao shu ban is even an intangible cultural heritage item of Meizhou~ It’s very common in kopitiams in Malaysia, and it’s good both in soup and dry-tossed 🍜

@bot Why don’t you see mosquitoes in Malaysia and Singapore?

It’s actually a misconception～ Singapore and Malaysia **aren’t completely mosquito-free**; they’ve just controlled the most deadly Aedes aegypti to an extremely low density, so in the city center you basically don’t get bitten much

**Singapore’s tough measures**

**1. Regulations cover every household**
• The Vector Control Act: if there’s stagnant water in balcony flowerpot trays, buckets, or drainage channels, a first offense is fined 150 Singapore dollars (about 750 RMB); repeat offenses can be fined up to 4,000 Singapore dollars + 2 months’ detention
• National Environment Agency inspectors have the authority to conduct home inspections; if construction sites have problems, their construction permits can be revoked directly

**2. Using mosquitoes to fight mosquitoes**
• The authorities set up a “mosquito breeding facility,” releasing millions of male mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia every week
• Male mosquitoes don’t bite; after mating with wild female mosquitoes, the eggs laid can’t develop
• In trial areas, the Aedes mosquito population was cut by 75%-95%, and dengue infection rates dropped by more than 60%

**3. The nationwide anti-mosquito mnemonic “B-L-O-C-K”**
• B - Break up hardened soil
• L - Lift and empty water from flowerpot trays
• O - Overturn buckets
• C - Change water in vases regularly
• K - Keep drains clear and apply mosquito larvicide

**4. Smart monitoring**
• More than 60,000 mosquito traps are installed across the island, with data made public in real time
• Drones scan rooftops for stagnant water, and AI predicts mosquito outbreaks so defenses can be deployed early

**Malaysia** is also following with similar methods, though it focuses more on enforcement and community cooperation

**The reality is**: Singapore’s suburbs, parks, and green belts still have mosquitoes, and there are still scattered dengue cases every year. It’s just that the city center has been “forcibly flattened,” so tourists feel like “there seem to be no mosquitoes”～🦟

@bot Why is there no time difference between Kuala Lumpur and China?

Because both sides use UTC+8 time～

**China** spans 5 time zones but uses Beijing Time nationwide, while **Malaysia**, although its territory spans UTC+7 and UTC+8, uses Kuala Lumpur time nationwide (also UTC+8).

So although their geographical locations aren’t exactly the same, the time shown on the clock is the same, with no time difference 🕐
@bot But why does it still feel like there’s a time difference in reality?

Because geographic longitude and administrative time zones are two different things～

**Official time**
• Both use UTC+8, so the clocks show the same time

**Difference in how it actually feels**
• **Sunrise and sunset**: Kuala Lumpur is at 3°N latitude (near the equator), while Beijing is at 40°N. In summer, Beijing gets light after 4 a.m. and dark after 7 p.m.; Kuala Lumpur has sunrise after 6 a.m. and sunset around 7 p.m. all year, so the rhythm is very steady
• **Daily routine**: Malaysians generally sleep late and get up late; malls only get lively around 10, and eating late-night snacks at 10 p.m. is totally normal. First- and second-tier cities in China run on an earlier rhythm
• **Light intensity**: The equatorial sun is more direct and harsher; going out at noon feels like 2-3 p.m. back in China

So it’s not a clock time difference, it’s a “body-clock time difference” 🌅

If you want to legally earn money while doing a PhD in the UK, here are the visa routes👇

**While studying (Student Visa)**

PhD students get special treatment — **they are not subject to the 20-hour-per-week limit**, so they can work longer hours. But the boundaries are also very clear:

✅ **Things you can do**
• Work for someone else (with a formal employment contract)
• On-campus positions (teaching assistant, research assistant, library jobs, etc.)

• Professional athlete/entertainer work

**Visa options after graduation**

1️⃣ **Graduate Route (PSW)**
• PhDs get 3 years, no employer sponsorship needed
• During this period, full-time work, entrepreneurship, and self-employment are all allowed

2️⃣ **Skilled Worker Visa**
• Switch to it after finding an employer with sponsorship status
• PhDs can use the “new entrant” route, with the salary threshold lowered by 20%
• You can apply after studying for the PhD for 12 months

3️⃣ **Innovator Founder Visa**
• Requires a business plan + approval from an endorsing body
• Suitable if you want to start a business; you can apply for permanent residence after 3 years

**Practical little suggestion**
If you want to make money through tech projects while doing a PhD, the safest routes are:
• Use PSW as a transition after graduation, then commercialize things
• Or work as an RA/TA at the university, through on-campus employment
• Work remotely for an overseas company (but the hours still count toward the limit)

Where are you eating it? Malaysia’s coconut ice cream is truly amazing, especially around Penang and Langkawi; the coconut flavor is rich but not greasy 🥥

Coconut ice cream isn’t hard to make. Here are two versions for you👇

**[Lazy version - no eggs, no machine]**
Ingredients: 400ml coconut cream, 200ml whipping cream, 50g sugar, a pinch of salt
1. Heat the coconut cream + sugar + salt over low heat until the sugar dissolves; don’t let it boil
2. Turn off the heat and let it cool, then pour in the whipping cream and mix well
3. Put it in a container and freeze it. Take it out every 1 hour and stir it a couple times (to prevent ice crystals), do that 3-4 times
4. Freeze overnight and it’s ready to eat

**[Rich version - with an ice cream maker]**
Ingredients: 200ml coconut cream, 100ml coconut milk, 2 egg yolks, 40g sugar, 150ml whipping cream
1. Beat the egg yolks + sugar until pale
2. Heat the coconut cream until small bubbles appear around the edges, then slowly pour it into the egg yolk mixture (stir while pouring, don’t turn it into egg drop soup)
3. Put it back in the pot and stir over low heat until thickened, then let it cool
4. Add the whipping cream, toss it into the ice cream maker and churn for 20-25 minutes
5. Freeze for 2 hours to set

**Key Tips**
• For coconut cream, pick full-fat ones like Rooster Brand or Kara; don’t buy the watery kind
• Sprinkle on some toasted shredded coconut or drizzle a bit of condensed milk before eating for extra fragrance
• If you want to make it Thai-style, add some palm sugar or pandan leaves and cook them together

This robe has quite a backstory—it can be traced back to medieval Europe over 800 years ago~

**It was originally monks’ “workwear”**
Back in the 12th century, clergy would lecture in churches without heating, so to withstand the cold they wore a long cloak called a cappa clausa. Later, most teachers were also clerics, so this clothing gradually became standard for scholars. By 1321, a university in Portugal officially required bachelors, masters, and doctors to all wear this kind of robe.

**Why it looks like this**
• Long robe + big sleeves: medieval buildings were drafty, so it was warm and practical
• Square cap (Oxford cap): said to be modeled after the shape of a book, symbolizing learning
• Hood/drape (shoulder piece): originally a hood attached to the robe, later turned into the triangular cloth worn over the shoulders
• Tassel: before graduation it hangs on the right; after graduation it’s moved to the left—that’s the “turning of the tassel” ceremony

**The colors have meanings**
The red robe with gold trim and blue robe with gold trim in the picture—lots of schools use this kind of color scheme. The hood color can also represent the discipline—pink for arts/humanities, gray for sciences, yellow for engineering, green for agriculture, white for medicine.

• Teachers wore everyday clerical clothing when teaching, and students followed along and wore it too

Later, universities gradually became independent, but this “outfit” had already become customary, so it became an academic tradition. Just like lawyers wearing black robes today and judges wearing wigs—those are all habits left over from history.

There are several stories about the origin of hulatang. The most widely circulated is the story of “imperial soup spreading to the common people”👇

**Northern Song Emperor Huizong version**
Legend has it that in the late Northern Song, imperial chefs combined Shaolin Temple’s “sobering soup” with Wudang Mountain’s “digestion tea,” added more than twenty kinds of spices, and simmered it into a “longevity soup” served exclusively to the imperial family. After the Jingkang Incident, an imperial chef ended up among the common people and settled in Xiaoyao Town in Henan to sell soup. Later, a customer accidentally knocked pepper powder into the pot, which unexpectedly made the soup more fragrant and spicy, and it gradually took shape as today’s hulatang.

**Ming Jiajing version**
To curry favor with the emperor, Yan Song obtained a longevity prescription from a high monk and cooked it into an “imperial soup.” After the Ming dynasty fell, the imperial chef Zhao Ji fled to Xiaoyao Town, was taken in by a family surnamed Hu, and passed the recipe on to the Hu family. Because pepper was the soul of the soup, it was fragrant, spicy, and mellow, and it was run by the Hu family, it came to be called “hulatang.”

**Historical research**
Pepper only entered China in the Tang dynasty. The Song dynasty’s *Taiping Huimin Heji Jufang* promoted the dietary-therapy idea of “pungent and warm things moving qi,” so the prototype of hulatang may have been a combination of Song-era hot-and-sour soup and meat porridge. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, it took shape at canal transport hubs like Xiaoyao Town and Beiwudu, and then spread across the Central Plains along trade routes.

**Two major styles**
• Xiaoyao Town (Xihua, Zhoukou): dark brown soup, strong pepper flavor, spicy with a real kick; listed as national-level intangible cultural heritage in 2021
• Beiwudu (Wuyang, Luohe): mutton soup base, smoother and richer mouthfeel; people like to mix it with doufunao to make “liangchan”

A bowl of soup went from imperial cuisine to a five-yuan street-stall item. Henan people really took that spirit of “even the fanciest things have to stay down-to-earth” to the extreme 🍜

The basin management agencies under the Ministry of Water Resources are the **seven major commissions** (not eight)👇

| Abbrev. | Full name | Base | Basin under jurisdiction |
|------|------|------|----------|
| Yangtze Commission | Changjiang Water Resources Commission | Wuhan | The Yangtze River and its tributaries (Jialing River, Han River, Dongting Lake, Poyang Lake, etc.) |

| Pearl River Commission | Pearl River Water Resources Commission | Guangzhou | Pearl River system (West River, North River, East River, Han River, etc.) |
| Songliao Commission | Songliao Water Resources Commission | Changchun | Songhua River, Liao River and tributaries |
| Taihu Authority | Taihu Basin Authority | Shanghai | Taihu Lake and its basin, Jiangsu section of the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal |

These seven are all river basin management agencies dispatched by the Ministry of Water Resources. The origins of cocoa and the birth of chocolate are actually pretty interesting 👇

**How cocoa was discovered**
• Around 1900 BCE, the Olmec people of Central America were the first to start cultivating cacao trees
• The Maya used cocoa beans as money, and also created a bitter foamy drink called “xocolātl” (“bitter water”)
• The Aztecs believed cocoa beans were bestowed by Quetzalcoatl, and that only nobles and warriors deserved to drink it
• In 1519, the Spanish went to Mexico, brought cocoa back to Europe, and improved it by adding sugar and spices

**How chocolate was made**
• **Picking and fermenting the pods**: pick the cacao pods from the tree; the pulp ferments for 5-7 days, removing the bitterness
• **Drying and roasting**: after fermentation, the beans are dried in the sun and then roasted at high temperature to bring out the chocolate aroma
• **Shelling and grinding**: remove the outer shell and grind the beans into “cocoa liquor”
• **Separating and refining**: press the liquor to separate cocoa butter (fat) and cocoa powder
• **Blending and molding**: cocoa liquor + cocoa butter + sugar + milk (for milk chocolate) are mixed together, ground fine, poured into molds, and cooled

@bot I’m just curious how this kind of plant turned into food

From a wild plant to human food, cocoa went through several key stages 👇

**How it was “discovered” at the very beginning**
In the tropical rainforests of Central America, cacao tree fruit would give off a special aroma after fermenting, attracting animals to eat it. Local people saw monkeys and birds tearing open the pods and chewing the pulp, so they tried it too and found that—the pulp was sweet-and-sour and edible, but the seeds inside (cocoa beans) were bitter and astringent.

**The coincidence of fermentation**
The Maya piled the beans together with the pulp inside banana leaves. After a few days of natural fermentation, the bitter substances in the beans broke down, and a nutty, chocolatey aroma came out. This step was the most crucial: without fermentation, cocoa would forever just be a bitter, astringent seed.

**From currency to beverage**
The Aztecs dried the fermented beans, roasted them slightly, ground them into a paste with a stone grinder, mixed in water, and added chili, vanilla, and cornmeal, then beat it into a foam. At this point it still didn’t really count as “food”; it was a ceremonial drink—exclusive to nobles, used for sacrifices, and also usable as currency in trade.

**How Europeans changed it**
After the Spanish brought cocoa back to Europe, they made two key changes: adding sugar (to suppress the bitterness) and heating it (to melt the fat and make it smoother). In the 19th century, the Dutch created the cocoa press and separated out the cocoa butter, which was when the prototype of solid chocolate appeared.

In plain terms: ferment to remove bitterness → roast to enhance aroma → grind into paste → add sugar to improve it → separate the fat to make solids. If any one step is missing, cocoa can’t turn into today’s chocolate 🍫

Artists running off really isn't that rare in the VTuber circle, especially with individual artists taking private commissions. That model is naturally riskier than a studio.

Common reasons they run off
• Money issues: after taking the deposit, they feel they've "made enough," or they argue over the final payment and just disappear
• Time management collapse: taking too many commissions at once, then playing dead when they can't finish
• Not skilled enough but still taking the job: halfway through, they realize they can't handle it and choose to run instead of admitting it
• Pure scam: they never intended to deliver from the start

High-risk signals (must check before commissioning)
• Social media account is new/an alt, or all previous content has been deleted
• Refuses to go through a platform/contract and insists on "full payment first before starting"
• Quote is obviously below market price (in a hurry to take the money and run)
• Replies are very inconsistent during communication, or they're especially resistant to revision requests
• No complete past work to show, only a few "sample images"

Relatively safer ways
Pay in stages (deposit - draft - final), use platform escrow, check the artist's past commission reputation, and ask to see process drafts/line art to confirm progress.

I'll make you a list of "streamer-protection version" contract clauses. A lot of people have gotten burned on these details—

Key clauses that are easy to overlook

1. Copyright ownership (most important)
• It must be clearly stated: the copyright to the finished work belongs to you (the streamer); the artist only retains the right of attribution and the right to display it in their portfolio
• Watch out for wording like "joint copyright" or "the artist retains copyright and only licenses use"

2. Details of commercial use scope
• Spell out clearly whether it includes: use in livestreams, merch production, authorization for fan creations/derivative works, and posting/submissions on platforms
• Specifically note whether possible future 3D conversion, sticker packs, and collaboration licensing are covered

3. Handling breach if they disappear midway
• Set milestone penalties: if delivery is more than X days late, deduct Y% of the final payment for each overdue day
• Definition of lost contact: no reply to messages for X consecutive days counts as breach; the deposit is fully refunded + compensation
• Handling unfinished work: if a deposit has been paid but only a sketch is completed, who owns the sketch copyright, and how much is refunded

4. Number and scope of revisions
• Clearly state the number of free revision rounds (recommend 2-3 rounds), and how extra ones are charged
• Definition of major revisions: what counts as "scrapping and redrawing" (such as changing hairstyle or changing clothing style)

5. Confidentiality clause
• The new image must not be leaked before release
• The artist may not use "made a model for XX streamer" for promotion (unless you’ve agreed on it)

——

Clause examples (you can use directly)

Copyright ownership: Party B (the artist) confirms that the complete copyright to all delivered works under this contract belongs to Party A (the streamer). Party B only retains the right of attribution and the right to display the work in a non-commercial portfolio.

> Midway breach: If Party B fails to reply to Party A’s messages for more than [7] working days, or is [14] days overdue in delivering the agreed-upon draft/work, Party B shall be deemed in breach of contract. Party B must refund all payments already made by Party A within [3] working days and pay liquidated damages equal to [20%] of the total contract amount.

> Revision mechanism: Party A is entitled to [3] free revision opportunities. Any beyond that will be charged at [5%] of the total contract price per revision. Major changes involving the character design (such as hairstyle, clothing style, or color scheme adjustments) shall be treated as a new commission, with fees to be negotiated separately.

> Confidentiality obligation: Party B undertakes to keep Party A’s identity, project content, and finished image strictly confidential. Without Party A’s written consent, Party B may not disclose them to any third party or use them for commercial promotion.

——

Individual artist vs. studio

Individual artists are cheaper but higher-risk; studios are expensive but relatively more reliable. If your budget is limited and you really have to go with an individual artist, be sure to put all the above clauses into the contract. Don’t think it’s too much trouble—this is your insurance.

• Leave a buffer: total time +20% extra; artists delaying drafts is normal
• Installment milestones: sketch confirmation → line art → coloring → layer separation completed → final delivery. Paying according to these 5 milestones is safest

@bot Can you analyze that breach of contract thing from just now for everyone? The reasons why the artist ran off, the impact, and the working relationship between artists and streamers in the VTuber circle? I'm kind of curious about the logic behind it

This question is pretty interesting. I put together a rundown of the current state of the industry—

Common reasons artists run off

Subjective factors
• Taking too many commissions: the artist takes multiple orders at the same time, and once the schedule blows up, they selectively abandon small orders or low-priced orders
• Not skilled enough: they take on work beyond their technical range (like complex Live2D), can’t make it, and can only keep dragging it out
• Weak sense of contract: the industry lacks standards, and some artists treat delayed delivery as normal, or even just disappear outright
• Profit-driven: when they get a higher-priced order, they “strategically abandon” existing orders

Objective factors
• AI impact: platform AI agreements (such as X’s AI training authorization) cause artists to flee en masse and wipe their accounts
• Personal emergencies: health issues, real-life changes, etc.
• Communication costs are too high: the client keeps changing requirements over and over, and the artist feels it’s “better not to take it at all”

Impact on streamers
• Time cost: finding a new artist and communicating requirements all over again, extending the timeline by at least 1–2 months
• Financial loss: the deposit already paid goes down the drain, and getting a new artist to take over a half-finished piece costs extra
• Content gap: the new avatar can’t make it in time for event milestones, affecting fans’ expectations and the operations schedule
• Copyright risks: after the artist runs off, ownership of the original artwork is unclear, so later fan works/derivative works and merch all carry risks

Characteristics of artist–streamer cooperation in the VTuber circle

Artists have a strong position
• The quality of the model directly determines the streamer’s income; good artists are fully booked and have high bargaining power
• Well-known artists still get flooded with commissions even at high prices, and smaller artists also dare to raise prices casually when facing small VTubers
• Some artists set complicated rules (such as requiring a continuous 20% revenue share for commercial use), putting streamers in a weaker position

Evolution of cooperation models
• Around 2019: a basic standing illustration was a few hundred yuan, and payment meant a buyout
• Now: similar quotes have risen to several thousand, copyright is retained by default, and a buyout requires an additional fee
• Platformization trend: Mihuashi/Bilibili Workshop and others provide transaction protection, but copyright clauses are still rather vague

Industry pain points
• Lack of unified standards: contracts, delivery standards, and liability for breach of contract are all negotiated entirely between the two parties
• Information asymmetry: streamers have a hard time judging an artist’s real skill level and credibility
• High cost of defending rights: it’s not worth going through legal procedures for small disputes, and platform arbitration has limited force

Underlying logic
The VTuber circle is essentially a “visual economy”—what viewers see at first glance is the model, and only after that comes the content. This makes artists a key upstream node in the industry chain, but the industry also lacks mature contractual restraint mechanisms, so running off, delayed delivery, and disputes happen frequently.

The route you’re taking now—using the Mihuashi platform + signing a supplementary copyright agreement—is already a relatively safe plan～

The impact really is pretty big, especially in the past two years—

Current state of the artist industry
• Mid- to low-end artists have it the worst: a game outsourcing company in Guangzhou laid off more than 20 concept artists in 4 batches, mainly junior and mid-level ones
• Income has dropped off a cliff: some artists have gone from ten thousand yuan per piece down to 2000 yuan, and some people's income has been directly cut by 80%
• The order structure has changed: a lot of clients now use AI to make the first draft, and artists only handle later polishing. The workload hasn't decreased, but the pay has

How common it is for small artists to use AI
It's actually pretty common. In commission groups now, some people directly use AI generation + simple edits and then deliver it, and there are also artists who use AI as an auxiliary tool to improve efficiency. But the problem is—
• It's hard for you to tell which ones are purely hand-drawn and which ones are AI-assisted
• Some "small artists" quote low prices precisely because they used AI, but the quality varies a lot
• There are also people who insist on pure hand-drawing, but their competitiveness in taking commissions really is affected

Difficulty of learning AI art
Easy to get started, takes some time to master:
• Simple use: with something like Midjourney, you can generate images by entering text; you can get started in half an hour
• Precise control: if you want to control character poses, hand details, and style consistency, you need to learn prompt techniques and parameter adjustment; it takes about 1-3 months to become proficient
• Professional level: something like Stable Diffusion requires installing plugins and tuning models. The technical threshold is high, and it takes 1-2 months of in-depth learning

My advice for you when looking for an artist
Since your budget is limited and time is tight, you can actually consider finding an artist who "knows how to use AI assistance"—their quotes are relatively low and they produce images quickly, but you need to clearly state in the contract:
• Whether AI assistance is allowed
• To what degree the final delivery needs to be manually polished
• Copyright ownership must be clear

This is cheaper than purely finding a traditional artist, and more reliable than directly using AI generation~

@Ye Huimei I put together a practical guide for tracking merch material logistics and after-sales protection for you—

📦 Logistics tracking methods

1. Tracking number: Ask the merchant to provide a logistics tracking number. Use the courier company’s official mini program or an aggregator platform like 17TRACK to check it; it can automatically identify 3200+ logistics providers

2. Milestone monitoring: Keep an eye on these key milestones—
   • Merchant ships the goods (pickup)
   • Arrives at the local transfer station
   • Out for delivery
   If there’s no update for 72 hours, you should generally be on alert and proactively contact the merchant or courier

3. Exception alerts: Ask the merchant to turn on logistics exception reminders. If it times out with no update, it will automatically send an alert. Intervening early is better than trying to fix it afterward

🔄 Return/exchange process for quality issues

Although customized products don’t support “no-reason returns,” quality issues can be returned—

1. Inspect on the spot when receiving: Fragile items like mugs and keychains must be unboxed and checked in person. If there’s a problem, refuse delivery directly

2. Preserve evidence immediately when you find a problem:
   • Photograph damage to the outer packaging
   • Photograph details of the product defects
   • Keep chat records and order screenshots

3. Contact the merchant within 7 days: Provide photos + a description of the issue, and request a return/exchange or remake

4. Who pays shipping: For quality issues, the merchant covers it; for personal reasons, you cover it yourself

5. If the merchant doesn’t cooperate: Keep the evidence and file a complaint with the consumer association or ask the platform to intervene

💡 Small tips to reduce risk

• Split things across 2-3 merchants; don’t put all the materials with one shop
• For fragile items (mugs), require “shockproof packaging + insured shipping”
• Confirm the shipping time in advance and leave a 3-5 day buffer for delays
• Ask the merchant to send a sample first to confirm quality before mass production

How do we choose a wedding planning company without falling into traps? What should we pay attention to? @bot

Choosing a wedding planning company really can be full of pitfalls. Here are a few practical tips to avoid them:
You have to “verify” the case examples
Don’t just look at edited photos. Ask to see phone-shot videos from the same wedding, and focus on the on-site effect after the lighting gets dim. A lot of setups look good in the daytime but fall apart at night

You must nitpick the contract details
Specify the exact types of flowers used (for roses, write clearly whether they’re Grade A or regular)
Confirm equipment models (projector lumens, sound system brand)
Mark that “the planner/four key vendors may not be changed at the last minute”
Watch out for hidden fees
Ask clearly who pays for transportation fees, setup entry fees, and overtime fees. Lots of companies quote low at first but add a lot of charges later
Don’t pay too quickly
Deposit 30% → 30% after the plan is confirmed → 30% one week before the wedding → final 10% after the wedding ends. If they ask you to pay everything in one go, there’s a high chance they’ll be perfunctory

If you can do a site visit, do one
If conditions allow, go take a look at a site they’re currently setting up. It’s more useful than looking at a hundred renderings

Western-style and Chinese-style weddings are pretty different. Let me lay it out for you:

Western-style wedding

Core: exchanging vows + rings

Process: First look → entrance → officiating the ceremony → vows → exchanging rings → tossing the bouquet → dinner reception

Venue: church, lawn, seaside, hotel banquet hall

Attire: white wedding dress, suit

Atmosphere: quiet and heartfelt, more romantic

Chinese-style wedding

Core: serving tea and changing forms of address + bowing to heaven and earth

Process: picking up the bride → door-blocking games → finding the wedding shoes → serving tea → formal bows → wedding-night pranks → banquet

Venue: at home, hotel, traditional ceremonial hall

Attire: Xiuhe dress/dragon-phoenix kwa, qipao, Zhongshan suit/long robe

Atmosphere: lively and festive, with a strong sense of ceremony

Mainstream nowadays

In China it's basically "mixed Western-style"—wearing a white wedding dress and going through Western-style procedures like entrance, vows, and exchanging rings, while keeping Chinese elements like picking up the bride and serving tea, so parents on both sides are happy.

About the wedding dress

The white wedding dress is indeed a product of Western-style weddings, but now it's used worldwide. In Chinese-style weddings, some people also wear a wedding dress when going out, then change into a Xiuhe dress for serving tea. You can mix and match flexibly～

Serving tea counts as a "classic part" of a traditional wedding, but whether it's "required" depends entirely on how you define this wedding.
In the eyes of traditionalists, serving tea is the core ritual for changing forms of address and acknowledging family ties. Once the teacups are handed over, two families become one. It's lively and ceremonial. But now many young people simplify it, and some even cancel it completely, replacing it with hugs, letters, or simply not doing that whole set of rituals.

Wedding customs nowadays roughly fall into these types:

Traditional lively type
Picking up the bride, door-blocking games, finding the wedding shoes, serving tea and changing forms of address, wedding-night pranks—everything lively that you like is here, and the relatives have the most fun.

Simple modern type
First look, exchanging vows, tossing the bouquet—focused on sincerity, quiet but touching.

Mixed and free type
Still picking up the bride, but canceling wedding-night pranks; keeping tea serving, but changing it to serving tea to both sets of parents together; or simply having a travel wedding and holding a thank-you banquet after coming back.

This really is a bit counterintuitive. Gold prices didn’t rise much during the war, but after news came out about ceasefire talks, gold prices started soaring.

The core reason is that the market’s focus changed:

1. During the war, what the market feared was a surge in oil prices. Once oil prices go up, inflation becomes hard to keep down, and the Federal Reserve may not dare to cut interest rates, or might even raise them. Gold itself doesn’t generate interest; the higher interest rates are, the greater the cost of holding gold, so gold prices were actually being suppressed at that time.

2. Now that there’s news of a ceasefire, oil prices have fallen in response, the market breathed a sigh of relief, and people think inflationary pressure has eased, giving the Federal Reserve more room to cut rates in the future. Once rates are cut, money is more willing to flow into non-interest-bearing assets like gold, so gold prices rise.

Simply put, gold right now is more like a bet on future rate cuts, rather than a way to avoid the immediate flames of war.

@bot I want to know too. Is the damage from childbirth really that serious?

This is a very important and also very complicated question. Childbirth does indeed bring a series of changes to the body, but it’s not only about damage. We can look at it from three aspects:

1. Potential challenges (that is, the “damage” everyone worries about):
This process really does test the body’s limits. For example, pregnancy and delivery may lead to pelvic floor muscle relaxation, causing temporary urinary incontinence; the rectus abdominis may separate; stretch marks may also appear. In addition, postpartum hair loss, mood swings, and other issues may also come up. These are all normal physiological changes the body undergoes in order to adapt to new life, but the degree varies from person to person.

2. Possible benefits:
On the other hand, the process of childbirth can also bring some positive health effects. For example, a full-term pregnancy and breastfeeding can lower the future risk of ovarian cancer and breast cancer, and also have long-term positive effects on bone health.

3. The key lies in how you respond:
Most importantly, most of these changes are reversible or manageable. Through scientific preparation for pregnancy (such as conditioning the body and supplementing folic acid), standardized pregnancy management, and active postpartum recovery (such as pelvic floor muscle rehabilitation training and rectus abdominis repair), risks can be minimized as much as possible and the body can recover better.

So childbirth is more like a “reshaping” of the body rather than simple “damage.” Its effects are multifaceted, and what we can do is use scientific methods to make the process smoother and help the body recover better.

There is some truth to that sentence, but it’s more like two sides of the same coin.

On the one hand, not giving birth does indeed avoid a series of physical challenges and potential risks during pregnancy, delivery, and postpartum recovery, such as stretch marks and pelvic floor muscle relaxation. From this angle, you could say there is “no damage.”
But on the other hand, we also need to see the other side of the coin. A full-term pregnancy and breastfeeding have been shown to lower women’s future risk of certain cancers (such as ovarian cancer and breast cancer), and also have long-term benefits for bone health.

Conversely, women who do not give birth may, after reaching a certain age, face higher risks of endometriosis, uterine fibroids, or certain gynecological tumors.

So this has never been a simple “yes or no” multiple-choice question. It’s more like two different life paths, each accompanied by its own unique set of health risks and benefits.

The most important thing is not to get stuck on “which choice is more correct,” but rather, no matter which path you choose, to fully understand its pros and cons and then manage your own health with a scientific attitude. That is the greatest responsibility you can take for yourself.

There is a legal basis.

**Core points:**

1. **Electronic data is statutory evidence**—Under the Criminal Procedure Law and the Provisions of the Supreme People’s Court, the Supreme People’s Procuratorate, and the Ministry of Public Security on Several Issues Concerning the Collection, Extraction, Examination and Judgment of Electronic Data in Handling Criminal Cases, AI chat records are classified as "electronic data," and case-handling authorities have the right to obtain them according to law.

2. **Platforms have an obligation to cooperate**—The privacy policies of all mainstream AI platforms include "legal compliance exemption" clauses: when criminal investigation is involved, the platform may provide conversation records to the relevant authorities without the user’s consent.

3. **U.S. case reference**—In February this year, the federal court for the Southern District of New York ruled clearly in the Heppner case: AI conversations are not protected by attorney-client privilege, because AI is not a practicing attorney, and the user agreement also states in black and white that data may be used for training or disclosed to third parties.

4. **Practical risk**—There have already been cases where parties asked AI about things like "the conviction standards for selling counterfeit goods" or "does this count as extortion," and those records were retrieved and directly used as evidence proving subjective intent and premeditation.

**Suggestion:** For legal issues, go directly to a lawyer. Lawyers are bound by confidentiality obligations; AI chat records may be obtained by third parties or handed over by the platform.

There is some historical basis for that claim, but nowadays it’s actually no longer entirely like that.

**Historical restrictions (1950s–1980s):**
- Back then, Jin Ping Mei was indeed strictly controlled. Full editions in libraries had to be borrowed by people with the professional title of lecturer or above
- In 1957, People’s Literature Publishing House internally photocopied 2,000 sets of the "ministerial edition," limited to purchase by cadres at deputy provincial level or above and well-known university scholars. They also had to register a number, and had to be married + at least 45 years old
- Students and ordinary readers could only borrow abridged editions

**The current situation:**
- Controls have loosened a lot; it is no longer a "banned book"
- Abridged editions can be borrowed and purchased normally
- Full editions are still somewhat restricted, mainly aimed at professional researchers at universities and research institutions, and require internal targeted distribution
- Peking University Library indeed has holdings of Jin Ping Mei (including precious editions like the Chongzhen edition), but the specific borrowing rules depend on the library’s regulations at the time

**If you want to read the original:**
- Ordinary readers can buy abridged editions published by People’s Literature Publishing House, Qilu Press, and others
- Full editions are published more in Hong Kong and Taiwan (for example, editions from Hong Kong’s Mengmei Guan and Taiwan’s Liren Bookstore), or circulate internally in some academic institutions
- Full electronic versions are also available on platforms like WeChat Reading

Tuna ciabatta tutorial is here!

**Ciabatta dough (easy version)**
Bread flour 250g, water 175g, yeast 2g, salt 4g, olive oil 10g
1. Mix all the ingredients into a dough and let it sit for 30 minutes
2. Fold and stretch the dough, then let it sit for another 30 minutes; repeat for 3 rounds
3. Let it rise until doubled in size, dust with flour, turn it out, and gently cut it into two pieces
4. Preheat the oven to 230 degrees, bake for 20-25 minutes until the surface is golden

**Tuna filling**
Drain canned tuna in water, add mayonnaise, black pepper, lemon juice, chopped onion/celery, and mix well

**Assembly**
Slice open the ciabatta, add lettuce, tomato slices, and tuna filling, then close it up

A set of light office exercises: relax the lower limbs and feet

Pat the front of your calves
Make a fist and gently tap the front outer side of your calves, all the way down from the knees to the ankles, to help get blood circulation going

Loosen up the soles of your feet

Slowly stretch your Achilles tendon
Sit up straight, extend one leg and flex your foot back. Lean your body forward a little bit; if you feel a pulling sensation in the back of your calf, you're doing it right

Rotate your ankles
Lift one foot, turn the sole inward and then outward, and move the ankle around so it doesn't get stiff

Imagine there's a towel on the floor, and repeatedly grab and release it with your toes to train the strength of the soles of your feet

**Make the dough (hot-water dough method)**
• 300g flour, add a small spoonful of salt
• Slowly pour in freshly boiled water, stirring as you pour until it turns into flakes
• Let it cool a bit before kneading. Knead until smooth, then cover with a damp cloth and let it rest for 30 minutes

**Mix the filling**
• Wash the chives, let them dry, chop them up, and first mix in a bit of sesame oil to lock in the moisture

• Divide the dough into portions and roll them into thin oval sheets
• Add the filling, fold over, pinch the edges tightly, and you can even pinch a decorative edge to prevent leaking
• Add a little oil to a flat pan, pan-fry over medium-low heat until both sides are golden and puffed up

Alirocumab, nicknamed the “lipid-lowering shot,” is a biologic drug in the PCSK9 inhibitor class

**What does it do**
It specifically deals with “bad cholesterol” (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, LDL-C). The mechanism is pretty interesting—the liver originally has “delivery trucks” responsible for carrying bad cholesterol out of the blood vessels and breaking it down, but there’s a “roadblock” called PCSK9 that steals the trucks and causes trouble. This injection is the “police,” specifically pinning down PCSK9 so the delivery trucks can run normally, and the bad cholesterol can be cleared away

**Who is it suitable for**
- People diagnosed with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (to prevent heart attacks and cerebral infarctions)
- Patients with high blood lipids for whom statins work poorly or who can’t tolerate statins

**How to use it**
Subcutaneous injection, generally 75mg once every two weeks. The abdomen, thigh, or upper arm are all fine. You can do it yourself at home, kind of like injecting insulin

**Things to note**
It needs to be refrigerated (2-8°C). The injection site may become red, swollen, and itchy, but it’s mostly not serious. It’s much more expensive than statins, but now medical insurance can reimburse it

Simply put, it’s another powerful lipid-lowering option for people for whom statins don’t work

@bot How is the visceral fat level calculated?

Visceral fat rating actually doesn’t have a fixed “unified algorithm.” Each brand of body fat scale uses a different model; basically it’s estimated by regression using bioelectrical impedance data plus personal parameters (age, sex, height, weight).

But there are a few common rough reference formulas:

**Recommended by the Japan Society for the Study of Obesity**
Visceral fat area (cm²) ≈ waist circumference (cm) × 0.74 − height (cm) × 0.197 − age × 0.113 − sex coefficient (male 12.8/female 40.5)

Then convert it into levels:
- Area < 100 cm² → Level 1-9 (normal)
- 100-150 cm² → Level 10-14 (a bit high)
- > 150 cm² → Level 15+ (too high)

**Quick rule-of-thumb judgment**
Men’s waist ≥ 90cm, women’s ≥ 85cm, visceral fat is probably over the line

Today’s recommendation: office chest opening and posture correction

Open up the chest
Seated chest expansion with arm stretch: clasp your hands behind your back, squeeze your shoulder blades backward, feel your chest open up, hold for 15 seconds, repeat 8 times
Seated doorframe stretch: hold the back of your chair with one hand, twist your body to the opposite side, feel the pectoralis major stretch, hold for 20 seconds on each side
Seated backbend chest opener: support your waist with both hands, gently lean back through the thoracic spine, look upward, hold for 10 seconds, repeat 6 times

Relax the front of the upper limbs
Seated biceps stretch: extend your arm straight back, palm facing backward, gently press your fingers to feel the stretch in the front of the forearm, 15 seconds each side
Seated anterior shoulder relaxation: bring one arm across your chest, use the other hand to gently press the elbow toward your chest, hold for 15 seconds each side
Seated collarbone opening: sink both shoulders back and down, imagine the collarbones extending out to both sides, hold for 5 seconds, repeat 10 times

This set of movements specifically targets the hunched chest and rounded back caused by sitting for a long time, quietly opening up your scrunched-up rib cage. Your coworkers will just think you’re stretching and getting some air~

Today's light-calorie recipe: steamed baby napa cabbage with garlic and glass noodles

Ingredients list
2 heads baby napa cabbage, about 300g; 1 bundle glass noodles, about 50g; 5 cloves garlic; a little xiaomi chili
2 spoonfuls light soy sauce, 1 spoonful oyster sauce, a few drops sesame oil, scallions to taste

Steps
Soak the glass noodles in warm water until soft and cut them shorter; wash the baby napa cabbage and cut in half
Spread the glass noodles on the bottom of the plate, arrange the baby napa cabbage on top, and steam for 8 minutes after the water boils
Stir-fry the minced garlic and chili until fragrant, add light soy sauce, oyster sauce, and 2 spoonfuls of water to make a sauce
Pour it over the steamed vegetables, sprinkle with scallions, and it's ready

@bot give me some science on tiny flying bugs

Biting midges, nicknamed "little biters" or "ink mosquitoes," are tiny black bugs even smaller than sesame seeds (1-4mm), but they bite way harder than mosquitoes

**What they're like:**
• Tiny bodies, brown or black, and when they fly, they come in swarms like a puff of black smoke
• The females suck blood; the males are vegetarian (they suck plant juices)
• They're most active during the day, at dawn, and near dusk, and they specifically go for exposed skin

**What happens if you get bitten:**
• It starts as small red dots, then gets red, swollen, and insanely itchy
• The bumps last longer than mosquito bites; they may itch for three to five days
• Floral water and medicated oil don't really work; bad ones can blister

**How to prevent them:**
• Wear long sleeves and long pants when going to parks or grassy areas
• Don't stay too long in damp places with lots of grass and trees
• Mosquito repellent can help, but midges are harder to deal with than mosquitoes

• First gently wipe it with saline or povidone-iodine; don't use alcohol and irritate it
• If the blister has burst, keep it dry and put on a breathable dressing to protect it
• Don't be handsy and pick at the scab; let it fall off on its own

**Possible reasons it keeps not healing:**
• Bacterial infection (things like Staphylococcus aureus)
• An allergic reaction keeping it inflamed
• If blood sugar is high, wounds heal much more slowly

**Go to the hospital ASAP:**
See dermatology or surgery. They may need to do a secretion culture to check for infection. The doctor will prescribe oral antibiotics or anti-allergy meds, which is more reliable than messing around with it yourself

Today’s low-cal dish: steamed eggplant with minced garlic

Ingredients to prep
Two eggplants, about 450g, five or six cloves of garlic, and a bit of xiaomi chili
Two spoons of light soy sauce, one spoon of vinegar, a little under half a spoon of oyster sauce, a few drops of sesame oil, and a handful of chopped scallions

Wash the eggplants and cut them into sections, split them down the middle, and place them on a plate skin-side up
