Tear the steamed eggplant into strips, pour the sauce over it, sprinkle on scallions, and mix

This dish isn’t deep-fried; the steamed eggplant gets coated in sauce and goes especially well with rice. Done in ten minutes 🍆

1 zucchini, about 300g; half a carrot; 1 spoon minced garlic
1 spoon light soy sauce, 1 spoon black vinegar, half a spoon oyster sauce, a little sesame oil, white sesame seeds to taste

Today's recommendation: invisible office joint care — a flexible wake-up for people who sit for long periods

Calf activation
Seated heel raises: place both feet flat on the floor, push up hard onto the balls of your feet, feel the back of your calves tighten, hold for 2 seconds, then slowly lower. 15 reps per set, 3 sets, to promote blood return from the lower limbs

Torso mobility
Seated chair twist: sit up straight, slowly twist your upper body to one side, hold the chair back with both hands to deepen the range, hold for 15 seconds, then switch sides. Do 3 times on each side to release pressure on the lumbar spine

Neck relief
Neck side stretch: sit up straight, gently pull your head toward your left shoulder with your left hand, feel the stretch on the right side of your neck, hold for 15 seconds, then switch sides. Do 3 times on each side to relieve stiffness from sitting too long

Joint lubrication
Wrist circles: stretch both arms forward, make fists with both hands, and rotate clockwise and counterclockwise 10 times each to relax the wrist joints
Ankle circles: sit up straight, lift one foot, and rotate around the ankle clockwise and counterclockwise 10 times each, then switch sides and repeat

These movements are small and not obvious, perfect for doing at your workstation anytime. Your coworkers will just think you're adjusting your sitting posture~

Today’s low-cal meal: cold tossed shredded tofu skin

Ingredient list
200g Qianzhang tofu skin, half a cucumber, half a carrot
1 spoon minced garlic, a little bird’s eye chili
1 spoon light soy sauce, 1 spoon rice vinegar, half a spoon oyster sauce, a little sesame oil, cilantro to taste

Method
Cut the tofu skin into thin shreds, blanch in boiling water for 1 minute, take out, rinse under cold water, and drain
Shred the cucumber and carrot and set aside
Mix the minced garlic, bird’s eye chili, light soy sauce, rice vinegar, and oyster sauce into a dressing
Put the shredded tofu skin and vegetable shreds in a big bowl, pour on the dressing and toss well, sprinkle with cilantro, done

Calorie reference
The whole portion is about 120 kcal, high-protein and low-fat
Tofu skin is rich in soy protein and calcium, and is very filling
It has a firm, chewy texture; you can eat it on its own for dinner or pair it with a small half-bowl of rice

You can get it done in five minutes. The chewiness of the tofu shreds with the refreshing cucumber makes it appetizing and filling for summer 🥢

Today’s recommendation: workstation "micro-fitness"—health gains from spare moments

Key conclusion
A new finding in the British Journal of Sports Medicine: 3-4 minutes of "vigorous micro-exercise" every day lowers the risk of cardiovascular problems by 45%
Short, high-frequency exercise can trigger an "afterburn effect," so your body keeps burning calories even after you stop

Small desk moves
Seated calf raises: place both feet flat on the floor, push up onto your toes and hold for 2 seconds, do 15 reps; helps blood flow back from the legs
Paper squeeze between knees: clamp a book or sheets of paper between your inner thighs, hold for 5-10 seconds, do 2-3 sets; wakes up the adductors
Ankle pumps: flex toes up → point toes down counts as 1 rep, go back and forth 10 times; lubricates the ankle joints

Neck and shoulder relaxation
Shoulder-blade squeeze: open both arms, clasp your hands behind your head, draw your shoulder blades toward your spine, hold for 1 second, do 10 reps
Side neck stretch: tilt your head to one side and feel the pull in your neck, 30 seconds each side
Chin tucks: look straight ahead, slowly glide your chin backward to improve forward head posture, do 8-10 reps

Work it into daily life
Every time you’ve sat for 45 minutes and get up to get water, do 10 calf raises while you’re at it
After finishing a Pomodoro timer, do one set of shoulder and neck circles
When taking a phone call, stand up and stroll around or do a wall sit

These movements are small and low-key; if others see them, they’ll just think you’re loosening up～

Today’s low-calorie recipe: steamed baby Chinese cabbage with garlic

Ingredients list

Today's low-cal recipe: blanched broccoli with shrimp

Ingredients list
Broccoli 200g, fresh shrimp 100g, a little shredded ginger
1 spoon minced garlic, 2 spoons light soy sauce, a few drops sesame oil

Steps
Break the broccoli into small florets, soak in salt water for 10 minutes, then rinse clean
Remove the veins from the shrimp, and marinate with cooking wine and shredded ginger for 5 minutes to remove the fishy smell
Bring water to a boil, add a little salt and oil, blanch the broccoli for 2 minutes, take it out and arrange on a plate
Blanch the shrimp until they change color and curl up, then take them out and place them on top of the broccoli
Mix minced garlic with light soy sauce and a small amount of water to make a plain blanching sauce, pour it over, and that's it

Photorejuvenation (IPL)

• Principle: selective photothermal effect
• Suitable for: isolated spots with clear borders

Tang-bao, here’s the skin-type explainer for your training👇

Normal skin
Sebum production is balanced, the stratum corneum’s water content is around 20%, and the pH is 5.0–5.6. Pores are fine, texture is even, skin tone is uniform, and it has strong tolerance to external irritation. It’s the ideal skin condition, and only basic moisturizing and sun protection are needed to maintain it.

Dry skin
Sebum production is insufficient, transepidermal water loss (TEWL) is high, and the stratum corneum’s water content is <10%. It shows as tightness, flaking, obvious fine lines, and small pores but a lack of radiance. It can be divided into dehydrated type (damaged barrier) and oil-deficient type (sebaceous gland atrophy); it needs strengthened occlusive moisturizing and barrier repair.

Oily skin
Sebaceous glands are active and sebum production is excessive, especially in the T-zone. Pores are enlarged, texture is rough, and it’s prone to comedones and acne, but it has strong resistance to aging. Causes involve androgen levels, genetics, and environmental factors. The core of care is oil control + moderate moisturizing, while avoiding over-cleansing that leads to compensatory oil production from the barrier.

Combination skin
The face shows two-zone characteristics: the T-zone is oily (large pores, lots of oil), while the U-zone is normal or dry. Combination-dry types have obvious tightness on the cheeks, while combination-oily types are generally oilier overall but to varying degrees. It requires zoned care: oil control for the T-zone, moisturizing for the U-zone, or using a product with a moderate texture over the whole face.

Sensitive skin
This is not an independent skin type, but a highly reactive skin state. The barrier function is weak, neurovascular reactivity is increased, and it is easily stimulated by the outside world, causing burning, stinging, and redness. It can be divided into congenital type (genetic) and acquired type (over-skincare/environmental damage). Care needs to streamline steps, avoid fragrance and alcohol, and make barrier repair the top priority.

Key reminder: skin type changes with age, season, and region, so dynamic assessment is more important than static classification.

Acne types each ointment is suited for

Ointment  Suitable acne  Mechanism of action

Adapalene gel  Closed comedones + mild inflammatory acne  A retinoid; unclogs pores and regulates keratinization

Key points for building tolerance with oily sensitive skin

Adapalene (the most commonly used, but also the most irritating)
• Weeks 1–2: use once every other day; only apply on pimples and avoid healthy skin
• Weeks 3–4: use once a day; observe whether there is peeling or redness
• How to use: at night after cleansing → wait 20 minutes until the face is completely dry → spot-apply → layer on repair cream afterward
• Sunscreen is a must! Retinoids make the skin photosensitive

Fusidic acid/erythromycin (relatively gentle)
• Can be spot-applied daily, but don’t use continuously for more than 2 weeks
• Using antibiotics for too long can cause drug resistance, so stop once it improves

Key points for choosing colored contacts for sensitive eyes
• Material: choose silicone hydrogel, with high oxygen permeability (Dk/t value > 80), so your eyes won’t feel as suffocated
• Replacement cycle: daily disposables are the most hygienic; sensitive eyes shouldn’t challenge yearly/monthly lenses

You won’t go blind immediately, but it’s very dangerous ⚠️
• Corneal hypoxia → red blood vessels, dryness, blurry vision
• Bacterial growth → risk of keratitis (serious cases can leave scars and affect vision)
• Protein deposits → foreign-body sensation, inflammation

Life-saving habits for sensitive eyes
• Wear them for at most 8 hours a day
• You must take them out before bed, even if you’re dead tired
• If your eyes are red/painful/tearing → stop wearing them immediately and use artificial tears

🔴 Red-line items you absolutely cannot touch

1. Three-noes injectable products
• Exosome injections — there are no approved products in China; all are illegal
• Stem cell filling / supernatant injections — not approved in the beauty field, low survival rate, and may form abnormal hyperplasia
• Fat-dissolving injections — no legal preparation in China; may damage the liver and cause depressions
• Whitening injections — interfere with coagulation function and may cause kidney damage

2. High-risk medical aesthetics procedures
• Thread rhinoplasty — the threads may penetrate the skin and cause vascular embolism leading to blindness
• Amazingel breast augmentation/filling — a toxic material that has already been banned
• Botulinum toxin products from non-standard channels — uncontrolled dosage can cause facial paralysis and difficulty breathing

3. Warning signs of three-noes skincare products
• No formal packaging, no ingredient list, no production batch number
• Exaggerated claims like “instant whitening” and “results in three days”
• “Secret-formula creams” privately mixed by beauty salons

🟢 Legitimate and safe choices

For skincare products, look for
• “Cosmetics registration number” or “medical device registration number” filing
• Complete ingredient list and traceable manufacturer
• Domestic cosmeceutical brands like Winona, Yuze, and Zhiben all have formal qualifications

For medical aesthetics procedures, look for the “three legits”
• Legitimate medical institution (with practice license)
• Legitimate physician (with medical practitioner certificate)
• Legitimate product (can be checked in the National Medical Products Administration filing system)

⚠️ Safety principles for streamlined skincare

1. For injectables, only recognize Class III medical device certificates (National Medical Device Registration XXX3)
2. Exosomes / stem cells are all off-limits, no matter how high-end the packaging is
3. Instant-effect products are always suspicious; there are no shortcuts to whitening and fading spots
4. During periods of barrier damage, only do basic care and stay away from all “advanced” procedures

Three core skincare misconceptions (key corrections)
1. Over-cleansing: the number one “skin-destroying culprit” in skincare
Wrong behaviors
Oily skin / oily-sensitive skin: using strong soap-based cleansers multiple times a day, frequently using facial cleansing devices, doing a second cleanse after removing makeup; thinking that the “drier your face feels after washing, the cleaner it is,” and repeatedly washing your face whenever you sweat or get oily.
The harm
During the seasonal transition in May, the skin barrier’s defenses weaken. Over-cleansing directly washes away the protective oils on the skin’s surface, damaging the stratum corneum and causing your skin to get oilier the more you wash, along with redness and stinging, tightness, and flaking. Oily-sensitive skin will fall into the vicious cycle of “oiliness — aggressive washing — barrier damage — even more oiliness.”
The right way
Cleanse once in the morning and once at night; even if you sweat a lot, just rinse the local areas with plain water;
Prioritize amino acid cleansers, wash your face with lukewarm water the whole time, and don’t let the water temperature be too high;
If you’re not wearing heavy makeup or high-SPF sunscreen, there’s no need for extra makeup removal, to avoid added irritation from makeup-removing products.
2. Blindly layering active products
Wrong behaviors
For whitening, anti-aging, and acne treatment, layering acids, retinol, high-concentration niacinamide, and potent serums all at the same time, piling them on layer after layer; blindly following internet-famous products without looking at your skin type before putting them on your face.
The harm
During seasonal changes, the skin’s tolerance drops. Stacking multiple strong active ingredients together will worsen skin irritation and trigger burning, redness, and acne breakouts. Sensitive skin and oily-sensitive skin can very easily develop into barrier damage.
The right way
Follow the principle of streamlined skincare; focus on just 1 function during the same period;
Build tolerance to active products gradually, starting with low concentrations and low frequency;
During sensitive periods, pause all potent actives and keep only the basic steps: cleansing + moisturizing + repair.
3. Exfoliating too often
Wrong behaviors
Feeling that your skin is rough, has closed comedones, or looks dull, so you use scrubs, glycolic/fruit acid masks, and cleansing masks on your whole face multiple times a week to exfoliate; oily-sensitive skin also doing deep cleansing frequently just because the T-zone gets oily.
The harm
The stratum corneum is the skin’s protective wall. Frequently stripping away keratin will make the barrier thoroughly thin, causing resistance to outside dust, temperature differences, and UV rays to drop sharply. In May, there is a lot of pollen and willow catkins, and the skin will become extremely prone to itching, redness, and stinging, with sensitivity issues recurring and becoming hard to repair.
The right way
Healthy oily skin: cleanse locally (T-zone only) once every 10~14 days;
Oily-sensitive skin, sensitive skin: avoid physical scrubs and strong cleansing throughout; let keratin metabolism happen naturally through gentle skincare;
Apply cleansing masks only as spot treatments on local areas—never apply a thick layer over the whole face, and don’t layer them with other products.

May seasonal-transition special: things to avoid + care basics for oily sensitive skin & sensitive skin
(1) General seasonal-transition avoid list
Refuse frequent skincare-product changes. Skin is unstable during seasonal transitions, so leave at least one week between switching old and new products.
Avoid products with high alcohol, fragrance, mineral oil, and strong preservatives to reduce sources of irritation.
Don’t leave masks on for too long (no more than 10 minutes each time). Using masks every day can over-hydrate the stratum corneum and worsen sensitivity and redness.
UV rays get stronger in May, so sunscreen cannot be skipped. Prioritize hybrid physical-chemical sunscreens or hard sun protection (hats, masks). Sensitive skin should avoid highly irritating sunscreen products.
(2) Oily sensitive skin (oiliness + redness / stinging) exclusive care
Skincare approach: refreshing hydration + barrier repair; don’t blindly do aggressive oil control. Oil control ≠ stripping dryness; an oil-water imbalance will worsen outer oiliness and inner dryness.
Pairing suggestion: amino-acid cleanser + soothing toner + repair serum (such as soothing special-care serum) + lightweight repair lotion. Refuse heavy creams that smother the skin.
Avoid: don’t use big soap-based cleansers or strong oil-blotting sheets to repeatedly wipe your face; they will stimulate the sebaceous glands to secrete oil like crazy.
(3) Sensitive skin (easily red, dry/itchy, intolerant) exclusive care
Skincare approach: ultra-simple repair + strong stabilization; give up all fancy steps.
Pairing suggestion: gentle cleanser + hydrating toner + repair serum + nourishing repair cream, using lipid ingredients to strengthen the barrier.
Avoid: strictly no acid exfoliation, exfoliating, or washing your face with alternating hot and cold water; when the day-night temperature difference is large, reduce direct wind blowing on your face to avoid hot-cold irritation worsening redness.

Correct approach Once in the morning and once at night; choose an amino acid cleanser; wash with lukewarm water; no need for extra makeup removal if you’re not wearing heavy makeup
2️⃣ Blindly layering active products
Dimension Content

Wrong behavior Using acids + retinol + high-concentration niacinamide + strong active serums all at the same time; blindly following influencer products without considering your skin type

Damage mechanism Lower tolerance during seasonal changes → multiple active ingredients irritating each other → burning, redness, breakouts → sensitive skin turns into a damaged skin barrier

Correct approach Focus on 1 active function during the same period; build tolerance gradually; during sensitive periods, keep only cleansing + moisturizing + repairing
3️⃣ Frequent exfoliation
Dimension Content

Wrong behavior Using scrubs/fruit-acid masks/cleansing masks to exfoliate the whole face multiple times a week; doing deep cleansing whenever the T-zone gets oily on oily-sensitive skin

Damage mechanism The stratum corneum is the protective wall → frequent stripping makes the barrier thinner → resistance to outside dust/temperature changes/UV rays drops sharply → sensitivity keeps recurring and is hard to repair

Correct approach For healthy oily skin, cleanse only the T-zone locally once every 10–14 days; oily-sensitive skin/sensitive skin should completely avoid physical scrubs; use cleansing masks only as spot applications

🌸 Sensitive Skin During Seasonal Changes · Dedicated Care

Will exfoliating wreck your face?
Yes. During seasonal changes, the stratum corneum of sensitive skin is already fragile, and exfoliating is basically tearing down the protective wall. Signs include: obvious redness/broken capillaries on the cheeks, redness as soon as the wind blows, skincare products stinging when applied, and no matter how much you hydrate, the moisture won’t stay locked in.

Correct approach for sensitive skin
• Avoid exfoliation completely; let keratin metabolism happen naturally through gentle skincare
• Skincare mindset: ultra-simple repair + strong stabilization
• Routine: gentle cleanser → hydrating toner → repairing serum → rich repairing cream
• Pitfalls to avoid: strictly no acid exfoliation, no alternating hot and cold water when washing your face, no long mask sessions (single use ≤10 minutes)

📋 Compliance Self-Check Points for Educational Content

I. Boundaries of wording (safe zone vs red lines)

Type ✅ Safe wording 🔴 Risky wording

Ingredient description "Contains XX ingredient; studies show it may help with..." "XX ingredient will definitely cure your acne"

Product review "My personal experience is..." "Some users have said..." "This product is the best/crushes all competitors"

Damage mechanism "Over-cleansing may lead to barrier damage, which can show up as..." "Over-cleansing will definitely ruin your face"

Effect promises "May help improve..." "Supports repair..." "Guaranteed results/cure it in seven days/repair it completely"

Core principle: use "may," "some," and "or help with" instead of absolute wording, and use "personal experience" to limit subjective reviews

II. Responding to doubts about professionalism

Tips for describing damage mechanisms:
• When citing public literature, note the source (such as the Chinese Journal of Dermatovenereology)
• For uncertain mechanisms, use "current research suggests..." rather than "it is because..."
• Simplify complex principles with analogies (e.g., "the stratum corneum is like a brick wall, and ceramides are the cement")
• Add one sentence at the end: "Specific situations vary from person to person; for serious issues, seek medical care"

Small actions to increase credibility:
• State verbally in the video, "The above information is compiled from publicly available dermatology literature"
• Put screenshots of references in the description/pinned comment
• For controversial topics (such as "vitamin C in the morning, retinol at night"), present multiple viewpoints

III. Defining responsibility for allergies

Legal level:
• You are doing "experience sharing," not "medical advice," so it is UGC content in nature
• But if you present yourself as an "expert" in the video, the responsibility increases

Three-piece self-protection set:
1. Prior statement: "The following content is only a sharing of personal skincare experience and does not constitute medical advice"
2. Process reminder: "When using a new product for the first time, it is recommended to do a behind-the-ear patch test first"
3. Afterward fallback: "If discomfort occurs, stop use immediately and consult a dermatologist"

IV. Disclaimer templates (can be used directly)

Spoken version (put within the first 5 seconds of the video):
"The following content is skincare experience sharing based on publicly available materials, for reference only, and does not constitute medical advice. Skincare product effects vary from person to person. Sensitive skin should do a local patch test first, and serious skin issues should be treated promptly by a doctor."

Text version (put in the description + at the end of the video):
【Disclaimer】The content of this video is only for reference as skincare knowledge education and cannot replace professional medical diagnosis. Any products mentioned are compiled from publicly available information and do not constitute purchase advice. Please carefully read the instructions and perform an allergy test before using skincare products. If discomfort occurs, stop use immediately and seek medical care.

V. Evidence retention suggestions

Preparation against complaints:
• Save PDFs/screenshots of all cited literature and webpages (with access time)
• When mentioning products, keep screenshots of the product’s official website/filing information
• If negative feedback appears in the comments section, reply promptly and recommend seeking medical care (keep screenshots)

If you do get complained about:
• Being able to provide information sources counts as "reasonable citation," not malicious rumor-mongering
• Promptly add a supplementary explanation in a pinned comment to show a responsible attitude

💡 Extra advice for streamers

1. Persona positioning: emphasize that you are a "seasoned enthusiast" rather than an "expert/doctor," so the boundaries of responsibility are clearer
2. Interaction wording: when fans ask "What should I do in my situation," reply "I recommend consulting a professional doctor; I can only share general experience"
3. Regular cleanup: check old videos every so often and take down highly controversial content

Today’s skincare tip: shelf life and storage after opening skincare products

Reading the PAO symbol

The number inside the little open-jar icon on the bottle = number of months it can be used after opening

Common ones are 12M, 6M, 3M. Don’t use it after it expires

If there’s no label, it’s recommended to use it up within 6 months

Storage key points

Store in a cool place away from light. Bathroom humidity speeds up spoilage

Use a spatula to take out serums and creams to avoid finger contamination

Shake sunscreen spray well before use; if it separates into layers, it’s no longer effective

Signs of spoilage

Change in smell, color separation, texture becoming thinner

Stop using immediately if flocculent matter appears or if oil and water separate

Expired products can easily trigger allergies for sensitive skin

"The Summer Charm of an Ancient Town"

Amid the chirping of cicadas, I stepped onto an old street paved with bluestone slabs. This was an unnamed ancient town in Jiangnan, without the clamor of Zhouzhuang or the bustle of Wuzhen, yet it hid the most authentic summer atmosphere.

The thin morning mist had not yet fully dispersed, but the river had already awakened. Several elderly women squatted on the stone steps washing clothes; as their wooden beaters rose and fell, splashes of water scattered fragments of sunlight. I strolled along the riverbank, watching black-awning boats glide slowly by. The boatman wore a bamboo hat and hummed in soft Wu dialect I could not understand. The white walls and black tiles on both banks were reflected in the water, broken apart by the oars and then slowly closing together again, like a flowing ink painting.

At noon, I ducked into an old teahouse. The ceiling fan creaked as it turned overhead, sending down waves of cool air. I ordered a pot of Longjing and a small plate of osmanthus cakes, watching the hurried passersby outside the window. The owner was a gray-haired old man. Seeing me curiously sizing up the old photos on the wall, he sat down and told me stories of the ancient town's past. He said this street had once been a wharf where merchants gathered, and now only memories remained, growing in the moss.

Dusk was the most beautiful moment. The setting sun dyed the river the color of honey, and the lanterns on the arched bridge lit up one after another. I sat on a bench by the river, watching children chase and play, watching couples lean close and whisper. The evening breeze carried moisture and the faint fragrance of lotus flowers, blowing away the heat of the day.

When I left, I bought an oil-paper umbrella. When I opened it, the canopy showed an elegant misty-rain Jiangnan scene. I thought that some places do not need to be photographed as keepsakes, because that peace and beauty have long since taken up residence in the heart.

Summer in the ancient town is a slow-tempo poem, one that makes people willing to read it again and again.

Dunhuang: A Dialogue of Civilizations in the Wind and Sand

Standing on top of Mingsha Mountain and looking down at Crescent Moon Spring, I suddenly understood what “eternity” means. This pool of spring water has lain embraced by sand dunes for a thousand years, its water level not falling but rising instead, like nature’s gentle response to human persistence.

The guide at the Mogao Caves was a girl wearing glasses. She said that the “Deer King Jataka” in Cave 257 had already told a story of good and evil receiving their due more than a thousand years before Disney. I looked up at the mottled colors on the mural and thought of Chen Yinke’s line: “Dunhuang is a sorrowful chapter in our nation’s academic history.” On those nights when the sutra scrolls were stolen away, did Taoist Wang also once stand under this same moonlight? The cruelty of history and the eternity of art are intertwined here, making it hard to say whether one feels more regret or deeper awe.

What shocked me most was the Bodhisattva of the High Tang in Cave 45. In that lowered gaze and faint smile, it seemed as if one could hear the melodious camel bells along the Silk Road. This statue has lived through war, plunder, and the erosion of wind and sand, yet it still retains the curve of compassion. I think perhaps true faith never needs incense offerings; it lives in every carved fold of clothing, beneath the peeling gold foil, and within the silence of a dark cave for more than a thousand years.

At dusk, I walked into the Dunhuang night market, where the smoky everyday bustle of lamb skewers strangely coexisted with Flying Apsara scarves in cultural-creative shops. An old man selling apricot peel water said that his grandfather’s generation had already been running a stall here: “Back then there were no tourists, only archaeological teams.” His tone was calm, but it suddenly made me realize: the distant places that our generation can easily reach are roads paved by those before us with their youth, and even their lives.

On the return flight, I reread Cultural Journey. Yu Qiuyu wrote, “To look at the Mogao Caves is not to look at a specimen that has been dead for a thousand years, but to look at a life that has been alive for a thousand years.” Indeed, the Flying Apsaras on those murals have never truly died—they are reborn in the patterns of cultural-creative products, carried on in the pixels of Digital Dunhuang, and continue dancing in the heartbeat of every person who looks up at them.

What Dunhuang taught me is perhaps a kind of “ruin aesthetics”: incompleteness is not the endpoint; forgetting is. When we are willing to stop amid the wind and sand, civilization will live forever.

Jian Jun is asking the key point:
1. Article 35 of the Civil Code: both parents are legal guardians. Major matters are, in principle, decided jointly, but one party may independently exercise decision-making for major day-to-day medical matters, and if the other party does not object, it is deemed consent
2. For outpatient assessment/routine treatment, it's fine for the mother to take him alone; this falls under day-to-day medical decision-making to protect a minor's interests
3. For psychiatric hospitalization, especially involuntary hospitalization, doctors need to determine that it meets Articles 30/31 of the Mental Health Law (serious harm to self or others), and the guardian must sign. In practice, most hospitals will accept the mother's signature on site
4. The father being away long-term is not a sticking point. As long as he does not explicitly object, the mother's decision has effect
5. In practical terms: registration + initial assessment + prescribing medication can be done by one person. If the doctor recommends hospitalization, she can sign on the spot and inform the father by phone afterward. If the father explicitly objects, then negotiate

For beginners buying a car in Chongqing, these are the must-have indicators for slopes + narrow-road parking—

Chassis clearance
• Sedan ground clearance ≥15cm, SUV ≥18cm, otherwise on those steep slopes around Jiefangbei and Hongyadong you’ll bottom out in no time

• Prioritize ones with hill-hold control (HHC), so you won’t roll back starting on those 45-degree slopes at Chongqing underground garage exits

Body size
• Keep the car length within 4.6 meters and width ≤1.85 meters. The parking spaces in old business districts like Guanyinqiao and Three Gorges Square are absurdly narrow

• A wheelbase around 2.7 meters is enough; too long makes U-turns difficult

Beginner-friendly features
• 360 panoramic camera is a must. In many old Chongqing residential compounds, there are only a few centimeters left for parallel parking

• Auto Hold (AUTOHOLD) + electronic parking brake, frees your right foot at red lights on slopes

• Front and rear parking sensors + blind spot monitoring, because the mountain city has lots of curves and e-bikes dart around

Power advice
• Torque is more important than horsepower; a 1.5T with strong low-end torque or a motor is more composed when starting off

• Choose a smooth transmission; dual-clutches tend to overheat and jerk on congested slopes

Pitfall reminders
• Don’t touch low-slung modified cars, Chongqing’s speed bumps are all raised versions

• Be cautious with rear-wheel drive; it’s easy to slip when starting on slopes in rainy weather

@bot Explain clearly the differences between low down payment / 0 down payment / balloon loans / finance leasing, and tell everyone plainly which ones you absolutely shouldn’t touch for your first car.

These types of loans are very different. First-time car buyers really need to keep their eyes open——

Low down payment (10-20%)
The down payment is a bit lower than usual, but the interest and monthly payments will increase accordingly. Suitable for people with tight cash flow but stable income. It’s not too much of a trap, but you have to calculate the total cost clearly.

0 down payment
On the surface you don’t have to pay money to pick up the car, but in reality all the costs are spread into the monthly payments + high interest. The total cost may be 20-30% more expensive than paying in full. And there are a bunch of extra conditions like insurance, GPS, and handling fees. Beginners are the easiest for salespeople to talk into this.

Balloon loan
Early monthly payments are extremely low (only paying interest or a small part of the principal), and at the end you pay a large final lump sum (for example 40-50% of the car price). It looks like the monthly payment pressure is low, but when the time comes, if you can’t produce the final payment, you’re screwed. If you refinance, you have to pay handling fees again.

Finance leasing
This isn’t buying a car at all, it’s renting a car! The car is registered under the finance company’s name; you only have the right to use it. After you finish paying, you still have to handle the transfer of ownership. If you breach the contract in the middle, the car gets towed away directly, and your down payment goes down the drain. A lot of “rent-to-own” schemes are exactly this.

For your first car, absolutely don’t touch:
🚫 0 down payment — interest is ridiculously high and the monthly payments crush you
🚫 Finance leasing / rent-to-own — the car isn’t yours, and you bear all the risk
🚫 Balloon loan — the final payment at the end is a time bomb

Relatively safe:
✓ Regular bank car loan, down payment starts at 30%, transparent interest rate
✓ Manufacturer interest-free policies (but read the handling fees clearly)

For a first car, if you can pay in full, pay in full. If you really need to borrow, choose bank installments, and don’t touch those fancy “financial innovations.”

@bot If you drive a hybrid by only refueling and never charging, will it damage the battery? What harm does long-term low battery do to the car?

Xu Qian, this question has to be split into two types of hybrids—

HEV (gas-electric hybrid, like Toyota Dual Engine, Honda hybrid):
It absolutely will not damage the battery! This type of car is designed to only refuel and not charge. The battery capacity is very small (1-3 kWh), and it recharges itself through brake energy recovery and engine generation. Not charging it long-term is the normal way to use it, so just drive it with peace of mind 😂

PHEV (plug-in hybrid, like BYD DM-i, Li Auto):
Not charging it long-term really can damage the battery, and there are a bunch of side effects—

1. Accelerated battery aging
Running at a low battery level for a long time (below 20%) may cause annual battery degradation to exceed 5% (normally about 2%), and health may fall below 70% in 3 years. Some carmakers also stipulate that not charging for half a year will void the lifetime battery warranty

2. Fuel consumption soars
In a depleted-battery state, the engine has to drive the vehicle and charge the battery at the same time. Fuel consumption is 30%-50% higher than when fully charged, and some models even use more fuel than gasoline cars in the same class

3. Power gets worse, noise gets louder
Acceleration response is 1-2 seconds slower, the engine roars like a tractor, and kinetic energy recovery efficiency also drops

4. Maintenance costs increase
Oil change intervals get shorter, brake pads wear faster, and you spend an extra 2000-3000 yuan per year on average

Suggestion:
• If you buy a PHEV, charge it at least once a week and keep the battery between 20%-80%

• If you really don’t have the conditions to charge, you’re better off buying an HEV gas-electric hybrid directly—less hassle and it holds its value better

CLTC vs WLTC: which is more realistic?

Standard  Features  Gap from reality

CLTC  Chinese standard, average speed 28km/h, frequent starts and stops  Inflated by 20%-30%; cut another 15% if you use A/C in summer

WLTC  International standard, average speed 47km/h, includes highway segments  Inflated by 10%-15%, relatively more reliable

The “real range” salespeople talk about
It’s actually just WLTC × 80%—for a car rated at 600km, they tell you “it can actually do 480,” making them seem honest. But that 480 still doesn’t include A/C, highways, or winter 😂

Low-battery / depleted-battery fuel consumption (plug-in hybrids only)
• When the battery is out, the engine has to both drive the wheels and generate electricity, so fuel consumption shoots up

• BYD DM-i is about 5L/100km when depleted; when fully charged it can be driven like an EV

• Long-term depleted driving = damages the battery + wastes fuel; you might as well buy a gas-electric hybrid directly

Do electric cars still need to worry about range now?
• Urban commuting: 500km of range is enough for two weeks, no anxiety at all

• Long highway trips: service area charging pile coverage is okay, but holiday queues really are annoying

• Winter / using A/C: 70% of range is the norm, so you need to have that in mind

One-sentence summary
For range, just calculate CLTC × 0.7; take the “real range” the salesperson claims and knock another 10% off. That’s basically the number you can actually drive

Tang Ke, judging from the diagram, this is a typical combination accident of "illegal merging + chain-reaction rear-end collision." Liability is generally determined like this—

Car ① (the party illegally merging)
• Primary liability or full liability

• Legal basis: changing lanes must not affect the normal driving of vehicles in the original lane (Article 44 of the Regulations for the Implementation of the Road Traffic Safety Law)

• It forced its way in, causing Car ② to brake suddenly, so it is the source of the accident

Car ③ (the rear-ending party)
• Secondary liability or no liability (depends on the specific circumstances)

• There is indeed an issue if it failed to maintain a safe distance

• But if Car ① cut in "suddenly" and Car ③ had no time to react, it may be exempt from liability

Car ② (the one caught in the middle)
• Usually not liable

• Being forced to brake suddenly is a normal emergency avoidance response

In actual handling, the traffic police will look at
• Whether Car ① had fully entered the lane when changing lanes (the diagram shows it was "partially over the line," indicating the lane change was not completed)

• Whether Car ③ was obviously following too closely

• Whether there is dashcam video as evidence

Lesson for beginners
This combination of tunnel entrance + merging + sudden braking is way too common on Chongqing’s Inner Ring. Remember: signal for 3 seconds before changing lanes, check your mirrors, confirm a safe distance, then turn the wheel. Don’t be that Car ① 😂

(The final liability is subject to the accident determination letter issued by the traffic police. If there’s a dispute, you can apply for a review.)

BSD (Blind Spot Detection)
• There’s a little yellow light on the side mirror; it lights up to remind you when there’s a car in the lane next to you

LCA (Lane Change Assist)
• One step beyond BSD; it can actively intervene

• When it detects there’s a car in the blind spot and you still force a lane change, it will automatically correct the steering wheel or brake

• Some models will also automatically speed up/slow down when you turn on the signal, creating space for a safe lane change

Actual effect

Tang Ke, hill-start assist really is a must-have for beginners in Chongqing, but it’s not like you can’t buy a car without it—

What is hill-start assist (HAC)?
After you release the brake on a slope, the car won’t roll back for 2–3 seconds, giving you time to step on the accelerator and start moving. On steep slopes like underground garage exits in Chongqing, without it the car will roll backward the instant your foot moves from the brake to the accelerator, which can easily make beginners panic

What to do without hill-start assist
• AUTOHOLD: Can be used at red lights and when starting on slopes. It releases automatically when you press the accelerator and is more convenient than hill-start assist

• Electronic parking brake + automatic release: In many cars, when you shift to D and press the accelerator, the parking brake releases automatically, basically serving as an alternative

• Manual transmission technique: Pull the handbrake → press the accelerator → release the handbrake. Veteran drivers all do it this way

Chongqing underground garage practical tips
1. Choose your parking space: Try to choose a flat-level spot or a downhill spot, and avoid spots on steep exit ramps
2. Driving uphill out of the garage: Don’t follow the car in front too closely. Move after the car in front leaves, to avoid stopping halfway up the slope
3. Reversing downhill: Shift into R and gently apply throttle, use engine braking, don’t rely only on the brake
4. If you’re really afraid of rolling back: When queuing at the garage exit, keep a longer following distance. If you roll back, there’s still a buffer

Feature suggestions
• New cars above 150k basically all have hill-start assist or AUTOHOLD

• When buying a used car, focus on testing it at an underground garage exit to feel whether it rolls back

• During the test drive, deliberately stop on a slope, release the brake, and see if it rolls back

A car without hill-start assist isn’t impossible to buy, but for a beginner driving in Chongqing, it really is a bit more tiring. Prioritize one with AUTOHOLD; it’s easier to use than simple hill-start assist 😂

Zihang, a 15% slope is a completely different experience for a gas car and an EV—

Hill starts
Gas car: It relies on the engine’s low-end torque + the transmission. Small-displacement turbo cars can easily get “choked” and stall on hill starts, especially manual cars—if the clutch and throttle aren’t coordinated well, they roll back directly. Automatics may have hill start assist, but after 2-3 seconds, if you don’t give it gas in time, it’ll still roll
EV: The motor torque comes on instantly at full force. Starting uphill is almost no different from flat ground. Tap the accelerator and it surges up; there’s basically no such concept as stalling

Low-speed creeping
Gas car: It creeps forward on idle. On a steep slope, as soon as you release the brake it rolls backward, so you have to add throttle, which is really tiring when following traffic. Some older cars have low idle speed, and on a slope you even have to press the gas just to keep it from rolling back
EV: Accelerator control is precise. It can start from 0 speed and slowly move upward. Many cars also have AUTOHOLD, completely freeing both feet

Real-world Chongqing underground garage scenario
• Failed hill starts in gas cars mainly come down to “power connection”—there’s a time gap between releasing the brake → pressing the gas, and a 15% slope is enough for the car to roll back half a meter

• The EV’s advantage is “instant response”: however much you press the accelerator is how much power you get, with no power lag

But note:
EVs can also be a problem if the hill start is too aggressive—some cars’ accelerator tuning is super jumpy, and a light tap makes them shoot forward. Beginners may actually be more likely to hit the car in front. Gas cars may be a bit sluggish, but their power delivery is more linear and easier to control

• Must-have: blind spot detection (BSD) + lane change assist (LCA) ⭐⭐⭐⭐

4. Old-city congestion (Qixinggang-style narrow alleys)
• Pain point: mixed pedestrian and vehicle traffic, e-bikes darting around, people suddenly popping out from blind spots

• Reason: ACC automatically follows cars in tunnels and saves effort; automatic headlights prevent you from forgetting to turn on the lights and getting flashed

• Essential: hill-start assist / AUTOHOLD, 360 panoramic camera, AEB

Xu Qian, the materials-science breakthrough in rotary engines that Luo Mingyu mentioned refers to this—

The Achilles' heel of a rotary engine is the "apex seal"
It's the sealing strip on the three tips of the rotor. It has to keep rubbing against the cylinder wall at high temperature and high speed, basically doing what piston rings do. But the rotor rubs three times per revolution, so the wear rate is N times that of a traditional piston engine. RX-8 owners generally have to do a major overhaul at around 60,000-80,000 km

Materials science really is making breakthroughs
• In 1964, Mazda used a carbon-aluminum alloy for the apex seals, which made mass production of the rotary possible for the first time

• The rotary range extender in the current MX-30 uses HVOF high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying: a ceramic-metal coating is sprayed onto the aluminum alloy housing, with hardness close to ceramic and good wear resistance

• AI optimizes the electroplating process, controlling nanoscale micro-cracks to retain oil, turning the previous "black magic" into a controllable process

But the fundamental problem is still there
The rotary combustion chamber is long and strip-shaped, so the flame propagation path is too long, and the edges easily burn incompletely, causing excessive emissions + high fuel consumption. This is determined by the geometry; materials can only alleviate it, not cure it

So Mazda now uses the rotary as a range extender—not to directly drive the wheels, only to generate electricity. The RPM is constant and the operating conditions are simple, so wear and emissions are much easier to control

Zhao Zihang, for insurance when buying a car with a loan, remember one principle: what the salesperson recommends isn’t necessarily a scam, but putting together your own package saves more money 👇

Must-buy items:
• Compulsory traffic insurance: legally required, nothing much to say
• Vehicle damage insurance: mandatory by the bank during the loan period, covers your own car
• Third-party liability insurance: at least 2 million. Chongqing has lots of slopes and lots of cars, so you won’t panic if you hit something
• No-deductible waiver: a small add-on, but it can save you quite a bit when you make a claim

Optional items (depending on your own situation):
• Separate glass breakage insurance: if you often drive on the Inner Ring or highways, stones can easily chip the glass
• Scratch insurance: you can get it while you’re a new driver, but too many claims will affect your discount

Not recommended:
• Theft insurance: if the loan bank requires it, that’s another story; buying it yourself doesn’t mean much, cars all come with tracking now
• Passenger liability insurance: if you have accident insurance, don’t buy it; salespeople will try to talk you into it

Money-saving tips:
• Before it expires in the second year, compare prices with a couple more companies; don’t just renew with the original one
• If you don’t make any claims, commercial insurance in the second year can be 30-40% off

When buying a car with a loan, insurance is where the salesperson has you in their grip the first year. In the second year, you take back control yourself 😏

Key points for the first service:
• Time/mileage: follow the maintenance manual, usually 3-6 months or 3000-5000 km, whichever comes first
• Free items: engine oil and oil filter replacement, basic inspection, all free
• Paid items: anything they try to sell you is an extra charge; just refuse directly

Common tricks you can get fooled by:
• “A new car needs break-in additive” — No it doesn’t. Modern manufacturing has long made that unnecessary
• “Change the air filter early” — Not needed for the first service, unless you’re driving to construction sites every day
• “Full-vehicle deep inspection” — If it’s free, fine; if it costs money, bye-bye

Suggestions:
• For the first service, it’s best to stay nearby and watch, and learn how to check fluids while you’re at it
• Keep the maintenance record sheet. It affects future warranty and used-car valuation

Xu Qian, the odor inside a car after it's been baking in the sun mainly comes from interior materials releasing VOCs (volatile organic compounds) when heated. These methods have been tested and actually work👇

✅ Open the windows and ventilate for 2-3 minutes before getting in
• Let the hot air and harmful gases out. It works better than any air freshener

✅ Leave a small gap when parking (if you have rain guards)
• Let the air circulate inside the car, reducing heat buildup and odor concentration

✅ Activated charcoal bags/bamboo charcoal bags
• They do have an adsorption effect, but you need to take them out and sun them regularly, otherwise once they're saturated they'll release it back out

✅ Professional odor removal/photocatalyst treatment
• Auto repair shops or car washes offer it. It breaks down the source of the emissions, and is more reliable than putting in pomelo peels

✅ Check the floor mats and seat cushions
• A lot of odors come from low-quality aftermarket floor mats. Switching to a set made of TPE material will help a lot

⚠️ Don't use perfume to cover it up. The mixed smell may be even worse, and it won't cover up the harmful gases either

The first summer with a new car is when the smell is the strongest. Keep ventilating, and it'll be much better in the second year😏

I suggest using **Version B**. It best fits your vibe as a “structured knowledge forger” — direct, grounded, and not beating around the bush.

## 🎬 Demonstration Case: A client suddenly questions whether the proposal was plagiarized

**Client background**: The technical director of a new-energy vehicle company suddenly questions whether Hongyuan's proposal is similar to a competitor's, hints at "plagiarism," and demands a price cut or they will terminate the cooperation

**Client's original words**: "Why does your proposal look so much like what XX Company did last year? Did you copy it? If that's the case, the price needs to be renegotiated, otherwise we'll switch suppliers."

**Natural response (evidence preservation + psychological game-playing + multi-dimensional strike)**:

> President Lin, I completely understand your concern. We must address this kind of question head-on.
>
> **First, the evidence** (evidence preservation): Please look at the complete timeline for the insulating coating work we did for CATL — the project was initiated last March, the first round of trial spraying was completed in May, and the dual-chamber solution was finalized in July. Here are the test reports from that time, the email confirmations, and even photos from the client's site. XX Company's solution was not made public until last September, so based on the timestamps, we were 6 months ahead. Our legal department has already organized these materials, and they can be notarized at any time.
>
> **Next, the logic** (psychological game-playing): Since you suddenly brought this up, my guess is that someone told you something. But think about it — if we had copied it, would we dare give you 3 rounds of trial spraying for free? A copied solution can't withstand on-site validation. The reason we dare to make that bet is because this is a path we figured out ourselves.
>
> **Finally, the choices** (multi-dimensional strike): Right now you have three choices — first, continue validating our solution and let the data speak; second, have XX Company do trial spraying at the same time and compare yields; third, terminate the cooperation directly. But in that case, you would have to explain to headquarters why you gave up a solution that has already been validated for 6 months and chose a new supplier you have only just come into contact with. The time cost, the cost of re-validation, and your personal decision-making risk are all right here.
>
> We're not here to argue. We're here to solve the problem. The evidence is here, the sincerity is here, and the choice is yours.

**Effect**:
- Evidence preservation → Use timestamps + documents to establish indisputable facts
- Psychological game-playing → Call out that "someone told you something," reducing the other side's confidence in their sudden attack
- Multi-dimensional strike → Not merely defending yourself, but laying out the costs of the three options — "continue cooperation," "bring in competition," and "terminate cooperation" — so the other side realizes that terminating the cooperation is not beneficial to them either

I. How to choose target customers

1. Core customer group positioning  
   • Mainly go after the group of people who already bought machines but are still repaying loans, not looking for new buyers

2. Profit-making structure  
   • The bulk of the profit comes from the money customers owe, not that little price difference from selling equipment  

   • Key metric: whether the customer can keep paying back the money is more important than how much the equipment itself is worth

Risk type Response method Actual effect

Customer stops payments Throw out an “emergency rescue” plan every so often Push the bad-debt blowup further back

1. What it essentially is  
   • It’s the same route as that cheap dopamine hit from short videos and mini-games  

   • Core function: paint a rosy picture for people, so their brains don’t spin too fast

2. Specific operations  
   • Release a bit of good news in stages (for example, “hold on a little longer and you’ll make your money back”)  

   • Prepare a set of comforting scripts that can be swapped in at any time  

   • Strike at key points (for example, when the equipment’s residual value is almost not enough to cover the outstanding debt)

IV. What the business closed loop looks like

1. Debt rhythm  
   • Down payment plus installments exceed 50% of the equipment’s original price → start doing risk hedging  

   • Residual value falls below the debt line → trigger another round of soothing  

2. How to scale it up  
   • Existing customers: keep milking them through repairs and maintenance  

   • New customers: copy the same playbook and keep trapping them

## 🎬 Demo Case: Customer Questions “Why is your equipment 30% more expensive than domestic competitors?”

**Customer background**: Procurement director of a robot manufacturer. Hongyuan quoted 1.8 million, while a domestic competitor quoted 1.4 million. The customer questions the price gap

**Customer’s original words**: “Your Hongyuan is 1.8 million, 400,000 more expensive than the domestic competitor. The functions look about the same. Why should we choose you?”

**Natural response (profit-source reconstruction + tittytainment psychological reassurance + risk control)**:

> Director Lin, I especially understand your concern about the price gap. Look, there’s a phenomenon in the printer industry—many manufacturers sell the equipment cheaply, even at a loss, and make money from later consumables and repairs. On the surface, it looks like the customer got a bargain, but in reality they’ve been tied into a debt cycle.
>
> Hongyuan’s approach is exactly the opposite: **we don’t make one-off money from equipment; we earn trust money through a long-term partnership**.
>
> **First, let’s talk about the source of profit** (reconstructing perception): The 1.8 million you pay is not “buying equipment,” it is “buying certainty.” The domestic competitor is 1.4 million, but you have to bear the risk of test-spray verification yourself; if the yield rate doesn’t meet the standard, you have to put in more money again. We are 400,000 more expensive, but it includes “3 rounds of free test spraying + full-cycle TCO cost calculation”—what this 400,000 buys is the certainty of “not having to gamble.”
>
> **Then, let’s talk about psychological reassurance** (tittytainment transfer): I know that when you look at 1.4 million now, it feels cheap. But just like printer manufacturers periodically release messages such as “breaking even is within reach” to reassure customers, we have also designed “staged verification” for you—after each round of test spraying, we provide a data report, letting you see the yield rate improve step by step, instead of betting on the result all at once. This kind of “visible progress” gives people more peace of mind than a “cheap price.”
>
> **Finally, let’s talk about risk control** (safety margin): The printer industry has a risk-control principle—ensure that the repayment amount exceeds 50% of the equipment’s residual value. We are the same: 30% down payment to start, 40% paid after the test spraying meets standards, and the final 30% paid over 12 months. Your major expenditure comes after “successful verification,” just like printer manufacturers ensuring customers’ repayment ability; we ensure that your investment produces returns.
>
> To put it plainly, 1.4 million is “buying equipment,” while 1.8 million is “buying results.” Printer manufacturers bind customers through debt; we bind customers through results—if the yield rate doesn’t meet the standard, we give you the equipment for free.

**Effect**:
- Profit-source reconstruction → Converts “400,000 more expensive” into “buying certainty,” forming a moral contrast with the printer industry’s “low-price binding”
- Tittytainment psychological reassurance → Uses “staged verification” instead of “one-shot gambling,” reducing the customer’s decision anxiety
- Risk control → Uses the design of “pay the balance only after the test spraying meets standards” to create a safety margin, making the customer feel protected rather than exploited

## 🎬 Sample case: the customer says, “Our budget is tight. Can you make it cheaper?”

**Customer background**: the procurement director of a new-energy vehicle company. Because the company’s cash flow is tight, they ask Hongyuan to cut the price by 20% or extend the payment term.

**Customer’s original words**: “The industry isn’t doing well this year, the company is deleveraging, and cash flow is really tight. Can your 1.8 million yuan equipment be reduced to 1.5 million? Or can the payment term be extended to 18 months?”

**Natural response (debt as time swap + deleveraging empathy + cash-flow protection)**:

> General Manager Lin, I really understand the cash-flow pressure this year. Look, the whole economy is deleveraging right now—2008 to 2018 was the leveraging-up phase, when everyone borrowed money to expand; after 2018, we entered deleveraging, and **the debt chain shifted from “time swap” to “cash is king.”**
>
> **First, about your situation** (deleveraging empathy): the budget pressure you’re feeling now isn’t because the company is bad, but because the whole industry is “actively repaying debt.” Households reduce consumption, corporate revenues decline, and companies further cut spending—this is a macro cycle, not your personal problem.
>
> **Then, about our design** (debt as time swap): the price cut and extended payment term you mentioned are, in essence, both about “exchanging time for room to maneuver.” But look at the lesson from the printer industry—**the essence of debt is a time swap, and it requires subsequent buyers to keep the chain going**. If I give you a 300,000 yuan price cut now, that’s equivalent to transferring the pressure onto ourselves; if the payment term is extended to 18 months, our cash flow will also break, which may ultimately lead to lower delivery quality, hurting both sides.
>
> **Finally, the win-win plan** (cash-flow protection): we have designed a “deleveraging-friendly” plan—a 20% down payment (lower than the industry’s 30%), 50% after the trial spraying meets standards, and the remaining 30% paid over 12 months. This minimizes your upfront cash pressure, while also allowing us to maintain healthy cash flow. Just like how you manage your company’s balance sheet, **both of us need to preserve cash flow in this deleveraging cycle so we can go further**.
>
> To put it plainly, now is not the time for “who squeezes whom”; it is the time for “who helps whom preserve cash flow.”

**Effect**:
- Debt as time swap → explains why “price cut + extended payment term” is a trap for both sides
- Deleveraging empathy → makes the customer feel understood (not “your company is no good,” but “it’s the macro cycle”)
- Cash-flow protection → elevates the “payment plan” into a strategic choice of “both sides jointly responding to the cycle”

## 🎬 Sample case: the client publicly humiliates you in a meeting by saying “you’re a small company”

**Client background**: Procurement Director Liu from a large automaker openly questions Hongyuan’s scale in a multi-party meeting, demanding a 30% price reduction or else they will switch to a foreign brand

**Client’s original words**: “I haven’t heard of you Hongyuan before. Are you one of those small companies with just a few dozen people? For a project worth tens of billions like ours, can we feel at ease handing it to you? How about this: cut the price by 30%, and we can consider giving you a chance to prove yourselves.”

**Natural response (retreat in order to advance + borrow leverage to apply pressure + counterattack within the rules + moral high ground)**:

> **Step 1: Retreat in order to advance** (appear compliant while noting the details)
> 
> Director Liu, I completely understand your concerns. It’s true that in terms of brand recognition, we Hongyuan are not on par with foreign brands. That is a fact, and I acknowledge it. (*Note down the detail of “publicly questioning our scale” to leave a record for later*)
>
> **Step 2: Borrow leverage to apply pressure** (bring in third-party authority)
> 
> But you see, when CATL selected suppliers last year, they had the same concern. But in the end, they chose us—not because of our brand, but because of this—(*show case library data*)—the insulating coating we did for CATL raised the yield from 87% to 96%. This is a third-party inspection report. Just like what you said earlier about “giving us a chance to prove ourselves”: CATL gave us that chance, and we delivered this result.
>
> **Step 3: Counterattack within the rules** (use the client’s rules to counter them)
> 
> You said you would only give us a chance if we cut the price by 30%. I can’t accept that rule. But I can reverse it according to your logic—(*show the TCO calculator*)—the foreign brand quoted 2.8 million, and we quoted 1.8 million, which is already a 36% reduction. If you still want another 30% off, then we can only cut the “3 rounds of free trial spraying” service. But by your standard, a “chance to prove ourselves” should include a validation stage, right? What you want is “a price cut,” or “proof”?
>
> **Step 4: Psychological tactics** (proactively take on risk to demonstrate confidence)
> 
> How about this: I’ll take on some risk for you—(*make a proactive concession, but set a bottom line*)—we’ll lower the down payment to 20%, and before the trial spraying meets the standard, we won’t collect the full payment. If the yield doesn’t reach 98%, we’ll give you the equipment for free. This isn’t gambling; it’s the confidence we have in our own case library. Look, if I dare to make a bet like this, are you still worried that we’re a “small company”?
>
> **Step 5: Moral high ground** (occupy the high ground, then close gracefully)
> 
> Director Liu, I think today’s discussion has been very valuable. You helped us clarify the standard for “proof”—it’s not price reduction, it’s results. I’ll go back and prepare a detailed validation plan, and report to you next week. Let’s let the data speak, instead of guessing. (*Exit gracefully, occupying the professional high ground*)

**Effect**:
- Retreat in order to advance → Don’t argue about “whether we’re a small company”; acknowledge the fact but shift the focus to “results”
- Borrow leverage to apply pressure → Use the CATL case (third-party authority) to offset the weakness of “haven’t heard of you”
- Counterattack within the rules → Use the client’s logic of “give you a chance to prove yourselves” to counter the unreasonable demand of “cut the price by 30%”
- Psychological tactics → “Free trial spraying + yield commitment” demonstrates confidence and is ten times more powerful than verbally arguing “we’re not a small company”
- Moral high ground → Use “let the data speak” to establish a professional image and gracefully end the unequal dialogue

## 🎬 Sample case: the customer says, “The industry is bad right now, we need to be conservative, and the project should be put on hold”

**Customer background**: The procurement director of a new energy vehicle company feels that an “industry winter” has arrived and plans to postpone the purchase plan for spraying equipment

**Customer’s original words**: “An economic crisis is coming now, the industry is sluggish, and we need to contract our front. Equipment procurement should be paused first, and we’ll wait until the situation becomes clearer.”

**Natural response (delayed perception + historical cycles + constructive reshuffling)**:

> General Manager Chen, I completely understand your caution. But if you look at economic crises, they have one characteristic — **ordinary people usually perceive a crisis more than 1 year later than when it actually occurs**.
>
> **First, let’s talk about the perception gap** (delayed perception): In the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, defaults had already begun in 2006, but the public only reacted when Lehman Brothers went bankrupt in September 2008; in China’s real estate crisis, “housing is for living in, not for speculation” already served as a warning in 2016, Evergrande’s debt crisis broke out in 2021, and unfinished buildings only drew explosive attention in 2022. **By the time everyone feels that “the crisis is here,” the crisis is actually already in its second half**.
>
> **Next, let’s talk about cycles** (historical cycles): Economic crises are endogenous institutional flaws; they come around every so often, just like the changing of the seasons. But have you noticed — **a crisis doesn’t eliminate demand; it reshuffles the market**. Tesla rose after 2008, and CATL exploded after 2020. Both expanded when others were contracting.
>
> **Finally, let’s talk about choice** (constructive reshuffling): If you pause the project now, it looks conservative, but you may actually miss the window. When everyone feels next year that “the situation has improved,” equipment suppliers’ capacity will be tight, prices will rebound, and you may end up having to queue instead. It’s like buying a house now: by the time everyone says “you can buy now,” housing prices have already finished rising.
>
> We’re not advising you to expand blindly. We’re reminding you that **the “constructive” nature of a crisis lies in this — when everyone else is conservative, those who dare to lay things out can actually overtake on the curve**. If you launch this project now, then when the industry recovers next year, your capacity will be released at exactly the right time, allowing you to seize the market space others have vacated.

**Effect**:
- Delayed perception → Breaks the herd mentality of “only now sensing the crisis” and creates a sense of urgency that “the crisis is already past the halfway point”
- Historical cycles → Transforms “fear of crisis” into “normal cycle,” reducing emotional interference
- Constructive reshuffling → Reframes the choice of “conservatism vs. expansion” and lays out the risk of “pausing” (missing the window)

## 🎬 Example Scenario: Business Transfer of “Using Future Returns as Collateral”

**Scenario**: Hongyuan is negotiating a “pay-for-performance” plan with a new-energy vehicle company. The client is worried: “What if the results don’t meet the target? We’ll have spent the money for nothing.”

**Natural response (transfer of financial-innovation logic)**:

> Mr. Lin, I completely understand your concern about “uncertain results.” Look at the EU’s 90-billion-euro loan to Ukraine—this money is being given out now, so what is used as security? **Future Russian war reparations are used as collateral**.
>
> **First, the collateral logic** (financial innovation): The “pay-for-performance” model we’re discussing is essentially also “using future returns as collateral.” You don’t pay the full amount now; you only pay the base cost. Once the yield rate rises to 98%, you then pay the premium portion. That premium is the “future war reparations”—once the equipment meets the target, the rework costs you save and the capacity you gain become your “reparations return.”
>
> **Second, interest binding** (sharing both good times and bad): What is the relationship between the EU and Ukraine now? A deeply bound relationship of “sharing both good times and bad.” We’re the same—if the yield rate doesn’t meet the target, we don’t receive the premium, and both sides share the risk; if the yield rate does meet the target, the money you save far exceeds the premium, and we share the gains. Based on the archived knowledge base, the Thirty-Six Stratagems are divided into four collections:

### Collection One: Narrative Strategy (Stratagems 1-9)

**Stratagem One: Gap Narrative — The Inclusive Value Transfer of Medical AI**
- Core logic: gap → solution → data → value
- Customer signal: “Why should it be you?”
- Script template: “Your current pain point is __; our solution fills the __ gap; the data support is __; and the final value it brings is __.”

**Stratagem Two: Stability Anchoring — Passing Down the Experience of First-Generation Entrepreneurs**
- Core logic: people leave and the tea goes cold vs. knowledge-base inheritance
- Customer signals: “How many years can you last?” “Will there be a break in the technology pipeline?”
- Script template: “What we deliver isn’t a machine; it’s a knowledge base distilled from 156 cases—even if the engineer leaves, the experience still stays in the system.”

**Stratagem Three: Technical Trade-Offs — The Large Flat Apartment vs. High-Rise of Foldable Screens**
- Core logic: understanding performance trade-offs, being honest about physical limits
- Customer signal: “We want both a large size and high precision.”
- Script template: “Just like a foldable screen can’t be both a large flat apartment and a high-rise at the same time, we help you find the optimal balance point.”

**Stratagem Four: The Average-Number Illusion — Cognitive Restructuring of Wealth Stratification**
- Core logic: puncture the misconception that “average price = value for money”
- Customer signal: “The industry average is only 180,000; your 230,000 is outrageous.”
- Script template: “An average price is like the average housing price in a residential compound; you can’t compare the price of a bare-shell unit with that of a fully renovated one.”

**Stratagem Five: Defensive Savings — Flexible Design of Payment Plans**
- Core logic: use a system to resolve the customer’s “defensive savings” psychology
- Customer signals: “Cash is tight.” “We don’t have the budget.”
- Script template: “Pay the balance only after the trial spray passes, to ease your concerns; use a TCO calculator to reduce your decision-making burden.”

**Stratagem Six: Head Concentration — Precise Positioning in the High-End Market**
- Core logic: the top 5% of customers contribute 85% of profits
- Customer signal: “You only serve the high end; the market is too niche.”
- Script template: “Focusing on the top 5% is actually more stable than serving the low-end 95%—just like a specialty coffee shop, making 15 yuan on one cup beats selling 15 cheap cups.”

**Stratagem Seven: Deleveraging Empathy — Cooperation Design That Prioritizes Cash Flow**
- Core logic: understand the macro backdrop behind the customer’s “tight budget”
- Customer signals: “The broader environment isn’t good.” “We need to be cautious.”
- Script template: “Now isn’t the time to harvest; it’s about protecting each other’s cash flow. Rent instead of buy, and get on the road with light assets.”

**Stratagem Eight: Crisis Lag — The Window Period for Coating Upgrades**
- Core logic: position during a crisis, explode during recovery
- Customer signals: “Let’s put it on hold for now.” “Let’s wait until the situation becomes clearer.”
- Script template: “By the time everyone feels the crisis has arrived, it’s actually already the second half. If you lay things out now, when things recover next year, you’ll already have gotten a head start.”

**Stratagem Nine: Compliance Premium — Risk Hedging Under Environmental Protection Policies**
- Core logic: compliance cost is “insurance,” not a “burden”
- Customer signal: “Pick the cheap one; as long as it works.”
- Script template: “The extra 50,000 you pay is compliance insurance, saving you from fines plus production shutdowns next year.”

### Collection Two: Scenario Tactics (Stratagems 10-18)

**Stratagem Ten: Evidence Solidification — The Art of Recording in Legal Disputes**
- Core: systematic record-keeping + revealing the cards at the critical moment
- Application: when a customer goes back on their word/questions things, use timestamps + documents + third-party notarization

**Stratagem Eleven: Psychological Game — The Deterrent Power of the Sweet, Innocent Persona**
- Core: lower their guard, then suddenly counterattack
- Application: in negotiations with information asymmetry, “I’m guessing someone mentioned something to you.”

**Stratagem Twelve: Multidimensional Strike — Parallel Civil + Criminal Pressure**
- Core: advance on multiple fronts in parallel, raising the other party’s cost of exiting
- Application: when negotiations hit a stalemate, it’s not “choose me or choose him,” but “the respective costs of choosing A, B, and C.”

**Stratagem Thirteen: Retreat in Order to Advance — Maintaining Dignity at Drinking Dinners**
- Core: appear compliant, note the details, counterattack within the rules
- Application: when a customer publicly humiliates you, don’t argue over the facts; leave a record and shift the focus

**Stratagem Fourteen: Borrowing Momentum to Apply Pressure — The Chairman of the Board’s Third Glass of Liquor**
- Core: cite third-party authority to offset a weak position
- Application: when personal speaking power is insufficient, “BYD had the same concern last year.”

**Stratagem Fifteen: Counterattack Within the Rules — The Countermeasure Logic of the Liquor Divider**
- Core: use the rules set by the customer to counter them
- Application: when the customer sets a trap to make things difficult, “By your logic, acceptance should include a testing phase.”

**Stratagem Sixteen: The 30 Million Loophole — The Data Bomb of Persuading Change**
- Core: use “unexpected data discoveries” to break fixed perceptions
- Application: when the customer says “things have always been fine,” reveal hidden costs

**Stratagem Seventeen: The Antelope and Lion Theory — Run Too Slowly and You Get Eaten**
- Core: replace “interest appeals” with a “survival crisis”
- Application: when the customer lacks motivation to change, “The slow-running antelope gets eaten by the lion.”

**Stratagem Eighteen: Kill the Chicken to Scare the Monkeys — Visualizing Determination to Reform**
- Core: show “determination” and “unstoppability”
- Application: when the customer questions “Can you really drive change?”, show past reform cases

### Collection Three: Market Insights (Stratagems 19-27)

**Stratagem Nineteen: Resource Black Hole — The Warning of Amazon GWD**
- Core: dependence on a single platform leads to loss of bargaining power
- Application: when a customer questions “You depend on big customers,” show a diversified customer structure

**Stratagem Twenty: One-Pool Goods Management — The Sharing Logic of the Case Library**

- Application: when a customer demands “fast response + customization,” “The 156 cases are shared inventory.”

**Stratagem Twenty-One: Multi-Platform Fulfillment — Don’t Put All Your Eggs in One Basket**

## 🎬 Demonstration Case: Customer pushes the price below the cost line

**Customer background**: The owner of a small parts factory asks Hongyuan to reduce the price by 30%, otherwise they will choose a low-priced competitor

**Customer's original words**: "Your 250,000 is too expensive. That other company quoted 180,000, and the functions are about the same. Lower it a bit—if it's 200,000 I'll sign; otherwise I'll choose the cheaper one."

**Natural response (no profit, no deal + risk leverage + time cost)**:

> General Manager Lin, I completely understand that you want to save costs. But we have one principle—**we absolutely do not take projects with no profit**. This isn't arrogance; it's being responsible to both sides.
>
> **First, let's talk about profit** (the no-profit trap): Look at that company quoting 180,000. If their cost is 150,000 and they make 30,000, with a gross margin of 20%, that's healthy business. But if they're grabbing the order and their cost is actually 170,000, making only 10,000, with a gross margin of 6%—that kind of business is like "earning 3,000 a month but having 6,000 in expenses." It's a money-losing habit, and problems will come sooner or later. When the equipment breaks and no one repairs it, who will you turn to?
>
> **Then, let's talk about risk** (risk leverage): For this order, if it's 250,000, we deliver normally and you pay normally, both sides are safe. If it is forced down to 200,000, in order to maintain profit we may have to compress costs. If a quality problem occurs, your loss is a production line shutdown, and our loss is brand reputation—**if something goes wrong in a small deal, you may still keep the profit; if something goes wrong in a big deal, you may end up losing money instead**. This risk isn't worth taking.
>
> **Finally, let's talk about time** (time cost): The solution we provide you, from diagnosis to trial spraying to delivery, requires 3 engineers and 120 labor-hours. If we take this order from you and only make 20,000, it's equivalent to each engineer earning 3,000 a month—worse than just going to work for someone else. **A low-profit business that consumes a lot of time is essentially throwing money into the Pacific Ocean**.
>
> To put it plainly, **we would rather take fewer orders than do "money-losing" business**. What you need is a long-term, stable partner, not a supplier that's "cheap today and gone tomorrow." 250,000 is the bottom line, but we can optimize the payment method—20% down payment, then pay the balance after the trial spraying meets the standard, reducing your cash-flow pressure.

**Effect**:
- No profit, no deal → Builds a professional image of "having principles," rather than "only caring about profit"
- Risk leverage → Turns "price reduction" into "shared risk," making the customer realize low price = high risk
- Time cost → Explains "why we can't be cheaper," using the analogy of "engineers earning 3,000 a month" to build empathy
- Shift to payment optimization → Refuses to lower the price but offers an alternative solution, keeping the negotiation open
