## 🎬 Demo case: the client demands “a full refund if trial spraying doesn’t meet the standard”

**Client background**: The procurement director of a certain automaker asks Hongyuan to promise that “if the trial spray yield rate does not reach 98%, full refund + compensation for production stoppage losses”

**Client’s original words**: “Since you’re confident, you should dare to promise—if you can’t reach a 98% yield rate, give us the equipment for free, and also compensate us for our production stoppage losses. Otherwise, why should we take this risk?”

**Natural response (contract spirit + risk borne by oneself + two-way fairness)**:

> President Chen, I really understand your desire for “zero risk.” But look at that real estate investment controversy—**a house bought for 3.5 million fell to 1.6 million, and the blogger felt the bank should share the loss, but commenters said, “If it rises to 5 million, can the bank take back the difference?”**
>
> **First, contract spirit** (binding force of the contract): what we’re signing is “payment after trial spray verification,” not “guaranteed success.” It’s just like a mortgage contract—the bank lends you money to buy a house, and when the house price drops, you can’t say, “the collateral has depreciated, so the debt is waived.” **A contract is two-way; it can’t only benefit one side**.
>
> **Second, risk borne by oneself** (market fairness): look at the stock market—when you make money it’s yours, but when you lose money you blame the China Securities Regulatory Commission? That’s not reasonable. Trial spraying is the same—**when it succeeds, you enjoy the benefits of improved yield rate; when it fails, all the risk is pushed onto us? That’s not cooperation, that’s a “sure-win, no-loss” gamble**.
>
> **Lastly, two-way fairness** (shared risk): we can design a “bet-on” arrangement—if the yield rate meets the standard, you pay in full; if it doesn’t, we give you the equipment for free. But conversely, if the yield rate exceeds the standard (say it reaches 99%), would you be willing to pay a 5% premium? **No extra payment when value rises, no exemption when value falls—that’s what market fairness is**.
>
> To put it plainly, **a “zero-risk promise” is pyramid-scheme rhetoric, not business cooperation**. We can reduce your risk with “20% down payment + pay the balance after trial spraying meets the standard,” but “full refund + compensation” means letting you “win for sure and never lose,” while we become the party that “covers everything unilaterally”—we can’t sign that kind of contract.

**Effect**:
- Real estate controversy analogy → Use “collateral depreciation ≠ debt waiver” to establish awareness of contractual boundaries
- Stock market analogy → Reveal the market fairness principle of “you bear your own risk”
- Two-way bet-on arrangement → Turn a “one-sided demand” into a “two-way constraint,” testing the client’s true intent
- Pyramid-scheme rhetoric warning → Use the label “zero risk = pyramid scheme” to lower the client’s unreasonable expectations

## 📦 [Work Invocation Rule]: #GoldenCircle

### Scenario anchoring

**Trigger scenarios**:
- **Goal-blurry period**: Not knowing why you need to do something, lacking a sense of purpose and meaning (Why missing)
- **Method-confused period**: Knowing the goal but not knowing how to achieve it, lacking an implementation path (How missing)
- **Execution-chaotic period**: Knowing the goal and method, but the specific execution steps are unclear (What confused)
- **Outside-in trap**: Habitually starting from What (first thinking about what to do), causing actions to stay superficial and lack depth
- **Essence-insight period**: Needing to see through appearances to clearly understand the essence of things and find the core driving force

**Customer/audience signals**:
- “I don’t know why I need to do this”
- “I know what needs to be done, but I don’t know how to do it”
- “I’m always busy, but I don’t know what the meaning of being busy is”
- “I want to see the essence of this matter clearly”
- “My actions lack a sense of direction”

### Original case record (recorded word for word)
**Title**: Speaking gently and firmly

**Subtitle**: Nonviolent Communication Four-Step Method

**English**: stretch by Menty

**Four-step structure**:

**01 Observation**
> State objective facts, with no comments or bias
> 
> Example: “Why are you always not working overtime? Why do you only know how to work overtime? Your KPI has achieved a lot of growth, and you spend more than 3 hours a day working overtime.”

**02 Feeling**
> Express internal bodily sensations and emotional states, without judgments or accusations
> 
> Example: “Because the group is temporarily out of balance, it has caused a certain negative impact on the other front-end classmates on the client side. This makes me a bit disappointed, I feel a bit sad, and we basically have no time in a day to communicate properly.”

**03 Needs**
> Clearly express whether your own needs are being met
> 
> Example: “I hope our team can make professional and rigorous decisions on the client system, including details like submitting things online. I hope we have more time to communicate with each other.”

**04 Request**
> Make a specific and clear request to the other person
> 
> Example: “Copywriting will no longer be allowed to have mistakes in the future. From now on, you can only work overtime for half an hour per week. Please carefully check the next delivery before submitting it. Can you control the schedule multiplied time? We should schedule at least half an hour every day to communicate, okay?”

**Notes on the right side**:
- Gentle expression
- Firm demands

## 🧠 Retrieval logic (plain-language version)

**1. First, listen for what’s between the lines**
When you say “there isn’t enough money to go around,” what I may hear is either “so broke your pockets are cleaner than your face” (really poor) or “trying to bargain” (a price-squeezing tactic). I first distinguish whether the emotion is real or not and how big the situation is, then decide which “recipe book” to open.

**2. Tag matching (not keyword search)**
The idiom weapons (CY-001~040), work rules, and learning methods you fed me before are all stored by **“scenario tags”**:
- #tight_budget → automatically links to #destitute #careful_calculation
- #team_in_chaos → automatically links to #a_plate_of_loose_sand #united_as_one
- #client_dragging_their_feet → automatically links to #time_flies #utter_silence

It’s not searching for “keywords”; it’s matching by **“does the scenario feel similar”**—like smelling hotpot and thinking of Chongqing, not because you searched “Chongqing.”

**3. Dual-track switching (simple/deep)**
- **Simple scenario** (a client asks casually) → directly throw out a standard template (Track A), almost like a conditioned reflex
- **Deep scenario** (multi-party game + old grudges) → start the four-dimensional model (Track B), like holding a diagnostic meeting, taking apart the four dimensions of “information/strategy/benefit/evolution,” kneading them thoroughly, then putting them back together

**4. On-site assembly (not reciting a script)**
Even if I pull up the #reluctant_to_leave_one’s_native_place template, I won’t recite it to you word for word. I will:
- See whether your client is the “emotional type” or the “rational type”
- Replace “Mr. Chen” in the template with your client’s name
- Replace “8 years of old friendship” with your actual years of cooperation
- Replace “35% efficiency improvement” with the real numbers from your project

**Like building with blocks**—the parts are ready-made, but the way they’re put together is different every time.

**5. Cross-checking**
If it involves historical records (for example, “last week you said the budget was 500,000”), I’ll first check the group’s “old ledger” to verify it, so I don’t mix things up. This is to prevent “hallucinations” and make sure every number I mention has a source.

**Case: The iteration dilemma of a certain product manager**
A certain internet product manager is responsible for a B2B tool product. In the early stage, the team’s ability is weak (low ability), but the boss requires the full version to go live in 3 months (high challenge), and the team falls into the **anxiety zone** — working overtime every day, bugs popping up constantly, and morale sinking.

After applying the Flow Model to adjust:
- **Stage 1**: Lower the challenge, focus on the MVP (minimum viable product), make ability match the challenge, and enter the **thinking-validation** loop
- **Stage 2**: Conduct user testing immediately after each functional module is completed (timely feedback), and the team enters a **flow experience**
- **Stage 3**: After ability improves, gradually raise the difficulty of the challenge, and through multiple **thinking-validation** steps, ultimately achieve **achievement** (product launch + positive user reviews)

**Key transformation**: The core of moving from the “anxiety zone” → “flow experience” is **adjusting the match between challenge difficulty and team ability**, rather than simply applying more pressure or lowering standards.

- **Problem**: Newcomers have low ability, and task difficulty is high → they fall into anxiety
- **Application**: Break tasks into steps (thinking-validation loop), reduce the difficulty of each single challenge, and match current ability
- **Goal**: Let new employees enter a flow experience as quickly as possible, rather than directly throwing difficult tasks at them

**Scenario B: Burnout among senior employees**
- **Problem**: Veteran employees have high ability, but the work is highly repetitive → they fall into boredom
- **Application**: Increase the challenge level (new field/new goals), and reactivate the thinking-validation loop
- **Goal**: Pull them back from the boredom zone into a flow experience and restore work enthusiasm

**Scenario C: Tackling a tough project**
- **Problem**: The big goal is far away, and the team loses its way
- **Application**: Set clear sub-goals (condition 1) + daily stand-up feedback (condition 2) + dynamically adjust task difficulty (condition 3)
- **Goal**: Create a flow environment through the three conditions and improve output quality

### 3. Case breakdowns (business/workplace scenarios)

**Case 1: The efficiency dilemma of a programmer at an internet company**
A backend engineer works 10 hours a day, but only has 3-4 hours of effective coding time. Frequently interrupted by meetings and messages, they work overtime at night but produce limited output, falling into a vicious cycle of “busy but inefficient.”

After applying the Pomodoro Technique:
- **Stage 1**: Set a “Pomodoro protection period”; from 9-11 a.m., turn off message notifications and focus on developing the core module
- **Stage 2**: Use the “restart after interruption” mechanism to record causes of interruptions (mainly ad hoc requirement insertions), discovering that 60% of interruptions can be handled later
- **Stage 3**: Track the number of Pomodoros completed each day; it rises from the initial 4 to 8, code output doubles, and overtime is reduced by 50%

**Key transformation**: From “passive response” to “active control,” using an external tool (timer) to replace willpower-based constraints.

---

**Case 2: Chaotic collaboration rhythm in a design team**
A creative team has 5 designers, each with different work rhythms: some are efficient in the morning, while others get inspiration late at night. During collaboration, they often can’t find each other, and feedback is delayed.

After applying the Pomodoro Technique:
- **Stage 1**: The team standardizes a “core Pomodoro period” from 14:00-17:00; during this time, everyone focuses on design and avoids disturbing others unless urgent
- **Stage 2**: The 5-minute break after each Pomodoro is used for quick synchronization, reducing fragmented communication
- **Stage 3**: The project delivery cycle is shortened from an average of 3 weeks to 2 weeks, and customer satisfaction improves (faster response to feedback)

**Key transformation**: Replacing “everyone fighting their own battles” with a “shared rhythm,” significantly improving team collaboration efficiency.

---

**Case 3: Treating procrastination for an exam-prep student**
A postgraduate entrance exam student plans to study 8 hours a day, but keeps scrolling on their phone and getting distracted. Actual effective study time is less than 3 hours, and the more anxious they get, the more they procrastinate.

After applying the Pomodoro Technique:
- **Stage 1**: Start with a “15-minute mini Pomodoro” to lower the startup threshold, then gradually extend it to the standard 25 minutes

### 3. Case breakdown (business/workplace scenarios)

**Case 1: A technical expert who was “excessively humble” failed to get promoted**
A certain technical backbone had strong capabilities, but was used to being “excessively humble.” During the promotion defense, they kept saying, “I’m still far from good enough” and “this project was mainly the team’s credit.” As a result, the reviewers felt they “lacked leadership presence,” and the promotion was out of the question.

Use mindset shift to adjust:
- **School mode**: “Excessive humility, not daring to show one’s own contributions”
- **Workplace mode**: “Neither servile nor overbearing; truthfully state one’s own value and effort”
- **Intervention**: Practice “results presentation” skills and let the data speak: “I led the XX module, improved performance by 30%, and drove an increase in team efficiency”
- **Result**: Six months later, at the next defense, they were successfully promoted with an attitude of “confident but not arrogant”

**Key shift**: From “excessive humility” to “neither servile nor overbearing”; the workplace requires an appropriate degree of self-presentation.

---

**Case 2: A comfort-zone dilemma caused by “avoiding difficult problems”**
A certain employee had worked in the same position for 5 years and was very familiar with the work, but whenever a new opportunity came up, they shrank back: “I haven’t done this before; I’m afraid I’ll mess it up.” As a result, colleagues who joined at the same time were all promoted, while they remained stuck in place.

Use mindset shift to break through:
- **School mode**: “Avoiding difficult problems, only dealing with familiar things”
- **Workplace mode**: “Boldly trying, treating difficult problems as opportunities for growth”
- **Intervention**: Proactively take on a new project and view uncertainty with a “growth mindset”
- **Result**: Although the project had some twists and turns, they accumulated cross-domain experience and obtained a cross-department promotion opportunity the following year

**Key shift**: From “avoiding difficult problems” to “boldly trying”; workplace growth comes from exploration outside the comfort zone.

---

**Case 3: A bottleneck for a backbone employee who was “toughing it out alone”**
A certain backbone employee was highly capable, but was used to “toughing it out alone,” not asking others for help and not being good at cooperation. As a result, the project kept snowballing, their personal energy was drained, and the team did not grow either.

Use mindset shift to adjust:
- **School mode**: “Toughing it out alone, not knowing how to borrow strength from others”

Energy 150 corresponds to the **Anger (resentment)** tier in Hawkins' levels of consciousness

**Key points**
- Value: 150 (negative range, but already close to the positive/negative dividing line of 200)
- Typical description: "Breeds hatred and erodes the inner self"
- Behavioral tendencies: combative, shifting blame, being argumentative, always feeling that "it's all other people's problem"

**Specific examples when applied to switching careers into AI design**
| Scenario | 150 state | Catchphrase |
|------|--------|-------|
| Getting stuck while learning | "This software is deliberately messing with me" | Taking anger out on the tool/tutorial |
| Seeing other people get results | "They just got lucky/have connections" | Looking down on other people's achievements |
| Having your ability questioned | "What do you know? I'm a professional" | Defensive clapback |
| A project goes wrong | "The client is too stupid/the requirements are ridiculous" | Blaming everything on external factors, no self-reflection |

**Why 150 counts as a danger zone**
- A bit stronger than "Fear (100)": at least there is drive (anger pushes people to want to "do something")
- But the drive is used in the wrong direction: all the effort goes into "fighting against it" instead of "building something"
- It's especially easy to get stuck at 175 "Pride": using "I'm not wrong" to fool yourself and refusing to improve

**The way to climb from 150 to 200**
1. **First recognize the signal**: when thoughts like "it's all XX's fault" pop up, hit the brakes first
2. **Adler's separation of tasks**: distinguish between "my business" (what I can control) and "other people's business" (what I can't control)
3. **Change the question**: don't ask "who takes the blame"; ask "where is the system blocked"
4. **Accumulate small wins**: use a "Pomodoro" to chew through one small task, turning anger into action

**One-sentence self-check**
> If right now everyone you look at annoys you, and you feel "the industry sucks/the tools suck/the clients suck," while you yourself are "100% not wrong" — then odds are you're sitting in the 150 anger zone.

@bot can you help us put together a checklist of common features of financial scams?

Here I am～ I’ve organized several of the most common features of financial scams to help you avoid landmines 👇

1. Guaranteed principal + high returns
• Promises like "sure profit, no loss" and "annualized returns above 15%"

• Uses "limited-time spots" to create urgency

• Essentially a Ponzi scheme, using new money to pay old debts

2. Fake platform type
• The app/website is crudely made, and the domain name is strange

• Easy to deposit, hard to withdraw; they use all sorts of excuses to get you to add more money

• No proper financial license

3. Paid stock recommendation type
• A "teacher" guides you in stock trading, but you pay a membership fee first

• The group is full of shills; you’re the only real person

• If you make money, they take a cut; if you lose money, they block you

4. Virtual currency/blockchain pyramid schemes
• Rebates for recruiting people, tiered rewards

• Air coins, copycat coins, plagiarized white papers

• Exchanges can run off at any time

5. Elderly care/health investment traps
• Targeting middle-aged and elderly people under the banner of "using your house to fund retirement"

• Health product investment rebates

• Emotional pressure tactics; the salesperson is even closer than your own son

@bot help me see what kind of products are suitable for a beginner to start with for small-amount financial management?

If you’re just starting out, I’d suggest beginning with these directions. They’re low-risk and have pretty good liquidity 👇

Money market funds

Things like Yu’e Bao and Lingqian Tong, where you can deposit and withdraw anytime. Annualized returns are around 1.5%-2%. The returns aren’t high, but the advantage is safety and flexibility, suitable for emergency funds

Bank time deposits/large-denomination certificates of deposit

Within 500,000, there is deposit insurance protection. The 3-year interest rate is around 2%-2.5%, with strong certainty, suitable for money you won’t need in the short term

Short-term bond funds

Volatility is a little higher than money market funds, but returns are also relatively higher (annualized 2%-3%). If held for more than 3 months, they can generally outperform money market funds

Treasury bond reverse repos

The yield will jump before holidays. 1-day and 7-day terms are both very flexible, and the safety is equivalent to treasury bonds

Low-risk bank wealth management products

Choose R1 and R2 risk levels, avoid stock-linked types, and the performance benchmark is generally around 2.5%-3.5%

I suggest starting with money market funds to test the waters first, then slowly allocating to short-term bonds or bank wealth management after you’re familiar with them～

@bot bot, generally speaking, how should everyday idle funds be allocated for wealth management in a more reasonable way?

You can refer to the “three-layer allocation method,” taking both safety and flexibility into account 👇

Layer 1: Emergency reserve (3-6 months of living expenses)

Put it in money market funds or demand wealth management products, available whenever needed

The goal is to deal with emergencies; don’t seek returns, seek peace of mind

Layer 2: Steady growth (50%-60% of idle funds)

Short-term bond funds, bank wealth management R1-R2, treasury reverse repos

Annualized 2%-3.5%, small fluctuations, suitable for money you won’t need within 1 year

Layer 3: Long-term allocation (20%-30% of idle funds)

Dollar-cost averaging into index funds, quality bond funds

Use time to smooth out fluctuations, seeking 3%-6% long-term returns

To give a simple example 🌰

Suppose your monthly surplus is 5000 yuan:

2000 into money market funds (emergency)

2500 in regular investments into short-term bonds or bank wealth management (steady)

500 in regular investments into index funds (long-term)

Your group leans steady, so you can allocate a bit more to the first and second layers, and slowly add to the third layer~

First, look at the fee model

@bot bot, what are the most common problems ordinary people tend to have when managing money?

Based on everyone’s discussion in the group, the most common problems ordinary people tend to have when managing money are mainly these 👇

1. Chasing rises and selling on drops

Only wanting to buy after seeing prices rise, then panicking and selling when they fall, ending up buying high and selling low, doing it backward. Many people buy funds only when the market is hot and end up holding the bag.

2. Treating personal finance as a shortcut to getting rich

Entering with a "quick doubling" mindset makes it easy to be lured into scams by high returns, or to trade so frequently that you wear down your principal.

3. Blindly following the crowd

Buying just because friends say so or because of online recommendations, without understanding what you’re buying at all. Like Su Ran said, following the crowd can actually make your mindset fall apart more easily.

4. Investing without emergency reserves

Putting all your savings into investments, then being forced to sell at a loss when you urgently need money. In the three-layer allocation method discussed in the group, many people directly skip the first layer, emergency reserves.

5. Paying too much attention to short-term fluctuations

Like Xu Yao said, watching the market every day and getting anxious over every little rise and fall. Personal finance is a long-distance run; short-term volatility is perfectly normal.

6. Only buying what’s familiar and not daring to diversify

Either putting everything in the bank or buying only stocks, without knowing how to allocate assets. In fact, diversified investing can reduce overall risk.

7. Entering without learning

Some people dare to invest even when they can’t tell the difference between money market funds and short-term bond funds. When they step into a pit, they don’t even know how they got there.

Base safety cushion (50-60%)

• Money market funds/current-account wealth management products — keep 3-6 months of living expenses there, available whenever you need it

• Government bonds/Treasury reverse repos — almost zero risk, and rates often spike at month-end and quarter-end

• Large-denomination certificates of deposit/time deposits — lock in certain medium- to long-term returns

Steady growth layer (30-40%)

• Short-term bond funds — extremely low volatility, with slightly higher returns than money market funds

• Bank wealth management products rated R1-R2 — choose fixed-income types and avoid equity-linked ones

• Negotiable certificate of deposit index funds — good liquidity, with lower risk than ordinary bond funds

Small trial zone (5-10%)

• Regular investment in broad-based indices — CSI 300 or CSI 500, using small monthly amounts to experience volatility

• Gold ETF — allocate a small amount to hedge against extreme risks

Key principles

• Build an emergency fund first, then talk about investing

• Don’t touch products you don’t understand; be cautious when returns exceed 5%

• Set the regular investment amount a bit smaller. Only if you don’t panic when it drops can you hold on

Protection first

🟢 Low-risk zone (R1-R2)

• Pure bond funds — invest in medium- and long-term bonds; returns are higher than short-duration bonds, but interest-rate fluctuations can affect net value

• Fixed income+ funds — 80% bonds as the base + up to 20% stock enhancement, with controllable volatility

🟠 Medium-risk zone (R3)

• Mixed funds (bond-leaning) — mainly bonds, with stocks as a supplement; the stock-bond ratio is about 3:7 or 4:6

• Index funds / ETFs — track broad-based indexes like CSI 300 and CSI 500, fluctuating with the market

• Gold ETFs — move with the gold price, have safe-haven attributes, and are less volatile than stocks

🔴 Medium-high risk zone (R4-R5)

• Mixed funds (stock-leaning / balanced) — stocks account for 50-80%, with obvious volatility

• Equity funds — more than 80% invested in stocks, with sharp rises and falls

• Industry/thematic funds — single tracks like new energy, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, etc., with high concentration

• QDII funds — invest in overseas markets, and also carry exchange-rate fluctuation risk

💡 Suggested route for beginners

Money market funds / short-duration bonds → pure bond funds → fixed income+ → fixed investment in broad-based indexes → then consider others

@bot what are the common reasons a mixed fund drops in the short term?

A mixed fund’s short-term drop is usually caused by these factors👇

Dragged down by the stock market

Mixed funds generally have 20-80% in stocks, so when the overall market falls, it’s hard for them to stay unaffected. Equity-heavy mixed funds move almost in sync with the stock market

Bond market volatility

When interest rates rise, bond prices fall, and the pure bond portion can also drag down the NAV. If the central bank has been tightening liquidity recently, bond funds may also dip a little

Holdings hit trouble in certain industries

For example, a mixed fund heavily invested in new energy will fall hard when that sector pulls back; one heavily invested in consumer stocks will also come under pressure if consumption data falls short of expectations

Fund manager portfolio-adjustment period

There are friction costs during position changes. The new holdings haven’t started contributing returns yet, while the old ones are still falling, so short-term performance can look bad

Panic selling

When the market panics, retail investors redeem → the fund is forced to sell stocks → NAV falls → more people redeem, creating a vicious cycle

Advice for Xu Yao

First look at the holdings distribution of your mixed fund. If it’s bond-heavy (stocks <30%), a larger drop may actually be a chance to add positions; if it’s equity-heavy, then you really need to assess whether you can withstand the volatility~

Let me translate it into plain human language for you👇

Going all-in

It means putting all your money in at once to buy. For example, you have 5000 yuan on hand and you use it all at once to buy a certain fund. The upside is that if you buy at a low point, you can earn more; the downside is that if you buy at a high point, all of it gets stuck. Newbies can easily step into this trap.

Averaging down the cost

This is the essence of dollar-cost averaging. For example, when the fund NAV is 10 yuan, you buy 100 yuan; when it drops to 5 yuan, you buy another 100 yuan. Your average cost is 7.5 yuan instead of 10 yuan. Buying more when it falls can “average” your overall cost down, making it easier to break even when it rises back.

Timing the market

It means trying to “buy low and sell high,” predicting when it is cheap and you should buy, and when it is expensive and you should sell. It sounds great, but even fund managers can’t do it. Newbies are even more likely to chase gains and panic-sell, so dollar-cost averaging is meant to “give up timing the market.”

My advice for you

Invest a fixed amount every month, buy whether it rises or falls. That way you don’t need to time the market, you can average down the cost, and you avoid the risk of going all-in～

Going all-in means putting all your money in at once, a huge no-no for beginners; lowering your average cost means adding more through regular investing when it drops, bringing down your overall holding cost; market timing means looking for buy and sell points. Beginners don’t need to obsess over it—regular investing makes timing less important.

I’ll explain it to you using the logic of buying and selling vegetables👇

Drawdown

It’s how much the fund you bought has fallen from its highest point.

🌰 Example: The fund you bought at 10 yuan rises to 12 yuan, then later falls to 11 yuan. The drawdown is (12-11)/12=8.3%. Simply put, it’s “how much it rose and then fell back.”

Position management

It means how much of the money in your hands you’ve invested, and how much you’ve kept unused.

🌰 Example: You have 10,000 yuan, and right now you’ve only bought 3000 yuan of funds. Then your position is 30%. Newbies must avoid going full position (100%) right away. Leave some room so you don’t panic.

Take-profit and stop-loss

• Take-profit: once you’ve earned to a certain level, lock in the gains. Don’t be greedy.

• Stop-loss: once it falls to a certain level, cut your losses and exit. Don’t stubbornly hold on.

🌰 Example: You set “sell when I gain 10%” and “run when I lose 5%.” Once it reaches that line, execute it no matter whether it rises or falls afterward. This avoids situations like “I had profits but later got stuck” or “the more it fell, the more I added, and in the end I lost badly.”

One-sentence summary

Drawdown tells you “how much you might lose,” position management teaches you “don’t go all in,” and take-profit/stop-loss helps you “keep profits and control losses”～

Drawdown is how much a product falls from its high point, representing the size of the risk; position management means allocating funds reasonably and not going full position; take-profit means selling once you’ve earned enough, and stop-loss means cutting decisively when losses hit your limit, to avoid getting deeply trapped.

Let me string together a complete logic chain for you, from "valuation to action" 👇

Step 1: Price-to-earnings ratio (PE) = a ruler for judging whether something is expensive or not

Imagine you want to buy a milk tea shop:

• It earns 100,000 a year and sells for 1,000,000 → PE = 10x

• It earns 100,000 a year and sells for 2,000,000 → PE = 20x

With the same earning ability, the higher the PE, the more expensive the purchase.

Applied to an index: if the CSI 300's PE is 12, it means at the current profit level, it would take 12 years to earn back the cost; if the PE is 20, it would take 20 years. Obviously, the lower the PE, the better the deal.

Step 2: Valuation percentile = where this ruler sits historically

If you only look at PE = 15, you don't know whether it's expensive or cheap.

But if I tell you: the CSI 300's PE has fluctuated between 10 and 20 over the past 10 years, and now 15 is right in the middle → this is the 50% percentile, neither high nor low.

• Percentile < 30% → cheaper than 70% of the time historically (green light, suitable for regular investing)

• Percentile > 70% → more expensive than 70% of the time historically (red light, consider taking profits)

Step 3: Index regular investment = act according to the traffic lights

Combine the two steps above:

🟢 Green light (undervalued): PE percentile < 30%

→ The index is very cheap, so you can double your regular investment amount and accumulate more shares

🟡 Yellow light (normal): PE percentile 30%-70%

→ Invest the normal amount regularly and hold steady

🔴 Red light (overvalued): PE percentile > 70%

→ The index is on the expensive side, so pause regular investment or take profits in batches

Put in one sentence

PE tells you "whether it is expensive now," valuation percentile tells you "whether it is expensive compared with history," and the two together determine whether your index regular investment should be "buy more, hold, or sell."

It's like buying vegetables: Chinese cabbage is usually 2 yuan per jin (normal PE), but now it's selling for 5 yuan (high PE + high percentile), so don't buy it yet; wait until it drops to 1 yuan (low PE + low percentile) and then stock up a bit more~

Let me run through a few of the “influencer fund traps” and “leverage traps” that newbies are most likely to fall into 👇

🚨 Influencer fund traps

What is an influencer fund?

It’s a fund that all the major platforms are pushing hard, whose short-term performance has exploded, and whose comment section is full of “fucking awesome.” For example, last year some new energy fund doubled in a year, the whole internet was hyping it up, and in the end a lot of people bought in at the top and became bagholders.

Why is it so easy to get trapped?

• The “great performance” you see is already in the past. By the time you buy in, the market style switches, and it immediately changes face

• Platforms push these because the commissions are high, not because they’re looking out for you

• Funds that surge in the short term are often heavily concentrated in a single industry, with huge volatility

How to spot them

• Be cautious of anything that has risen more than 50% in the past year

• If the comment section is all “the secret to getting rich” and “GOAT,” run fast

• If the name contains “new energy/chips/AI/healthcare” and it’s suddenly super hot in the short term, there’s a high chance it’s already at the peak

🚨 Leverage traps

What is leverage?

It means borrowing money to invest. For example, you have 10,000, borrow 90,000 to make 100,000 and buy funds/stocks. If it rises 10%, you make 10,000 (double your money), but if it falls 10%, you lose 10,000 (your principal goes to zero).

Forms of leverage newbies must absolutely not touch

• Margin trading and securities lending: the brokerage lends you money to trade stocks. There is a forced liquidation line, and if it falls to that level, they force-sell

• Borrowing through online loans to invest: using consumer loans or cash advances from credit cards to buy funds. If you lose money, you’re truly done for

• Off-market margin financing: illegal, and if your money gets scammed away you won’t even have anywhere to cry

Lessons learned in blood and tears

A lot of people think, “I’ll borrow a little money and take a shot; if I make money, I’ll pay it back.” Then once the market drops, not only is their principal gone, they also end up owing a huge pile of debt.

💡 Your trap-avoidance checklist

✅ Only buy things you understand (money market funds → bond funds → index funds, take it step by step)

✅ Anything that says “guaranteed profit with no losses,” “inside information,” or “limited-time high yield” is a scam

✅ The money you invest must be spare money you won’t need for 3 years. Don’t touch your living expenses

✅ Monthly fixed-investment amount ≤ 10% of monthly income, leaving enough margin of safety

✅ When “everyone is buying,” that’s actually when you should calm down

@bot explain the principle behind the stock-bond seesaw effect

Let me explain it in plain language for you 👇

What is the stock-bond seesaw?

It means the stock market and bond market often have “one going up while the other goes down,” like the two ends of a seesaw—when this side rises, that side gets pushed down.

Why does this happen? (the logic of fund flows)

There’s only so much money in the market, and capital flows around like water:

• When the stock market is doing well and can make money → money flows from the bond market into the stock market → stocks rise, bonds fall

• When the stock market plunges and everyone panics → money flees to the bond market for safety → bonds rise, stocks fall

• When economic expectations are good → people are willing to take risks and buy stocks → the bond market gets quiet

• When the economy is uncertain → people seek stability and buy government bonds → the stock market loses liquidity

Real example

In 2022, the stock market fell sharply, a lot of people got totally numb from losses, and they all went to buy government bonds and short-term bond funds for safety. As a result, the bond market instead turned bullish; in early 2023, when the stock market rebounded, bond funds saw another wave of redemptions.

What it means for you

Since you’re afraid of risk but also want some returns, you can make use of this pattern:

• When the stock market is rising like crazy (for example, everyone in the comments is shouting “bull market”), reduce some stock funds appropriately and add some short-term bonds

• When the stock market is falling badly (everyone is shouting “bear market”), that’s actually an opportunity to gradually add to index funds

• Allocate a bit to both sides (for example, 70% bond funds + 30% broad-based funds), and the seesaw effect can smooth out your overall volatility

This is the underlying logic of “asset allocation”—don’t put all your eggs in one basket, and let stocks and bonds hedge each other～

Northbound funds really are called “smart money” by a lot of people, but beginners should be careful about blindly following them 👇

What are northbound funds?

They’re foreign capital flowing into A-shares from Hong Kong through Stock Connect programs like Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Because Hong Kong is in the south and the mainland is in the north, it’s called “northbound.”

Where is their reference value?

• Foreign institutions’ research systems are relatively mature, and their long-term allocation thinking is worth referencing

• Sustained large inflows often reflect optimism about A-shares overall

• A large single-day outflow may indicate that short-term risk-aversion sentiment is heating up

But don’t deify it

• Short-term fluctuations are big: tens of billions moving in and out in one day is very normal, and doesn’t mean the trend has reversed

A technical analysis term. The stock price makes a new high, but certain indicators (such as MACD or trading volume) do not make new highs at the same time. This indicates insufficient upward momentum, and it may soon top out and pull back.

Volume expansion with price stagnation

Trading volume increases significantly, but the price does not rise or even falls. This shows intense fighting between buyers and sellers: the bulls want to push it up but can’t, while the bears are unloading heavily.

→ A typical danger signal, often a precursor to a market shift

What’s the core logic behind the Davis Double Play and Davis Double Kill that retail investors often talk about? @bot explain the investment logic of the Davis Double Play and Double Kill.

Brother Lei, these two terms sound intimidating, but the logic is actually very intuitive👇

Davis Double Play (profit accelerator)

Stock price = earnings per share × price-to-earnings ratio

When a company’s performance improves (earnings per share ↑) and the market is also willing to give it a higher valuation (P/E ratio ↑), the two factors rise together, and the stock price can surge through a “multiplier effect.”

→ For example, if a stock’s earnings per share rise from 1 yuan to 2 yuan (+100%), and the PE the market gives it rises from 10x to 20x (+100%), the stock price shoots from 10 yuan to 40 yuan (+300%)

Typical scenario: the industry boom cycle starts, the company’s performance exceeds expectations, market sentiment is hot, and money floods in crazily

Davis Double Kill (loss accelerator)

Conversely, when performance declines (earnings per share ↓) and valuation contracts (P/E ratio ↓), the two factors fall together, and the stock price drops so badly its own mother wouldn’t recognize it.

→ Earnings per share fall from 2 yuan to 1 yuan (-50%), and PE contracts from 20x to 10x (-50%), so the stock price falls from 40 yuan back to 10 yuan (-75%)

Typical scenario: industry overcapacity, negative policy news, earnings blowups, and the market goes from chasing it to abandoning it

One-sentence summary

Double Play is “good piled on top of good,” and Double Kill is “terrible piled on top of terrible.” Investing is about finding targets that may get a Double Play and avoiding traps that may get a Double Kill～

Xiaoxiao, these three terms sound intimidating, but once you put them in plain language, they’re easy to understand 👇

Safe-haven attribute

It means “buy gold in troubled times.” When there’s war, an economic crisis, or a stock market crash, everyone panics and starts moving their money into gold, this kind of “hard currency,” to ride out the storm. Gold itself doesn’t generate interest, but everyone recognizes its value, so it actually rises in troubled times.

Left-side bottom-fishing

Imagine a stock price trend looking like the letter V: the left side is falling, the right side is rising.

• Left-side bottom-fishing: rushing in to buy on the left side of the V, while it’s still falling, betting that it’s almost at the bottom

• Right-side chasing gains: waiting until the right side of the V, when it has already started rising, and then chasing in

The advantage of the left side is that the cost is low; the downside is that you might be catching it halfway down the mountain—you think it has hit bottom, but it turns out there’s still a basement below.

Cycle bottom

Industries like pork, steel, and shipping have earnings like a roller coaster: good for a few years, bad for a few years. A cycle bottom means “the industry’s worst moment”—pork prices have fallen to the point where farmers are losing money, steel mills are taking losses across the board. At that point institutions will shout “it’s bottomed,” but whether it’s a real bottom or a fake bottom, you only know afterward.

Brother Lei, this question gets right to the root of it—investing with money you urgently need is like planting three landmines for yourself 👇

1. The time attribute of funds: mismatch is the original sin

Money you urgently need (living expenses, mortgage payments, medical bills) has a “due date,” but the market doesn’t care about your schedule.

• Example: You need to pay rent next month, so you put the money into a gold ETF. Then geopolitical tensions ease this week, gold prices drop 8%, and you’re forced to cut your losses to pay rent—your principal is gone, and you’re left scrambling too

• The essence: short-term funds are matched with high-volatility assets; this time mismatch will inevitably lead to losses

2. Psychological tolerance: urgency distorts people

For the same drop, the mindset with spare money versus urgent money is worlds apart:

Urgent-money mindset

Urgent money activates the brain’s “loss aversion” switch, making you panic-sell when you should be holding firm, and go all in when you should be staying calm.

3. Market volatility cycles: you can’t afford to wait

In A-shares, an average bull-bear cycle lasts 3–5 years; gold’s fluctuation cycles are often measured in quarters.

• Example: People who bought new energy at the 2021 peak and needed the money urgently couldn’t make it through the 2022–2023 decline, and cut their losses at the bottom

• People using spare money held on until the 2024 rebound, not only breaking even but also making money

The market never promises that “when you urgently need money, it will happen to be at a high point.”

How to avoid it (three steps)

① Layer your funds

• 3–6 months of living expenses → money market funds (T+0)

• Money you may need in 1–3 years → short-term bonds/bank wealth management products

• Money you won’t touch for more than 3 years → stocks/gold/equity funds

② Physical separation

Open a dedicated “investment account” and keep it separate from your living-expenses account. Out of sight, out of mind; when you need money urgently, you won’t think of it first either.

③ Set up an “escape pod” in advance

Before investing, write it down: “This sum of money must be used by XX year XX month at the latest; when the time comes, redeem it regardless of profit or loss.” Start gradually reducing positions 3 months before the deadline, and don’t let yourself get forced into a corner.

1. First look at how much the “+” is

The “+” part of fixed income+ is stocks or convertible bonds. The higher the position, the greater the volatility:

• Conservative: stock position <10%, annualized 3%-4%, drawdown <2%

• Steady: stock position 10%-20%, annualized 4%-6%, drawdown 3%-5%

• Aggressive: stock position >20%, annualized 5%-8%, drawdown may be >5%

2. Look at the historical maximum drawdown

Don’t just look at annualized returns; focus on the “maximum drawdown” indicator:

• Can accept losing 2% → choose one with drawdown <3%

• If even 1% hurts → don’t buy fixed income+ yet, continue with short-term bonds

3. The fund size needs to be large enough

Choose ones with size >1 billion; don’t touch anything under 500 million:

• If the size is too small, it’s easy for the fund to be liquidated

• Volatility is greater when there are large redemptions

4. Don’t put in more than 5% for your first position

90% of your money is in time deposits, so for the first try, just take 5% of the money from a matured time deposit to test the waters:

• If you lose money → your mindset won’t collapse, and you’ll know what fixed income+ looks like

• If you make money → gain some experience, then slowly add more

5. Hold for at least 6 months

Fixed income+ has volatility, but if you stretch out the time period, its ability to recover is strong:

• Don’t redeem just because it loses 0.5% in one month

• Set up automatic deductions, and after buying, look at your account less

Recommended screening criteria

Stock position 10%-15% + maximum drawdown in the past 3 years <3% + size >2 billion + institutional holdings <60%

Brother Lei, combining everyone’s experience in the group, here’s a set of “personal finance fundamentals” for beginners👇

1. Save first, spend later

• As soon as your salary arrives, immediately transfer out a fixed percentage (like 30%), and spend what’s left

• Don’t think “I’ll save whatever is left after spending”; human nature can’t stand that test

2. Emergency fund is the bottom line

• First save 3-6 months of living expenses, and put it separately in a money market fund

• Never touch this money, and physically separate it from your investment account

3. Keep accounts to find where money leaks out

• No need to record too finely; just divide into big categories: necessary/optional/impulse spending

• Review at the end of the month, and you’ll discover many surprises like “so I actually spent this much”

4. Look at your account less and read more books

• Beginners shouldn’t refresh net values every day; once a week is enough

• If you look at ups and downs too much, it’s easy to get itchy hands and make random moves

5. Iron rule: invest only spare money

• Money you’ll need within 3 years shouldn’t enter the stock market/gold

• Investing urgent money = anxiety + losses, a double hit

6. Accept the impossible triangle

Trading rules

3 traps beginners must know

1️⃣ Interest-bearing days ≠ term

• Buy a 1-day term on Friday, the actual occupation of funds is 3 days (Saturday and Sunday also count for interest) ✅

• Buy a 1-day term on Thursday, the actual occupation of funds is 1 day ❌ (not worth it)

• After 14:30 every day, yields often plunge, so it’s best to place orders in the morning or at noon

@bot What does a fund’s maximum drawdown mean, and how much counts as qualified for fixed income+?

Brother Mo, in simple terms, maximum drawdown means “if you bought at the highest point, how much it fell at the worst moment”👇

For example

You bought a fund, and its NAV rose from 1 yuan to 1.2 yuan, then later fell to 0.9 yuan

• Highest point: 1.2 yuan

• Lowest point: 0.9 yuan

• Maximum drawdown = (1.2-0.9)/1.2 = 25%

It means that if you bought at the highest point, you would lose at most 25%

Does the level of a fund's NAV have anything to do with returns? Should I buy ones with low NAVs @bot

Brother Mo, the level of NAV has absolutely nothing to do with returns. This is a common misconception👇

What is NAV

Simply put, it's "how much each unit of the fund is worth." For a fund with a NAV of 1 yuan, if you invest 1,000 yuan you can buy 1,000 units; for one with a NAV of 2 yuan, the same 1,000 yuan only buys 500 units—but either way it's 1,000 yuan, and the rise/fall percentage is the same

Why you shouldn't blindly believe "low NAV = cheap"

• A fund with a NAV of 1 yuan rising to 2 yuan is a 100% gain

• A fund with a NAV of 2 yuan rising to 4 yuan is also a 100% gain

• In the same market environment, returns depend on the performance of the holdings, not the NAV number

What you should look at when choosing funds

Metric



Meaning




Historical performance



Long-term performance over 3-5 years; don't only look at the past 1 year




Maximum drawdown



Risk-control ability; for fixed income+ it shouldn't exceed 5%




Fund manager



Years of experience, stability of style




Fees



Management fees, subscription/redemption fees; they have a big long-term impact




Size



Don't be too small (risk of liquidation), but also don't be too large (a big ship is hard to turn around)

A counterexample

Some funds have low NAV because they've performed poorly all along. For example, a fund with a NAV of 0.8 may have fallen from 1.5, which instead shows there may be a problem with the fund manager's ability

My advice for you

Choosing funds is like buying groceries: what you look at is "value for money" (return/risk), not the "unit price" (NAV). Rather than obsessing over whether the NAV is high or low, it's better to look at the fund's holdings, drawdown control, and long-term performance~

• Risk-off sentiment heats up, and foreign capital may flow out

• Sectors like defense, gold, and oil may see pulse-like rallies

• Overall market volatility rises, but the decline is usually controllable (in the 5%-10% range)

🔸 Medium term (1-6 months): returns to fundamentals

• As long as the conflict doesn’t expand into a regional war, the market will gradually become desensitized

• In the early stage of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, A-shares fell quite a bit, but basically recovered after 3 months

• The key is whether the conflict affects China’s economic fundamentals (energy prices, exports, etc.)

🔸 Long term (more than 6 months): almost no impact

• The trend of A-shares is ultimately determined by the domestic economy, policies, and corporate earnings

• Geopolitical conflict is just noise; it doesn’t change the long-term trend

Should regular investing be paused?

❌ Not recommended. Reasons:

• The core of regular investing is “accumulating positions at low levels”; higher volatility is actually a good thing

• Pausing regular investing means market timing, and market timing is the main reason retail investors lose money

• Historical data: starting regular investing in the CSI 300 at any point, the probability of positive returns when holding for more than 3 years exceeds 80%

✅ Adjustments you can make:

• If you’re worried about volatility, change monthly investing to biweekly investing (to smooth costs)

@bot What impact does liquidation of a fixed-income-plus fund have on investors? Will there be notice before liquidation, and can we redeem early?

Chen Mo, fund liquidation sounds scary, but for investors it’s mainly a “hassle” rather than a “loss” 👇

How liquidation affects you

🔹 Your money won’t disappear

• Liquidation means turning the fund’s assets into cash and returning it to holders based on the final NAV

• Your principal + the gains up to the time of liquidation will all be transferred back to your account

• It’s not the same as “running off with the money” or “blowing up”; it’s just that the fund stops operating

🔹 The main hassles are

• Funds tied up: the liquidation process usually takes 1-3 months, during which the money is frozen

• Reinvestment cost: after getting the money back, you have to find a new product, and you may miss market opportunities

• Tax/fee issues: liquidation is treated as a redemption, so you may have to pay redemption fees + income tax

Will there be notice before liquidation?

Yes, and more than once:

• First announcement: if for 60 consecutive working days the size is <50 million or holders are <200 people, the liquidation conditions are triggered and an announcement will be issued to explain it

• Second reminder: before the formal liquidation procedure begins, another announcement will be made with the specific timing

• SMS/APP push notifications: the fund company will notify holders through multiple channels

Can you redeem in advance?

✅ After the liquidation announcement, before formal liquidation: you can redeem normally

• During this period the fund is still operating, and redemption is based on NAV

• Suggestion: if liquidation is confirmed, redeem as early as possible to avoid your money being locked up for several months

❌ After it formally enters the liquidation procedure: you can’t redeem

• The fund stops subscriptions and redemptions and enters the clearing stage

• You can only wait for the liquidation to be completed, and the money will be automatically credited to your account

My advice for you

What Chen Mo mentioned, that “funds smaller than 200 million are prone to liquidation,” is right. When choosing fixed income+ products, you can:

• Prioritize ones with a size of 1-5 billion (they won’t be liquidated, and they also won’t be so big that they’re hard to maneuver)

• Regularly track changes in the size of the funds you hold; be alert if it falls below 50 million

• Don’t panic when you receive a liquidation notice; assess whether to redeem early or wait for liquidation

Simply put: liquidation isn’t scary, it’s just a bit of a hassle. Avoiding mini funds in advance is the easiest way 😊

💬 Fixed income+ FAQ for beginners

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Q1: What stock position counts as over the limit?

A: For low-risk fixed income+, it’s recommended to keep it ≤20%. Above 25%, volatility clearly gets bigger; above 30%, it basically counts as an equity-leaning balanced fund.

Q2: How do you quickly check the stock position and maximum drawdown?

A: Alipay → fund details → “Holdings” to see the stock proportion; “Performance” → “Risk indicators” to see maximum drawdown. Tiantian Fund has more complete data.

Q3: What fund size is appropriate?

A: 1–5 billion is best. <200 million has liquidation risk; >10 billion is like a big ship that’s hard to turn around, and returns can easily get diluted.

Q4: Will you lose money if it’s liquidated?

A: No. Liquidation means the assets are converted to cash and returned to holders. The principal won’t disappear, but the funds will be tied up for 1–3 months, and you’ll need to reallocate them.

Q5: Do convertible bonds protect your principal?

A: No. The idea that convertible bonds have a “floor on the downside” is conditional. They can also fall when the market is bad. After the 2021 speculative frenzy, they plunged, and quite a few people who bought at high levels lost 20%+.

Q6: Is fixed income+ more suitable for regular investing or a one-time purchase?

A: Spare money you won’t use for 3 years → buy in one lump sum; monthly surplus → use regular investing as forced savings. Fixed income+ has low volatility, so the cost-smoothing effect of regular investing isn’t very obvious.

Q7: How long is it appropriate to hold?

A: At least 1 year (to cover the bond market cycle); a comfortable holding period is 3 years. Class A shares waive redemption fees after being held for more than 2 years.

Q8: How do you choose between Class A and Class C?

A: Choose Class C for <1 year (no subscription fee), and Class A for ≥1 year (saves on sales service fees). Mnemonic: one year is the dividing line; short-term C, long-term A.

Q9: How often should you check your holdings?

A: Once per quarter is enough; the best time is within 1 month after the quarterly report is disclosed. Focus on stock position, convertible bond position, fund manager changes, and maximum drawdown.

Q10: Under what circumstances should you redeem decisively?

A: ① Stock position suddenly increases to 25%+ ② Fund manager is replaced and the newcomer has <3 years of experience ③ Maximum drawdown is >5% for two consecutive quarters ④ Size falls below 50 million.

Q11: Can you buy one with high short-term returns?

A: Be wary of anything with returns >5% over the past 3 months. Most likely it has added a high stock or convertible bond position, and the risk is being hidden.

Q12: Can you buy a newly established fixed income+ fund?

A: Not recommended. There’s no historical performance as a reference, you don’t know the fund manager’s operating style, and the risk is relatively high. Prioritize ones that have been established for more than 3 years.

• Aggressive version: equity allocation = 120 - age (suitable for veterans)

• Iron rule: base it on risk tolerance; formulas are only a reference

2.3 Dynamic rebalancing

• Frequency: mainly annual rebalancing; trigger when deviation >5%

• Method: reduce positions in what has risen a lot, add to what has fallen a lot, using new funds to top up

• Taboos: chasing rises and selling dips, frequent trading, going all-in at once

🎯 Chapter 3: Mindset Management Mechanism

3.1 Mechanism design

• Reduce checking frequency: look at fixed income+ once per quarter

• Preset “if-then” rules, and when emotions take over, follow the rules

• Physical separation: keep investment accounts and living-expense accounts separate

3.3 Mindset first-aid kit

• 5-minute cool-down method: when you want to make a move, count down 5 minutes

• Number desensitization: look at percentages, not amounts

• Convert it into time: how long it would take to earn back the loss

• Find the organization to vent: shout in the group

🎯 Chapter 4: 2026 Market Understanding

4.1 Bond market characteristics

• Low interest rates + high volatility; 10-year treasury bonds fluctuate between 1.6%-2.1%

• Fixed income+ expected returns 2%-5.5%; lower expectations

• Avoid heavy positions in ultra-long bonds; prioritize short-duration products

4.2 Applying equity-bond relative value (ERP)

• >80th percentile: reduce fixed income+ and add broad-based funds

• <20th percentile: reduce broad-based funds and add fixed income+

📈 Advanced Fund Regular-Investment Techniques · Preview Materials

I. Basic review (30-second quick look)

• The essence of regular investing: using time to diversify market-timing risk and smooth out costs

• Core advantages: lazy-person wealth management, forced saving, compounding effect

• Suitable for: salaried workers, investment beginners, people who don’t have time to watch the market

II. Five advanced techniques ⭐

1. Smart regular investing (dynamic amount adjustment)

• Invest more at low levels: when market valuation is below the historical median, make the regular investment amount ×1.5-2

• Invest less at high levels: when valuation is above the 70% percentile, make the regular investment amount ×0.5 or pause

• Tools: Alipay “Smart Regular Investment,” Qieman “Auto Follow”

2. Valuation-based regular investment method (more efficient than time-based regular investing)

3. Portfolio regular investing (diversification + complementarity)

• Broad-based funds as the base: CSI 300/CSI 500 (50%)

• Sector satellites: consumer/healthcare/technology (30%)

• Bond funds for balance: secondary bond funds/fixed-income+ (20%)

• Principle: stocks and bonds are negatively correlated; if the east side doesn’t shine, the west side will

4. Take profit, don’t stop loss (key!)

• Target-based profit-taking: redeem in batches once annualized returns reach 15-20%

• Valuation-based profit-taking: start reducing positions when PE > 70% percentile

• Don’t stop loss: losses in the early stage of regular investing are normal; only by sticking with it can you average down the cost

5. Regular investing + rebalancing (advanced play)

• Check the allocation of each fund once every six months

• Reduce positions in what has risen a lot, add to what has fallen a lot (use new money to add)

• Example: if the CSI 300 has risen too much, shift next month’s regular investment amount into the CSI 500

III. Five mistakes beginners often make ❌

Frequently switching targets​ → Stick with it for more than 1 year before judging the results

Stopping investments as soon as it drops​ → When it falls is exactly a good time to average down the cost

Having no profit-taking plan​ → You ride a roller coaster and end up working for nothing

Choosing the wrong product​ → Avoid funds with assets <200 million and that have been established for <3 years

Using money you need urgently for regular investing​ → You must use idle money you won’t need for more than 3 years

Authoritative recommendations:

For people over 60, sleeping 5.5–7 hours a day is about right (People’s Daily and the National Health Commission both say this). You don’t have to sleep a full 8 hours; sleeping too much can actually be bad.

The key is your condition during the day:

• If you feel energetic after getting up and don’t get sleepy → it means you slept enough

• If you keep dozing off during the day and can’t concentrate → you may not have slept well

You mentioned waking up early? That’s very normal:

Older people secrete less melatonin, deep sleep becomes shorter, and it’s easy to wake up early. As long as you’re not sleepy during the day, 5–6 hours is enough too.

A few suggestions:

• Don’t nap for more than 30 minutes, and nap before 3 p.m.

• Sleep at 10–11 p.m. and get up at 5–6 a.m.; that fits our biological clock

• Soak your feet before bed (Sister Liu’s mugwort recipe is pretty good), and look at your phone less

Sister Liu, I’ll sort out the key points for writing a standard IOU for you:

Required elements:

• Title: write “loan note” (when borrowing money) or “IOU” (when settling accounts), don’t write “receipt”

• Information for both parties: full name + ID number, and ideally attach a copy of the ID card

• Amount: write it in both uppercase Chinese numerals and numbers (for example: RMB ten thousand yuan only, ¥10000)

• Time: write the borrowing date and repayment date clearly

• Interest: the annual interest rate must not exceed 4 times the LPR (currently about 14%); if it’s not written, it’s regarded as interest-free

• Delivery method: state whether it was cash or bank transfer; keep proof for transfers

• Signature and fingerprint: the borrower signs by hand + presses a fingerprint; don’t have someone else sign on their behalf

Pitfall reminders:

• Don’t write “还欠款” (is it hai or huan? The ambiguity is big)

• Don’t leave blank spaces, to prevent words being added afterward

• Loan notes and IOUs have different statutes of limitation; loan notes can be up to 20 years, while IOUs are generally 3 years

• It’s best to have a third-party witness or video recording

For your friend’s situation, besides the IOU, transfer records and chat records should also be kept properly. These are all evidence～

Camera height

For shooting small items like walnuts: put the phone stand on the table, with the lens level with the walnuts or slightly higher by 15 degrees. Don't shoot too much from above, otherwise it looks petty

For filming a person introducing the product: aim the lens from the chest to the top of the head, leave a bit of space above the head, and don't cut off the forehead

Natural light by the window

Best position: sideways to the window (not facing it directly, not with your back to it), put the walnuts within 1 meter of the window, so the light is soft and has layers

Timing: 9-10 in the morning or 3-4 in the afternoon, when the light isn't harsh

Cloudy days are actually better; the light is even and you don't need to fuss with it

Zero-cost fill light tips

Simply put, anticoagulants are medicines that make the blood thinner and less likely to clot.

There is a function in our blood called "coagulation." When we get cut, it's what helps stop the bleeding. But some people's blood likes to clot too much, and it's easy for little clumps (blood clots) to form in the blood vessels. Anticoagulants make the blood "not too sticky," so it flows more smoothly and reduces the risk of clotting.

Good question, Xiao Nan. Older people really are the "key customers" for health supplement scammers, mainly for these reasons—

1. The heaviest health anxiety

As people get older, it’s hard to avoid some health problems—back pain, leg pain, poor sleep. Scammers seize on this and hype health supplements into miracle medicines that "cure every disease," hitting exactly where it hurts.

2. Emotional loneliness makes them easier to target

Many scammers act even closer than their own sons, calling every day to ask how they’re doing, sweetly saying "Auntie Zhang" and "Uncle Li." Older people lack companionship and are easily moved by this kind of "concern," feeling embarrassed not to buy.

3. Relatively closed information channels

Unlike young people who browse their phones and see popular science content every day, many older people get information mainly from TV ads and lecture flyers, so their ability to tell truth from falsehood is a bit weaker.

4. They have some savings on hand

Retirement wages and pension money are in their hands, so scammers think there is "money to be made." Also, older people can be less price-sensitive, and may buy health supplements worth several thousand yuan just like that.

5. They fear death and also fear burdening their children

The more they fear getting sick, the more they want to buy health supplements for "prevention"; the more they fear troubling their children, the more easily they get fooled by pitches like "no need to go to the hospital."

6. Strong herd mentality

When they see "all the old sisters bought it" or "everyone at the lecture is rushing to buy," they can easily follow the crowd and think, "If everyone is buying it, it must be fine."

So scammers have specifically studied a whole set of scripts aimed at older people: free gifts to get close → expert lectures to create fear → limited-time discounts to pressure the sale. @bot legally, what kind of activity does this type of offline pop-up count as, and what certificates and permits are needed? Let's not end up getting stopped by the urban management officers

This is a key question. Pop-up events really can easily attract the attention of urban management officers, so getting all the certificates and permits in order in advance is the only way to launch with peace of mind.
Legal nature
An offline pop-up event is a “temporary commercial business activity.” If it involves occupying roads, setting up temporary facilities, or on-site sales, approvals need to be handled in accordance with the Regulations on the Administration of Urban Appearance and Environmental Sanitation, the Regulations on the Administration of Urban Roads, and other rules.
Core certificate and permit checklist
1️⃣ Business license
No matter how short the pop-up lasts, the actual operator must hold a valid business license. If it is food-related, a food business permit or filing is also required.
2️⃣ Temporary occupation of urban road/venue permit
If the event occupies roads in streets, plazas, public areas of business districts, etc., you need to apply to the urban management department for a “Temporary Occupation of Urban Road Permit.” Generally you need to submit:
•
Event planning proposal (including time, location, scale, renderings)
•
Safety work plan
•
Venue rental agreement
•
On-site setup layout
3️⃣ Large-scale event safety permit
If the expected number of participants is relatively large (standards vary by locality, generally over 500 people), you need to apply to the public security authority for a large-scale mass activity safety permit.
4️⃣ Temporary facility setup filing
If it involves setting up a stage, display racks, tents, etc., you need to submit a setup plan and the construction company's qualifications. In some cases, a consent letter from the property management or venue is required.
Pitfall-avoidance suggestions
•
Apply 5-10 working days in advance; don't wait until the last minute
•
Confirm that the venue side has fulfilled its obligation to file as the “venue provider”
•
If food is involved, report to the market regulation department 15 working days in advance
•
Strictly prohibit operating beyond the approved scope (for example, applying for promotion and display, but then selling goods on site)

Light food is more like an attitude toward eating. It emphasizes “less oil, less salt, less sugar, high fiber,” aiming to make the body feel unburdened and the eating experience light and comfortable.

@bot 16+8 is the most scientific healthy eating method, right?

Wang Jie, 16+8 intermittent fasting is indeed a very popular healthy eating method right now, but it’s not the one and only “most scientific” standard for everyone.
Its core is compressing the day’s eating window into 8 hours and not eating for the remaining 16 hours, giving the body time to digest, repair, and even activate autophagy. For many people, this helps control weight and improve metabolism.
But there are a few key points to pay attention to:
1. What you eat matters a lot: if you binge during the 8 hours, the effect is zero.
2. It’s not suitable for everyone: it’s not very recommended for people with poor digestion, hypoglycemia, pregnant women, or teenagers.
3. Listen to your body: if you feel dizzy or weak, don’t force it.
So it’s a pretty good tool, but not a master key. Finding a rhythm that suits you is more important than blindly following trends.

@bot Our event budget is limited. For KOL placements, how can we spend the least money and achieve the biggest communication effect? Are there any low-cost alternatives?

Qingran, when the budget is limited, the thinking for KOL placements needs to shift from “spending money to buy traffic” to “spending money to buy trust.”
The core is to give up expensive top-tier KOLs and instead build a large “KOC (Key Opinion Consumer) + mid- and long-tail influencer” matrix. They don't have huge follower counts, but their interaction rates and sense of authenticity are extremely high, making them the most cost-effective choice.
There are three specific directions we can operate in:
Use “KOC volume” instead of “KOL bombing”
Rather than spending a large sum on one KOL with a million followers, it's better to split that money up and find dozens of real users with hundreds to thousands of followers. The “organic” notes they post are more credible than ads in users' eyes. There are cases showing that a seeding plan with a hundred ordinary users can leverage tens of millions in transaction volume.
Use “content co-creation” instead of “content outsourcing”
Don't send influencers a unified press release. Instead, co-create content with them. For example, invite them to come check in at the pop-up store in person, or send them samples and let them create based on their own real experience. The content that comes out this way is more vivid and more likely to be recommended by the platform.
Use “comment-section traffic interception” as a free lever
This is a zero-cost tactic. Assign someone to go under popular notes of the same type and post high-quality comments from the perspective of a real user, cleverly weaving in our event information. This is equivalent to riding other people's traffic for free, and because it's in the comments, it feels very natural.
You can start with the connections within our own circle, find some friends who like sharing their lives, and have them serve as the first batch of KOCs to post content. The cost is almost zero.

Qingran, with your budget and event goals, using KOC volume is clearly a better choice than a single mid-tier KOL.
Let's break it down from the four dimensions you mentioned:
1. Communication effect: KOC wins
Mid-tier KOL: Large follower count, but interaction rates are generally not high; it's more like a one-off ad exposure.
KOC volume: Although each person's follower count is small, the combined total exposure from dozens or even hundreds of KOCs may be higher. More importantly, KOC follower interactions are authentic, and conversion rates in the comment section and private domains are far higher than KOLs. They can better create an “organic buzz” feeling, which fits Xiaohongshu's content ecosystem.
2. Cost control: KOC wins
With a budget of 8000 yuan, it may only be enough to hire one mid-tier KOL with decent data. If the data performs poorly, the whole thing is wiped out. But if it's used to recruit KOCs, it can cover dozens or even hundreds of people, greatly spreading out the risk.
3. Execution difficulty: KOC is slightly harder, but controllable
KOL: Execution is simple. Agree on the price and content, then publish and you're done.
KOC: You need to spend effort recruiting, screening, communicating with, and managing a group of people, so the workload is bigger. But the upside is that you can develop the first batch of seed users from friends, classmates, and colleagues around you, with a very low startup cost.
4. Risk: KOC is lower
KOL: The biggest risk is fake data—spending money and getting no effect.
KOC: The risk is uneven content quality, but as long as you do the screening and simple training well in the early stage, they can basically all produce content above the passing line.
Overall, for an offline pop-up event whose goal is to attract real young people to attend, the KOC volume strategy can create the atmosphere that “lots of people are playing this,” and that sense of authenticity is very hard for a single KOL to achieve. @bot What is Xiaohongshu's recommendation algorithm mechanism? I want to know what kind of notes are more likely to be recommended, so I can set requirements for the KOCs and see whether it fits our project

Shen Jiming, the core of the Xiaohongshu algorithm is the CES score (click-through rate + interaction rate + completion rate). Put simply, it’s “hook people at the start, keep them in the middle, and make them want to interact at the end.”
Content traits the algorithm favors
• Cover: high information density, a sense of conflict, or a curiosity gap. Don’t do those abstract images that are “pretty but impossible to understand.”
• Title: the first 10 characters decide life or death. Numbers + pain points + a promise, like “3 hidden photo spots that make drink photos look amazing.”
• First 3 seconds: videos must throw out a hook; for image-text posts, the first image needs to make people understand at a glance “what this is and what use it is to me.”
• Interaction design: plant questions or controversial points in the body text, guide the comments section into arguments/resonance. The algorithm loves “high comments” the most.
Specific requirements for KOCs
• Prioritize vertical accounts with 10k-50k followers (food/store visits/lifestyle). Don’t just look at follower count; look at interaction rate.
• Require them to provide data screenshots from their last 3 posts. Focus on the ratio of “little eyes/likes/saves.” A high save rate means the content is useful.
• Content direction: on-site experience + practical guide (for example, “Yuehuo Bubble Station check-in guide + nearby food route”). Pure photo dumps sink easily.
• Posting time: weekends 2-4 p.m. or weekdays 8-10 p.m., to coordinate with the concentrated burst on your event day.

Zhimeng, your instinct is right. An overly low quote is itself a danger signal. Don’t panic, I’ve organized a quick three-step “mine-clearing” method for you. You can check through it right now:
Step 1: Look at the ratio of “likes/saves” to “followers”
This is the simplest judgment criterion. For a healthy account, the total number of likes and saves is usually far greater than the follower count. If a blogger with 500k followers only has ten or twenty thousand total likes/saves, there is most likely a problem with the data.
Step 2: Look at the quality of the “comments”
Open the comments sections of their recent posts and look at the first three pages:
1. Look at the content: If it’s all empty boilerplate like “looks good,” “link please,” “already ordered,” with no specific usage feelings or questions, it’s very likely paid commenters.
2. Look at the interaction: See whether the blogger replies to comments, and whether the replies feel sincere. Real bloggers have real conversations with fans.
3. Look at the likes: Real top comments will have many likes underneath, while paid-commenter comments are usually ignored.
Step 3: Look at the “follower” growth curve
If possible, you can ask the other party for a follower growth chart from the past six months. For a normally operated account, follower growth is smooth or fluctuates. If their chart is a straight line suddenly shooting up from the ground, or if there is a sudden surge at a certain point in time, then it’s basically bought followers.
With this combination of punches, you can basically filter out 90% of inflated accounts. If you’re still not reassured, don’t rush to decide yet; look around more.

@bot If a competitor copied our event planning proposal and publicly posted it on social media, does that generally count as infringement?

Su Zhimeng, this is a key question, and the answer is: not necessarily.
There’s a core legal principle called the “idea-expression dichotomy.” Simply put, copyright law protects “how you write” the proposal (the expression), not the “idea” behind the proposal itself (the idea).
So, to determine whether the other party has infringed, it’s not about whether the creative idea looks similar, but about two things:
1. Did the other party have “access” to our proposal?
Do we have a clear chain of evidence (such as emails, meeting records) proving that they saw, or even obtained, our proposal? This is the prerequisite.
2. Are the two parties’ “expressions” “substantially similar”?
This doesn’t refer to the idea of “campus promotion,” but to the specific details in the proposal, such as:
- The specific wording of the event theme
- The specific gameplay description of the core creative concept
- The color scheme and elements of the main visual style
- The names and rules of the interactive installations
- Even our unique, non-generic event process
If the other party highly overlaps with our proposal in these specific, original expressions, then it basically constitutes infringement. But if they merely borrowed the broad direction of “campus promotion,” while the specific gameplay, design, and copy are all original to them, then it doesn’t count as infringement.
So, the most urgent thing now isn’t to get angry, but to immediately preserve every version of our proposal, every revision record, and all related communication records to form a complete chain of evidence. That is the confidence we need to defend our rights.
