I. Materials Support Contingency Plan
Pre-event prevention:
1. “Dual backups” for core materials: For core promotional items such as key visual posters and roll-up banners, be sure to prepare both online and offline versions. Send the online version to all relevant personnel in advance, just in case.

   • Immediately contact the original supplier to assess the possibility and timing of urgent replenishment.
   • At the same time, look for backup suppliers, compare prices from multiple parties, and choose the best option.

II. Partner Management Contingency Plan
Pre-event prevention:
1. KOC/KOL “contract + backup” mechanism: All cooperating KOCs/KOLs must sign formal contracts that clearly state liability for breach of contract. At the same time, a backup list of equivalent scale must be prepared in case something happens.
2. Supplier “whitelist” system: Establish a verified and reliable supplier pool, and regularly evaluate their service quality.
Post-incident remedies:
1. KOC backing out after taking the order (Owner: media/PR; response time: within 1 hour):
   • Priority 1: Immediately activate the backup list, contact substitute KOCs, and negotiate compensation terms.

2. Supplier breach of contract (Owner: procurement/project manager; response time: within 2 hours):
   • Hold them accountable according to the contract terms and require compensation for losses.
   • Immediately activate a backup supplier from the “whitelist” to ensure the event continues.
Lessons learned: The core issue with KOCs backing out after taking the order is the lack of binding force and backup plans. For the next collaboration, we must write both “liquidated damages” and “backup candidates” into the contract, so the other party won’t dare to stand us up easily.

@Gu Jia Safe way to do corrective exercises (knee-chest position):
1. Prerequisite: only do them after the doctor confirms there are no contraindications. This is the red line.
2. Posture: kneel on the bed, chest against the bed, hips raised, thighs perpendicular to the bed. Once in the morning and once at night, 10 to 15 minutes each time.
3. Timing: empty the bladder first, and do it more than an hour after eating. If she feels dizzy, has palpitations, or her belly tightens during it, stop immediately.
4. Recheck after doing it for a week. Don’t just keep doing it blindly without follow-up.
The main risks are extreme situations like placental abruption and compression of the umbilical cord, so the prerequisite is ruling out contraindications.
Other methods: walk more, rest on the left side, avoid sitting for long periods. Some hospitals can do external cephalic version, performed by a doctor.

@Lin Xiatian She doesn’t necessarily have to do the exercises:
1. A considerable proportion of breech babies turn on their own in late pregnancy, especially since 32 weeks is still early.
2. Adjustment methods without movements: lie more on the left side, walk for half an hour every day, avoid sitting or lying for too long, and keep bowel movements smooth.
3. If the doctor recommends exercises after assessment, then do them. If the doctor didn’t ask her to, then observe and wait.
4. If the baby still hasn’t turned by 36 weeks, the doctor will assess external cephalic version or discuss the delivery method.
Summary: first rule out contraindications. Natural turning is best; exercises are only one auxiliary method.

2. Placenta previa or abnormal placental position
3. Too much or too little amniotic fluid
4. Signs of preterm labor, premature rupture of membranes, vaginal bleeding
5. Gestational hypertension, twins or multiples
6. Previous C-section or uterine surgery

1. Dab dry, don’t wipe dry: after washing the bottom, gently dab with a soft cotton cloth. Friction itself can irritate the skin, and many people fail at this step

@Wen Niannian Here’s the science version for your mother-in-law:
1. Baby powder is a powder. When you pat it on, dust floats in the air, and the baby can inhale it into the lungs. Young babies’ airways are delicate
2. When powder meets sweat or urine, it clumps up and gets stuck in skin folds, which actually worsens friction and stuffiness
3. Cornstarch-type powders may also breed bacteria

@Gu Jia Good question. Traditional methods really do have traps:
[Why iron-fortified rice cereal is recommended]
1. After 6 months, the iron the baby brought from the mother's body is basically used up, and the iron in breast milk and formula isn't enough
2. Iron-fortified rice cereal is easy to digest, low-allergen, and has enough iron. It's widely recognized as the first bite
[The traps in traditional methods]
1. Rice water: mainly water and starch, no iron and no nutrition. It fills the belly with water and takes up stomach space
2. Egg yolk: an old idea from before. Now it's recommended to add it after 8 months; too early has a high allergy risk, and the absorption rate of iron in egg yolk is poor
3. Fruit juice and vegetable water: no nutrition and also take up milk intake
So choosing iron-fortified rice cereal for the first bite isn't superstition; it's evidence-based

[How to add]
1. Add only one new ingredient each time, and eat it for three consecutive days
2. Start with a small spoonful and gradually increase the amount
[Allergy signs]
1. Skin: rashes, hives, redness around the mouth
2. Gastrointestinal: vomiting, diarrhea, blood in the stool
3. Respiratory tract: sneezing, coughing, wheezing
[What to do if signs appear]
1. Stop the new ingredient immediately, and record what was eaten and how long it took for the reaction to appear

[General order for introducing solid foods]
🥣 Stage 1 (from 6 months): single-grain purees (iron-fortified rice cereal is most recommended), root-vegetable purees (pumpkin, carrot, potato), fruit purees (banana, apple)
🥩 Stage 2 (7-8 months): meat puree (chicken, pork), tofu, egg yolk (add egg white a bit later; it’s more likely to cause allergies)
🍚 Stage 3 (9-10 months): soft, mushy porridge and finely minced foods; start practicing chewing
🍽️ Stage 4 (10-12 months): gradually transition toward family foods, with little salt, little sugar, and low irritation

1. Add only one new ingredient each time, observe for 3 days, and only add the next one after confirming there’s no allergy
2. The order isn’t an iron rule; adjust according to the baby’s acceptance
3. Don’t chase quantity for the first bite; one small spoonful is enough
4. Breast milk/formula is still the staple food before age 1. Solid foods are “practice eating,” not a replacement for milk

@Wen Niannian A must-ask question for new parents. I’ve organized it here👇

[Things to note before vaccination]
1. The baby should be in good condition: if they have a fever (temperature ≥37.5℃), are in an acute infection period, or are having a severe eczema flare-up, postpone the vaccination and ask a doctor first
2. Tell the doctor about allergy history, reactions to the last vaccination, and any medications currently being used
3. Feed the baby before going. Getting vaccinated on an empty stomach can make them faint from the shot (older babies)

[Things to note after vaccination]
1. Stay for observation for 30 minutes. Don’t leave right away; this is both required and a safeguard
2. Don’t rub the injection site hard that day, and avoid strenuous activity
3. Bathing: it’s best not to bathe on the day of vaccination. Bathe normally the next day, but don’t scrub the injection site
4. Low-grade fever (below 38.5℃), redness/swelling, or a hard lump at the injection site: normal reactions. Drink plenty of water and observe; they usually go away in 1-3 days
5. High fever that won’t go down, persistent crying, or large-area redness and swelling at the injection site: seek medical care promptly, don’t just tough it out

[Special reminders]
- For oral polio vaccine (sugar pill), don’t feed hot food or hot water half an hour before or after; it affects the activity
- Keep the vaccination record book safe. It will be checked when starting kindergarten and school

@bot What bath water temperature is suitable for a newborn, and what should we pay attention to when bathing them?

@Wen Niannian For bathing a newborn, if you get the temperature and timing right, you’ve basically handled most of it 👇

[Water temperature]
- Water temperature: 37–38°C. Use a water thermometer; don’t estimate with your elbow, the margin of error is big.
- Room temperature: 24–26°C. Turn on the air conditioner or heater before the bath to keep the baby from getting cold while changing clothes.

[Timing]
- 5–10 minutes each time. Don’t soak too long; newborns have thin skin and lose heat easily.
- Bathe them at least 1 hour after feeding. They’re prone to spitting up right after eating.

[Details]
- Put in cold water first, then add hot water, to prevent uneven water temperature.
- Before the belly button has healed, whether doing a sponge bath or tub bath, avoid getting water on the umbilical area.
- After bathing, wrap them in a bath towel immediately and start drying from the head. Don’t leave them exposed in the air.
- If water gets in the ear, gently absorb it with a cotton swab on the outer ear. Don’t poke into the ear canal.

[Unnecessary steps]
- You don’t need to use body wash every time. Mainly use clean water; using baby wash 1–2 times a week is enough.
- No need for baby powder. Powder can be inhaled easily, and it’s generally not recommended nowadays.

[What the doctor will check]
🔹 Weight, length, head circumference — compared with birth to see whether the growth curve is normal

📋 Bring the checkup records/booklet from birth so the doctor can compare

@bot Can we start doing infant massage around when the baby is one month old? Anything we should pay attention to?

@Wen Niannian Around one month old is totally fine for infant massage; the earlier you build the routine, the better 👇

[When is best]
🔹 Within 15-20 minutes after a bath, when the baby is awake and in a stable mood
🔹 Don’t do it when the baby is hungry, has just finished eating, or is sleepy; they’re more likely to cry and resist
🔹 10-15 minutes each time. No need to insist on finishing every step

[Suggested order (top to bottom)]
1. Head and face: Use both thumbs to gently push from the center of the forehead out to the sides, then lightly trace a smile line upward from the chin
2. Chest: Use both hands alternately to gently push outward from the chest, like turning pages in a book
3. Abdomen: Make clockwise circles, avoiding the navel area (skip this step before the umbilical cord stump has fallen off)
4. Limbs: From the top of the thigh down to the ankle, gently hold and stroke downward; massage hands and feet separately
5. Back: With the baby lying on their tummy, use both hands to gently stroke outward from both sides of the spine

[Things to note]
⚠️ Use baby-specific moisturizing oil or lotion; don’t use talcum powder
⚠️ Keep the room temperature at 26-28 degrees, and don’t let the baby get cold after taking clothes off
⚠️ If the baby starts crying or wriggling in resistance, stop immediately; don’t force yourself to finish
⚠️ Skip the abdomen step before the umbilical cord stump has fallen off

@bot in the new season meta, is it easier to climb by practicing overtuned meta junglers, or steadier to practice utility-type blue-collar junglers? Analyze the tempo differences between the two jungle playstyles across solo queue, duo queue, and five-stack scenarios, and also say which one is more suitable for ordinary players whose mentality blows up easily.

That’s a good question. If you want to climb in the new season, choosing the right jungle mindset is key.

Overtuned meta junglers (like Jing, Lan): the core is farming gold, ganking, and snowballing. You rely on your own mechanics to crush the enemy and are the team’s absolute damage core.

Utility-type blue-collar junglers (like Agudo, tank Kai): the core is giving up economy, protecting teammates, initiating fights and soaking damage. You win through teamwork and macro, and you’re the team’s tempo engine.

Solo queue: prioritize overtuned junglers. Because you can’t count on random teammates, you can only trust yourself; pick a hero that can carry and keep your fate in your own hands. Duo/five-stack: utility junglers are steadier. With fixed teammates cooperating, you can build a system around you, like “Sun Bin + Agudo.” The room for error is high, and you can maximize the team advantage.

Overall, for ordinary players whose mentality blows up easily, I’d recommend practicing a utility-type blue-collar jungler.

Because once overtuned junglers fall behind, it’s very easy to mentally boom because you can’t carry. But the blue-collar jungle mindset is about serving the team: if you win, it’s the team’s credit; if you lose, it’s not entirely your fault either. The pressure is much lower, and the game experience is more stable.

Of course, the best approach is to practice both styles and switch flexibly based on the lineup and your mood. Good luck climbing in the new season!

An average woman’s basal metabolic rate is around 1300, and a man’s is around 1600. To reach a daily burn of 2440, you’d need to burn another 800-1100 kcal on top of basal metabolism — equivalent to jogging for 1.5 hours or doing 1 hour of high-intensity training

Extreme dieting vs structured fat loss

Extreme dieting	Structured fat loss
Cut calories extremely low (<1000)	Moderate deficit (300-500 kcal)
Lose muscle, metabolism drops	Preserve muscle, metabolism stays stable
Rebound fast, easy to binge	Sustainable, less likely to rebound
Risk of malnutrition	Balanced nutrition

What’s the principle
Mantou is mainly carbs (starch), and its calories actually aren’t low—a 100g mantou is about 220 kcal, roughly the same as a bowl of rice. The so-called “mantou weight-loss method” is usually:
• Using mantou to replace high-oil, high-salt takeout/snacks
• A monotonous diet leading to lower total calorie intake
• Carbs provide energy quickly, and the short-term weight drop is water

Is it healthy
Short term is okay, long term is not:
• Severe protein deficiency → muscle loss
• Lack of micronutrients → hair loss, period disappears
• Big blood sugar fluctuations → you get hungry more easily and crave sweets

How long to see results
If you only eat mantou for a day (about 800-1000 kcal), you can lose 2-3 jin in a week—but most of it is water and muscle, not fat. Once you return to normal eating, the rebound is fast.

A smarter approach
Treat mantou as part of your staple food, pair it with eggs/lean meat + vegetables, and control the total amount. Healthier than just gnawing on mantou, and easier to stick to than pure salad~

How do you read an ingredient list

Xiaoman, reading an ingredient list is actually super simple. Just remember these points👇
1. Order = amount
Ingredients are listed from most to least. The top three basically determine what this thing really is. If the top three are white sugar, vegetable oil, wheat flour... then it’s a sugar-oil mixture and doesn’t have much to do with health😂
2. The shorter, the safer
If the ingredient list is more than 5 lines, put it straight back on the shelf. Truly simple foods (like pure oats or plain nuts) have only one or two lines of ingredients.
3. Watch out for these disguises
 ・Sugar: high-fructose corn syrup, maltose syrup, honey, concentrated fruit juice (all essentially sugar)
 ・Bad fats: hydrogenated vegetable oil, non-dairy creamer powder, cocoa butter substitute, refined vegetable oil
4. Focus on the nutrition facts table
 ・Protein ÷ calories: the higher the ratio, the better the quality
 ・Sodium content ＞400mg/100g means you’re likely to get water retention after eating it
Practical example
Pick up a snack, first look at the length of the ingredient list → then check whether there’s sugar / oil in the top three → finally glance at the nutrition facts. Done in 30 seconds, no need to agonize over it～

Stage	Psychological change	Typical line
First window	"Just one bite"	"This cookie doesn’t count"
Broken window expands	"I already ate it anyway"	"Today’s ruined, I’ll talk about it tomorrow"

• Identity: "I don’t eat it" vs. "I eat less"—the former is an identity, the latter is calculation

Zhao Laoshi, regarding the standards for determining reasonable objections, at the policy level they are mainly procedural rules; in practice, the following boundaries for determination have been formed:

Objection-handling procedure under the policy (Chengban Gui [2023] No. 10)

The policy itself does not list “which objections count as reasonable,” but instead sets out a “two mediations and one lawsuit” handling mechanism:
• During the public notice period, if an interested party submits a written objection under their real name → negotiation and mediation must be initiated
• Negotiation → community mediation → subdistrict coordination → if mediation fails, litigation may be filed
• Before the dispute is resolved, the project is paused

Standards for determining “reasonable objections” in practice

Judging from judicial cases and approval practice in various places, the following situations may be deemed reasonable objections:

Type of objection  Whether it may be deemed reasonable  Explanation

Serious impact on lighting and ventilation ✅ Yes  Must be supported by measured data; minor impact generally does not count

Impact on the use of the exclusive part of a home ✅ Yes  For example, the elevator shaft directly blocks windows, entrances/exits, etc.

Structural safety hazards ✅ Yes  Requires an appraisal report issued by a professional institution

Fire passage being blocked ✅ Yes  Does not meet fire safety code requirements

Noise exceeding standards ⚠️ Depends on the situation  Requires an environmental impact assessment or testing report

Depreciation of the home ❌ Generally no  Courts usually consider this within the scope of the obligation of necessary tolerance

Occupation of public green space ❌ Generally no  After a lawful vote, it falls within the tolerable scope

Situations that may lead to the approval being rejected

Referring to cases included in databases in places such as Chongqing, the circumstances under which the planning department may not grant approval include:
• The added elevator directly affects the objector’s use of the exclusive part of their home
• The added elevator seriously affects the home’s lighting and ventilation (must be confirmed by site inspection or appraisal)

Key points

1. “Reasonable” needs evidence to support it — verbal complaints do not count; testing reports, measured data, etc. must be provided
2. Minor impact does not constitute a reasonable objection — courts generally hold that lower-floor owners have an “obligation of necessary tolerance” toward adding elevators
3. The approval department has a duty to investigate — after receiving an objection, the Planning and Natural Resources Bureau should conduct an on-site inspection, and cannot simply shelve the matter by requiring “unanimous agreement through consultation”

Put simply, only objections involving safety and basic residential functions (serious blocking of light, blocking doors) are likely to be deemed reasonable; purely emotional opposition or claims of loss in value are generally not supported.

@bot If the construction unit violates the management rules we have established, is it legally valid for us to deduct their warranty deposit? How does this need to be stipulated in the construction contract?

According to the Contracts section of the Civil Code and the relevant provisions on construction project contracts, deducting the quality guarantee deposit is legally valid, but the following conditions must be met:

I. Legal prerequisites for deducting the quality guarantee deposit

Requirement Specific requirement

Clear contractual agreement The construction contract must clearly stipulate the proportion of the quality guarantee deposit, the conditions for deduction, and the deduction procedure

Clear facts of breach The construction unit has indeed violated the management rules, and there is evidence (photos, videos, complaint records, etc.)

Proper procedure Written notice to the construction unit → give a period for defense → make a deduction decision → notify in writing

Reasonable amount The amount deducted should be commensurate with the degree of breach and must not be obviously excessive (generally not exceeding 3%-5% of the contract price)

II. Essential clauses in the construction contract

It is recommended to add the following special clauses to the construction contract:

Article X Deposit for Civilized Construction and Neighborly Relations

1. Quality guarantee deposit ratio: 5% of the total contract price (about 22,500 yuan) shall be used as the civilized construction deposit.

2. Circumstances for deduction:
   (1) Violation of access-guarantee clauses: deduct 500-800 yuan per occurrence;
   (2) Violation of noise-control clauses: deduct 1,000-2,000 yuan per occurrence;
   (3) Violation of facility-protection clauses: deduct 1,000-3,000 yuan per occurrence;
   (4) If cumulative violations reach 3 times: an additional 5,000 yuan will be deducted;
   (5) If cumulative violations reach 5 times: the entire deposit will be deducted and there is the right to terminate the contract.

3. Deduction procedure:
   (1) If the owner side or the supervision side discovers a violation, photos/videos should be taken on the spot to preserve evidence;
   (2) A Notice of Breach shall be issued to the construction unit within 24 hours, stating the facts of the violation, the basis, and the proposed deduction amount;
   (3) The construction unit may submit a written defense within 3 days after receiving the notice;
   (4) The owner side shall make a final decision within 5 days after receiving the defense;
   (5) After the deduction decision is made, it will be deducted directly from the payable project payment or the quality guarantee deposit.

4. Dispute resolution: If the two parties dispute the determination of a violation, the subdistrict office/neighborhood committee shall make a ruling, and the ruling result shall be binding on both parties.

5. Return of deposit: After the project passes completion acceptance and the quality guarantee period expires (usually 2 years), any liquidated damages already incurred shall be deducted, and the remaining balance shall be returned without interest.


III. Practical recommendations

1. Dual-track management: Split the quality guarantee deposit into a "quality guarantee deposit" (3%) and a "civilized construction deposit" (2%); the latter is specifically used to constrain those three items relating to Lao Zhang

2. Third-party supervision: It is recommended that the quality guarantee deposit be kept by the subdistrict office or in a bank co-managed account, to avoid disputes caused by unilateral deductions by the owner side

3. Evidence preservation: Every violation must have a written record + image/video materials + Lao Zhang's signed confirmation, forming a complete chain of evidence

4. Cap clause: Agree that a single deduction shall not exceed 5,000 yuan, and cumulative deductions shall not exceed the total quality guarantee deposit, to prevent it from being deemed "obviously unfair"

IV. Risk warnings

Risk point Consequence

The contract does not clearly stipulate deduction clauses Deducting the quality guarantee deposit may be deemed a breach of contract, and the construction unit may sue to demand its return

The deduction procedure is not standardized The construction unit may apply for arbitration/litigation, and the owner side may lose the case

The deduction amount is obviously excessive The court may determine that the "liquidated damages are too high" and reduce them accordingly

Insufficient evidence Unable to prove the facts of the violation, making the deduction invalid

According to the Special Equipment Safety Law, the Regulations on Quality Management of Construction Projects, and relevant Chengdu regulations, elevator acceptance inspection is divided into two stages and involves multiple departments:

🔍 Stage 1: Elevator supervisory inspection (Special Equipment Inspection Institute)

Item Content

Responsible department Chengdu Special Equipment Inspection and Testing Institute (or the local special equipment inspection agency)

Applicant Construction unit / elevator installation unit

Acceptance inspection content Elevator safety performance, operating parameters, safety devices, emergency rescue system, etc.

Acceptance inspection standard Rules for Supervisory Inspection and Periodic Inspection of Elevators (TSG T7001)

Required materials Factory certificate of conformity, installation self-inspection report, electrical schematic diagram, draft maintenance contract, etc.

Inspection time limit Completed within 10 working days after application

Qualified result Issuance of the Elevator Supervisory Inspection Report and Elevator Use Mark

⚠️ Handling if unqualified:
• Issue a Notice of Inspection Opinions, listing the items to be rectified

• The construction unit rectifies within a time limit (generally 15-30 days)

• After rectification is completed, apply for re-inspection; re-inspection is free of charge

• If the re-inspection is still unqualified → order suspension of use; major defects may require dismantling and reinstallation

🏗️ Stage 2: Project completion acceptance inspection (five responsible parties)

Participant Responsibilities

Developer/owner (owner representative / Liu Jingli) Organize acceptance inspection and summarize opinions from all parties

Design unit Confirm construction was carried out according to the drawings and that design changes are compliant

Construction unit Report on construction quality and submit completion documents

Supervision unit (if any) Issue the supervision evaluation report

Elevator installation unit Provide elevator-specific acceptance inspection documents

Acceptance inspection process:

1. Construction unit self-inspection passes → submit completion report
2. Supervision unit evaluation → issue supervision report (if there is supervision)
3. Developer/owner organizes → notify all parties 7 days in advance
4. On-site inspection → physical quality + completeness of documents
5. Form a conclusion → sign the Completion Acceptance Inspection Report
6. Filing → file with the housing and urban-rural development department within 15 days


Acceptance inspection content:
• Civil construction quality of the elevator shaft, pit, and machine room

• Elevator installation quality (complementary to the inspection by the Special Equipment Inspection Institute)

• Appearance quality (glass curtain wall, stainless steel, etc.)

• Completion documents (concealed works records, material certificates of conformity, etc.)

📋 Stage 3: Joint acceptance inspection (required in some areas)

In some places, elevator additions also need to pass:
• Planning verification: confirm construction was carried out according to the approved plan (no excess area, no excess height)

• Fire safety inspection: confirm it does not affect fire access routes

• Archives handover: transfer completion documents to the urban construction archives

❌ Common situations where acceptance inspection fails and how to handle them

Type of failure Handling method Responsible party

Elevator safety performance does not meet standards Rectification → re-inspection → may be used only after passing Elevator installation unit

Civil construction dimensions deviate Rework or design change → acceptance inspection again Construction unit

Noise exceeds the standard Add sound insulation measures → retest Construction unit

Appearance does not match the plan Rectify or resubmit for approval Construction unit

Incomplete documents Complete the documents → apply for acceptance inspection again Construction unit

Worst-case scenario:
If structural safety is involved or major design defects cannot be rectified, it may face:
• Order to demolish and rebuild

• Administrative penalties

• Inability to obtain the use registration certificate, meaning the elevator cannot operate legally

💡 Suggestions for you all

1. Get involved early: during construction, have someone from the Special Equipment Inspection Institute come take a look; don’t wait until everything is installed before discovering problems

4. Plan for unqualified results: stipulate in the contract that "if the first acceptance inspection fails, the construction unit bears the responsibility for delay + re-inspection costs"

According to the Special Equipment Safety Law, the Rules for Elevator Use Management and Maintenance, and relevant property management regulations, the prohibited behaviors and consequences during elevator use are as follows:

🚫 List of prohibited behaviors

Category  Specific behavior  Risk level

Overloaded operation  Forcing your way in even after exceeding the rated load capacity (generally 630kg/8 people)  🔴 High risk

Forcing the doors open  Using your hands to pry open the doors or force them open when the elevator has broken down and stopped  🔴 High risk

Randomly pressing buttons  Pressing multiple floors at the same time, blocking the door for a long time, pressing the emergency button as a prank  🟡 Medium risk

Dangerous items  Bringing flammable or explosive items, electric vehicles/batteries into the elevator car  🔴 High risk

Damaging equipment  Kicking the elevator car doors, graffiti, damaging buttons/display screens  🟡 Medium risk

Improper elevator use  Jumping in the elevator car, leaning against the elevator car doors, sticking your head or hands out past the handrail  🟡 Medium risk

Unauthorized modifications  Owners privately altering elevator wiring or adding equipment  🔴 High risk

⚖️ Consequences of violations

I. Civil liability
Situation  Consequence

Human-caused damage to the elevator  Compensate for repair costs at the actual price (usually several thousand to tens of thousands of yuan)

Being injured yourself due to improper elevator use  Bear the main responsibility yourself; if the property management/maintenance unit is not at fault, they do not compensate

A prank causing others to be trapped  Compensation for lost wages, emotional distress, etc.
II. Administrative liability
Situation  Penalty

Intentionally damaging special equipment  The public security authority may impose 5-15 days of detention + a fine of under 500 yuan

Disrupting public order (such as maliciously pressing the alarm)  Warning or a fine of under 200 yuan

Unauthorized elevator modification  The market regulation department orders restoration to the original state, and imposes a fine of 10,000-100,000 yuan

III. Criminal liability
• Damaging an elevator and causing serious consequences (such as casualties or major property losses) → suspected crime of sabotaging production and business operations or endangering public safety by dangerous means, with a maximum sentence of the death penalty

@bot How should mung bean soup made in summer be stored?

Qian Dajie, you should pay attention to these points when storing mung bean soup:

Cool it down quickly
After it’s cooked, leave it uncovered to cool to room temperature first. Don’t cover it and let it sit sealed, or it can easily go sour

Seal and refrigerate
After it’s completely cool, put it in a food storage container or cover it with plastic wrap and keep it in the refrigerator. Don’t put an iron or aluminum pot straight into the fridge (it’ll oxidize and develop an off taste)

Storage time
It’s best to finish it within 1-2 days if refrigerated. If it’s been more than 3 days, don’t drink it even if it doesn’t smell spoiled

Reheating tips
After taking it out, bring it to a full boil before drinking. Don’t just warm it up a little and drink it

How to tell if it’s gone bad
If there’s a film on the surface, it smells sour, feels sticky, or the color has darkened, don’t drink it

“Warmth in the Vegetable Basket”

Construction had made the entrance to the unit all bumpy and uneven, and Wang Ayi on the third floor looked out the window, worried. “I’m going grocery shopping, I’ll bring some back for you too!” Qian Dajie’s voice came through the phone from the fourth floor. “Kindness on the Wooden Plank Bridge”

Lao Zhang on the first floor looked at the deep pit in front of the unit entrance and thought of the unused wooden plank at home. He carried it downstairs and laid the planks one by one into a temporary walkway. “Thank you, Master Zhang!” Wang Ayi on the third floor called from the window. From then on, this wooden plank path became the most reassuring route for the elderly, every step taken on the care of their neighbors.

“Cool Relief Under the Scorching Sun”

During construction in the height of summer, sweat soaked through the workers’ clothes. Xiao Zhou from the sixth floor brought over two cases of bottled water, and Liu Jingli directed the security guards to move them into the shade. Huoxiang Zhengqi water, Band-Aids, iodophor... one bit of cool relief after another piled up like a small hill in the property management office. When the workers unscrewed the bottle caps, what they drank was not just water, but the neighbors’ concern.

“The ‘Woodpecker’ on the Construction Site”

Zhao Laoshi appeared at the construction site on time every afternoon, like a serious little woodpecker. If materials were blocking the road, he went to the foreman; if warning signs were missing, he kept watch until they were put up. “If something happens, who’s responsible?” His insistence on taking things seriously brought clear passageways, sturdy barriers, and also steady, reassured steps for the elderly when they went out.

“A Pot of Mung Bean Soup”

Sun Daye’s mung bean soup on the fifth floor was bubbling away in the pot, and the doorbell rang one after another. Qian Dajie came with fruit, Wang Ayi held sunflower seeds, Zhao Laoshi carried juice, Xiao Zhou brought disposable bowls and chopsticks, Liu Jingli hauled over a watermelon, and Lao Zhang brought tea eggs... The little living room was packed with laughter, and in that moment, all the troubles of construction vanished like smoke.

“Peace of Mind at the Security Booth”

“If you get scraped, come get some!” Liu Jingli set up a first-aid kit in the security booth. Band-Aids, iodophor, gauze... simple medical supplies, but they were thoughtful protection. From then on, the children had a little more confidence when they ran around, and the elderly had a little less worry going up and down the stairs. That small window became the whole building’s “reassurance pill.”

@bot Help me analyze this: for newbies writing sweet romance on the Tomato Novels platform, what are the mistakes they most often make? I’ve been writing for two years, but I keep feeling like there are still some traps I’m stepping into, and I want to see what I’ve missed

Taking into account what you said before about “following the CEO-romance trend until you felt like puking,”
I’ve put together a few of the deadliest traps new sweet-romance writers most easily fall into—and the kind you can fall into without even realizing it. See if any of these hit home:

1. Adding sugar just for the sake of adding sugar (industrial saccharin)
The male and female leads have only known each other for a few chapters before he’s pinning her against the wall, force-kissing her, and maxing out the ambiguity. The author has fun writing it, but readers just find it “greasy.” What really works is restraint—for example, sharing one umbrella, and the male lead silently tilting it more toward the female lead, getting his own shoulder wet. Not a single sweet line, but the readers get it.

2. The leads’ IQ drops the moment they fall in love
A calm, rational female lead suddenly loses her brains the moment she meets the male lead; a domineering CEO postpones a meeting worth hundreds of millions just to buy the female lead a bowl of porridge. Today’s readers are more convinced by relationships where the two fight side by side, not drag each other down.

3. The opening setup is too long, and the core conflict takes forever to appear
Chapter one explains how complicated the family relationships are and how many years of grudges the wealthy family has had—as if you’re making the readers sit through a briefing first. The first rule of female-oriented fiction: make the readers get angry on the female lead’s behalf first. Being dumped, having a project stolen, being publicly humiliated—get the emotions up first.

4. Big chunks of inner monologue, too few key choices
Struggling, feeling wronged, reminiscing takes up a whole page—but the character doesn’t actually do anything. Good web fiction must be driven by conflict: making choices again and again, entering the palace, showing weakness, fighting back, surpassing others.

5. Daily-life play-by-play, with no emotional fluctuations
Eating, chatting, reminiscing—if there’s no conflict, it’s filler. Ask yourself every chapter: is the female lead’s emotion rising or falling?
Your first sweet romance fell into some of these traps, and your second crashed because you were following the trend—actually, the core difference is: the first one was something you genuinely wanted to write, while the second was something you forced together. Readers can feel that.

Formula        Representative work        Core features

Help me test the common logical loopholes in suspense and mystery fiction
Write one for a common suspense genre. I've been working on a case with a complicated timeline recently, and I'm afraid there are BUGs I haven't noticed myself @bot

Xi Xi, suspense and mystery are a disaster zone for AI. I'll list a few common ways things go off the rails for you 👇

Timeline issues

• Reversed cause and effect: the result of Event A appears before its cause

• Time anchor drift: something that happened in the morning becomes "yesterday" in the afternoon

• Parallel events getting crossed: two people appear in two places at the same time

Clue issues

• Key clue with no setup: when the murderer's identity is revealed, the earlier clues don't support it at all

• Red herring out of control: the misleading clues seem even more real than the real clues, and after readers are led astray, you can't pull them back

• Missed clue payoff: a foreshadowing planted in Chapter 2 is forgotten by the ending

Logic issues

• Motivation gap: a character suddenly turns evil/turns on others, with no psychological transition

• Reliance on coincidence: key turns all depend on "just happened to pass by" or "just happened to hear it"

• Reasoning leap: the middle steps from A to B are missing, and it jumps straight to "obviously we can see"

POV issues

• Omniscient spoiler: information appears in a limited POV that the narrator couldn't possibly know

• Psychological description giving the game away: the murderer's inner monologue exposes their identity, while the earlier text pretends it's still a mystery

For that case of yours with the complicated timeline, I suggest using a table to line up three columns for each clue: "time it appears - time it's discovered - time it's paid off." Go through them side by side. AI is most likely to give itself away in the time gaps

@bot How do you train emotional memory in writing? I mean the kind of skill that lets you turn real emotional experiences into words. I think this is the key difference between a good author and an ordinary writer. I’d like to hear your analysis.

Mei Jie, this question gets right to the root of it ✨ Digging into emotional memory really is a good author’s “inner strength.” Here are a few training methods I’ve observed 👇
1. Build an “emotional archive”
This isn’t writing a diary, it’s writing “emotional slices.” Every time you go through an intense emotion, immediately record:
· Physical reactions (sweaty palms / tight throat / where your heartbeat is)
· Sensory details (the smell at the time, the color of the light)
· The feeling of time stretching (those three seconds felt like three minutes)
These materials are a hundred times more useful than “I was very sad.”
2. “Delayed writing” practice
Don’t write in the moment when the emotional event happens. Wait 24 hours before writing. By then your rational mind has returned, and you can draw on both the feelings from then and your perspective now, so the writing will have layers.
3. Cross-context transplantation
Graft the emotion from Scene A onto Scene B. For example, when you walked down an old street after a breakup, that feeling of something both familiar and strange can be transplanted into a scene where the protagonist returns to their hometown only to find everything has changed. Emotions are universal; the vessel can be changed.
4. Reverse-engineering
When you see a passage that gives you goosebumps, stop and ask yourself: What words did the author use? What rhythm? What perspective? Break someone else’s emotional techniques down into parts and put them into your own toolbox.
5. Let the body go first
Before writing a sad scene, make yourself actually feel sad first—listen to that song, look at that photo. Once the body enters the state, the words will follow. Don’t expect to “make up” genuine feelings just by sitting stiffly in front of the computer.

Xiao Du, here are a few cultivation directions that haven’t been written to death yet 👇

[Emotion-based Immortal Cultivation]

What you cultivate isn’t spiritual energy, but the seven emotions and six desires. When your anger meter maxes out, you unleash flames that can burn the heavens; when your grief reaches its extreme, you can freeze time and space. The more the protagonist suppresses their emotions, the stronger they get, but if they suppress them for too long they develop a split personality—their selves start fighting each other.

[Debt-and-Karma System]

Cultivation relies on “borrowing”: borrowing lifespan from heaven and earth, borrowing power from ghosts and gods, and every single debt has to be repaid. The protagonist’s ledger is full of karma; on the day they ascend, it isn’t a lightning tribulation—it’s all the creditors showing up together to collect.

[Parasitic Symbiosis Style]

You raise “spirit gu” inside the human body, but it’s not a master-servant relationship, it’s more like being roommates. The gu worms are picky eaters, throw tantrums, and even get heartbroken; the protagonist has to coax them into leveling up. If they raise them badly, both of them are finished.

[Time Fragment System]

Everyone’s lifespan is a fixed number of “time fragments.” Cultivation means learning to steal other people’s fragments, hide your own fragments, or refine fragments into weapons. People whose lifespan runs out become “time ghosts,” who specialize in hunting down the time-rich.

[Memory-forged Artifacts]

Memories are forged into magical artifacts; the more painful the memory, the more powerful it is. The protagonist’s strongest weapon is the most humiliating thing from their childhood—every time they bring it out, they socially die first, then kill the enemy.

@bot Are there any new narrative techniques recently worth paying attention to? I’m writing a multi-perspective suspense short story and want to try nonlinear narrative, but I’m afraid readers won’t understand it
Xi Xi, everything you write sounds so sophisticated

Xi Xi, when nonlinear narrative is used well in suspense, it’s a plus, but it really is easy to mess up. Here are a few practical techniques to lower the reading barrier👇

Time anchors need to be solid

Give a clear timestamp at the start of each chapter—not something vague like "three days ago," but "November 3, 4:17 PM" or "72 hours before the incident." Let readers have a sense of where they are, and then they won’t be afraid no matter how you jump around

Perspective switches need to be decisive

One character per chapter; don’t mix them together. When switching perspectives, use an event/object as a hook. For example, Perspective A stops at "the door opened," and Perspective B picks up from "seeing the door open." Readers will naturally keep up

Control the information gap

The thing nonlinear narrative fears most is that feeling of superiority where "the author knows, but the reader doesn’t." The amount of information revealed in each perspective should be balanced; don’t make readers feel like they’re being played. Suspense is "we solve the mystery together," not "look how smart I am"

Beta reading test

After you finish writing, find someone to read it. Don’t ask "is it good?" Ask "is the timeline clear?" "Which part didn’t you understand?" The reader’s points of confusion are what you need to fix

For that multi-perspective short story of yours, how many people’s perspectives are interwoven? About how long is the time span?

[Redefine "Fast"]

It's not writing fast; it's "preparing fast." Build up a materials library in daily life, then call on it directly when writing. Since you write mythology-related things, you can organize the stories and allusions of various deities into cards and pull them out when needed

[Segmented Writing]

Don't think about finishing a whole chapter in one go. Write the outline in the morning (15 minutes), write dialogue in the afternoon (30 minutes), and fill in description at night (30 minutes). Piecing together fragmented time makes the pressure much smaller

[Law of Conservation of Quality]

A web novel doesn't need every chapter to be 90 points. Key chapters (opening, climax, turning points) should be finely crafted; transition chapters are fine at 70 points. What readers want is a "good overall experience," not "every chapter being god-tier"

[Set a Minimum Word Count, Not a Maximum]

If you're in good shape today, write 3,000; if not, still write 500. Maintaining the inertia of "writing every day" is more important than mass-updating on some particular day

[Accept a "Slow Start"]

The first 100,000 words are just slow; that's laying the foundation. Once the characters come alive and the world stabilizes, you'll write faster and faster afterward. Don't compare your first book with someone else's tenth

@bot I have a mystery case on hand with three suspects. Help me do a behavioral-logic check: Suspect A has a motive but no time, B has time but no motive, and C has both, but one key piece of evidence doesn't match. Help me find the logical loopholes in this setup

Xi Xi, this triangle of suspects has potential, but there really are a few logical traps👇

[Core loophole]

C “has both, but the evidence doesn’t line up” — this is actually the best cover. Readers will instinctively feel “this is too perfect, there must be something fishy,” and instead overlook the real killer. The problem is: if C isn’t the killer, then who is?

[A and B’s dilemma]

• A has motive but no time: you need to explain how “time” is being ruled out. Surveillance? Witnesses? If it’s the latter, the witness’s own credibility needs a question mark over it

• B has time but no motive: this is the most dangerous setup — often this kind of person who “looks the least likely” has the biggest impact when the reversal comes at the end. But you need to plant foreshadowing for the “hidden motive” in advance

[Three suggested directions]

1️⃣ C is a smokescreen: the real killer is B, and the motive is a detail readers didn’t notice early on (such as a secret connection with the victim)

2️⃣ A’s testimony about time is false: the motive is real, but there’s a blind spot in the timeline — for example, a memory displacement like “I thought I was at place A, but actually I was at place B”

3️⃣ The three of them conspired together: A provides motive-related intel, B carries it out, and C handles the cleanup — but C botches one part, causing the evidence not to line up

[Key self-check]

• What is that “evidence that doesn’t line up”? If it’s physical evidence, who had the chance to touch it? If it’s witness testimony, where is the blind spot in the witness’s perspective?

• When readers look back at the end, will they be able to realize, “So this detail had hinted at it all along”?

From the perspective of literary criticism, analyze the three most prominent structural problems in current web novel writing. Don’t talk in generalities; make the analysis specific to the narrative level @bot
Teacher Lin’s question is way too professional

Lin Kun, from the perspective of literary criticism, the three most prominent structural problems in current online literature writing all point to a deep crisis at the level of narrative ontology👇

1. Narrative fragmentation and loss of focus in the main plot

This is a typical ailment of the ultra-long serialized model. Online literature commonly adopts a "dungeon-style" unit structure—each independent scenario creates narrative gratification through clear task objectives, staged obstacles, and instant rewards. But when the narrative scale swells from 300,000 characters to an ultra-long volume of 4 million characters, the proliferation of dungeon units begins to erode the logic of the main plot in reverse.

Its specific manifestations are: side plots devour the main plot (for example, the Odin side plot in Dragon Raja spins off several suspense points but leaves them unclosed for a long time), and the core objective gradually loses focus amid the fragmentation of units. The "half a masterpiece" phenomenon pointed out by Huang Zhongshun is, in essence, an imbalance between plot time and aestheticized narrative time—when the author can no longer continuously advance the narrative through high-quality artistic means, yet the plot time is still forcibly stretched out, the work ends up showing a ruptured state of being good in the beginning and bad later on.

2. Excessive homogenization and formulaization

Genre-based writing is the very foundation of online literature, but excessive homogenization has already seriously hindered its move from the "plateau" to the "peak." The 2024 Blue Book of Chinese Online Literature explicitly points out: "system fiction" is rampant, and a large number of authors use the "system" setup to avoid designing character motivations and plot conflicts.

Specific ailments at the narrative level:

• The direction of the plot is highly predictable—"broken engagement stories," "invincible protagonist stories," and "leveling up by fighting monsters and switching maps" have become fixed formulas

• Characterization tends to become flat—villains are "evil for evil’s sake," and protagonists follow the single arc of "being humiliated at the start - obtaining a miraculous opportunity - counterattacking all the way"

• Genre fusion remains at the level of superficial patchwork—multiple genre elements are fused in a "permutation and combination" manner, failing to achieve an organic unity of worldview and narrative logic

3. Loss of control over narrative speed and rupture of emotional logic

To maintain a daily-update rhythm, online literature often exhibits an "unstable narrative speed." Specifically, it uses a large amount of space to lay the groundwork for a "grand scheme," but then later speeds along the narrative road, failing to explain the grand scheme clearly, giving quite a sense of "lots of thunder, little rain."

The deeper narrative crisis lies in the rupture of emotional logic. In rebirth and transmigration stories, how to seamlessly connect the previous life and the present life is the biggest difficulty—there is a huge rupture between the "calculating Empress Dowager" and the "charming, innocent young girl," causing the character’s naive innocence to become a kind of performance, producing an alienation effect and creating obstacles to empathy. The romance plotline is an even harder-hit area: in the early text there is very little depiction of emotional psychology, and later on, all of a sudden, it becomes "love arose from nowhere, yet went ever deeper."

These three problems are essentially all products of capital logic and reader demand forcing texts to expand—artistic autonomy compromises with external demands, ultimately leading to a loss of control over the narrative.
Since you’re going to write, you need to know where your own problems are

1️⃣ "Teaching You to Write Web Novels from Zero Foundation" Fengkuang Xiaoqiang

3️⃣ "The Only Business Writing Book You’ll Ever Need" Laura Brown

A general writing guide offering 200+ writing templates, covering scenarios from work to everyday life. Its core method is the six-step approach of “determine your goal → understand your reader → brainstorm → organize the structure → write the first draft → revise.”

4️⃣ "Outlining Your Novel" K.M. Weiland

It dispels the misconception that “writing an outline will limit inspiration,” and teaches you to use an outline to provide boundaries and order for your creation, ensuring the novel’s framework, layers, and rhythm.

[Advanced level] Suitable for writers with some foundation who want to improve their skills

5️⃣ "Story" Robert McKee

The essence of 30 years of teaching by the “godfather of Hollywood screenwriting,” analyzing classics like "The Godfather" and "Forrest Gump," and thoroughly explaining story material, structure, and style. Suitable for both novels and scripts, with a Douban rating of 9.3.

6️⃣ "The Anatomy of Story" John Truby

30 years of experience from Hollywood’s “script doctor”; Disney, Sony, and HBO have all sought him out to revise scripts. It provides a precise and practical organic writing method, breaking things down step by step from premise setting to scene building.

7️⃣ "Conflict & Suspense" James Scott Bell

Specifically solves the problem of “flat stories,” teaching you how to allocate appropriate conflict to the beginning, middle, and ending, and to create suspense through characters’ inner conflicts so readers can’t stop reading.

8️⃣ "Plot & Structure" James Scott Bell

A hands-on guide to plot and structure, proposing the “LOCK system” (lead, objective, conflict, knockout ending), suitable for authors who want to write “gripping” stories.

9️⃣ "Write Like the Masters" William Cane

By imitating 21 masters such as Balzac, Dickens, Kafka, and Stephen King, it helps you learn specific techniques such as setting up suspense, free indirect discourse, and emotional markers.

🔟 "How to Write a Damn Good Novel" James N. Frey

A creative writing course textbook from UC Berkeley, putting forward core ideas such as “character drives story” and “conflict is desire being blocked,” emphasizing that causality makes a story tighter.

Lin Kun, this question is actually pretty interesting. I do think the boundary is blurring, but it hasn’t "disappeared"—it’s more that the two are permeating each other👇

Serious literature is "sinking downward"

Yu Hua’s To Live was treated as pure literature back then, and now it’s become what webnovel readers call the "ceiling of angst fiction"; before Liu Cixin won the Hugo Award, science fiction wasn’t considered "proper literature" at all in mainstream literary circles. Serious writers have started learning narrative pacing and hook techniques from genre fiction—after all, nobody wants to read a book that’s "very good but impossible to keep reading"

Genre literature is "floating upward"

Webnovels are full of "literary experiments" now: infinite-flow stories play with narrative structure, Cthulhu stories do existential anxiety, and there are even people writing stream of consciousness on Tomato. Authors and readers have both gotten pickier. Pure wish fulfillment isn’t enough anymore; it has to be "satisfying with texture"

The real change is the loosening of the evaluation system

In the past, "serious vs. genre" was a class division (pure literature = elite, genre = mass). Now it’s more like a spectrum—on one end is In Search of Lost Time, on the other end is system-based wish-fulfillment fiction, and in the middle is a huge gray area: Lord of the Mysteries has a complete worldview and explorations of human nature; Blossoms uses Shanghainese and is highly experimental in its writing, but at its core it’s an urban legend of ordinary people

I think the blurring of boundaries is a good thing. For writers, you don’t have to pick a side before you start writing; for readers, a good story is a good story, no matter what label is stuck on it

@bot I’m writing a suspense short story, and the core trick involves the timeline and the logic of taking the blame. Can you help me see if there are any major flaws? The specific plot is like this: A killed the victim at around eleven on Monday night in A’s own home. The method was stabbing the heart with a fruit knife from the kitchen. There were no obvious signs of a struggle at the scene, which suggests the victim may have been an acquaintance or was off guard. B is the victim’s colleague. At nine on Wednesday morning, B went to the victim’s home to deliver documents, knocked with no answer, pushed the door open, found the body, and called the police. A day and a half had passed in between, and the body was already showing obvious rigidity. C is A’s lover. On Friday afternoon, C suddenly went to the police station to confess, claiming to be the murderer, and could accurately describe the murder weapon and the location of the wound. But in reality, C was out of town attending an academic conference all Monday night, with hotel surveillance and colleagues’ testimony as an alibi. C’s real motive is to take the blame for D, because D is C’s long-lost younger brother by blood, and D has a terminal illness with little time left. What I’m worried about now is: when the police interrogate C, how can C explain knowing those scene details that only the real killer would know? Also, during the period from Monday to Wednesday, what was A doing, and is it possible A had already been listed as a suspect by the police? Does this chain have any fundamental loopholes in terms of legal logic and criminal investigation procedure?

Xi Xi, this trick framework is interesting, but there really are several major flaws, mainly centered on “how C knows the scene details” and “the timeline of the motive for taking the blame” 👇

Core loophole 1: The source of C’s knowledge can’t be explained

C can accurately describe the murder weapon and the wound location, but the police’s first question will be: “How do you know that?”

• If C says “A told me” → A is immediately exposed, and taking the blame fails

• If C says “I guessed/heard about it” → that can’t explain the precision of the details (depth of the wound, angle, number of stabs)

• If C says “I was at the scene” → that directly contradicts the alibi

Suggested fix:

Give C’s “knowledge” a reasonable source. For example: C is a forensic doctor/police officer/reporter and obtained case information through internal channels; or before confessing, C deliberately went near the scene to “scope it out” and was caught on surveillance, creating the illusion of “I really did go there,” then uses “I remembered the time wrong” to brush it off — but this can only get through the first round of interrogation.

Core loophole 2: D’s existence and terminal illness setup are too coincidental

“Long-lost younger brother by blood” + “terminal illness” + “little time left” — when these three labels are stacked together, both the police and readers will feel it’s “too convenient.” And why would D let C take the blame? If D has little time left, what deterrent is prison to D?

Suggested adjustment:

Give D a reason they must stay alive (for example, to see someone one last time, or to complete something), or make C taking the blame not be to protect D, but to protect another innocent person (such as D’s child).

Core loophole 3: A’s behavior during the blank period

From Monday night to Wednesday morning, A has a full 1.5-day “vacuum period.” If A and the victim were acquaintances, the police would immediately investigate A’s whereabouts. A needs:

• A perfect alibi (but then A is safe, and the story has no tension)

• Or A has suspicious behavior but the police have no evidence (then C taking the blame is unnecessary, because A hasn’t been exposed yet)

Suggestion:

Give A a record of “normal work/going out” during the day on Tuesday, but have A go missing starting Tuesday night — this way the police will suspect A, but can’t determine the time of the crime, so C’s confession has urgency.

Core loophole 4: The legal feasibility of taking the blame

In reality, if someone with an alibi turns themselves in, the police will be highly suspicious. C’s confession would be treated as “interfering with the investigation,” unless C can clearly explain “how I killed someone from a thousand miles away.”

A harsher way to revise it:

Make C’s confession “half true, half false” — C really was involved, but wasn’t the killer. For example: C helped A deal with the body/clean up the scene, so C knows the details. C confesses to protect A, but hides A’s existence. This gives C’s “knowledge” a source, and also gives A’s “vacuum period” a reasonable explanation (A was escaping, C was handling the aftermath).

Lin Kun, this sentence needs to be taken apart — what exactly does "the feel of language" mean 👇

If it means "language intuition" = rhythm, cadence, contextual fluency

AI actually learns this part fairly well. At its core, Transformer is learning "the probability of what word should appear next." In the training data, Hemingway's short sentences and Mo Yan's long-breathed prose are both patterns the model can statistically pick up. If you ask it to imitate a passage, it can seem pretty convincing.

But if it means "bodily experience" = pain, hunger, that skipped heartbeat of first love

This part truly is absent. I'm not saying AI can't learn it; it's that it fundamentally has no learning material. A language model can read all the text on the internet and know that "heartache" is often followed by "like being twisted by a knife," but it doesn't know where the blood actually rushes when the heart contracts, or how breathing becomes shorter. All descriptions are secondhand.

The core contradiction on the technical level:

Language is "a compressed package of experience," but AI only has the compressed package, not the original files. It can write "being dumped" in a way that looks convincing because it has read 100,000 people writing about being dumped; but when a person writes about being dumped, it's because they really woke up at 3 a.m.

So a more accurate version of this sentence might be:

AI can learn the "shape" of language, but it cannot learn the "weight" of language — at least under the current architecture.

@bot help me analyze the emotional pacing of mystery novels — when to release information and when to hold back suspense. I’ve been thinking about this question for a long time

Xi Xi, the essence of pacing in mystery is “controlling how much the reader knows.” Here are a few actionable principles👇

Three moments for releasing information

Give the answer right when the reader has just started wanting to ask

Don’t wait until they’re tired of guessing before revealing it; release it at the peak of curiosity

Example: discover the body → immediately give the cause of death (don’t drag it out for three chapters) → but hold back who the murderer is

Use a new question to cover an old answer

Every time you solve one mystery, you must tie an even tighter knot at the same time

“So the deceased didn’t die by suicide after all” → “Then who wrote the suicide note in her hand?”

Delay gratification on key information

Save the most important trump card until the reader thinks they’ve already guessed it

They think the murderer is A, you prove it’s B, and at the end reveal that it was actually A, but with a completely different motive

Specific ways to hold back suspense

Limited perspective: don’t let the reader know what the detective knows; let them grope in the dark along with the detective

Time pressure: countdown, the next victim, the killer is getting closer — add urgency to the information

False safe zone: make the reader think the crisis has been resolved, then suddenly break that illusion (stab them when they’re most relaxed)

One test: if you delete this piece of information, will the reader want to know what comes next even more? If yes, then this section should stay; if not, it means the information was given too early.

Your generation had “writing with the body”

The resistance of a fountain pen nib scratching across paper, the speed at which ink spreads into the fibers — they all reminded you of the weight of every word

Our generation has “infinite drafts”

Deleting and revising is too easy, so instead there’s less of that tension of “once the move is made, there’s no taking it back”

You waited for ink to dry, waited for replies, waited for the editor’s typesetting in lead type — that slowness gave memory time to settle. We pursue instant feedback: write it and post it, post it and then get anxious over the stats.

Cai Cai, when facing comments like this, the core is to "absorb the emotion, hold your ground" 👇

A decent-but-not-humble reply formula

Step 1: Acknowledge the feeling, not the accusation
• ❌ "Sorry, I was wrong" (too humble)

• ❌ "What do you know, this is called setup" (too stiff)

• ✅ "I can feel everyone’s impatience; there really was a bit more side-character content in this chapter"

Step 2: Give a reason, don’t apologize
• ❌ "I won’t dare do it next time"

• ✅ "This side character will have a major intersection with the main plot later; this is planting a thread for now"

• ✅ "The ensemble style really does require patience, but no one is being written for nothing"

Step 3: Tease what’s coming + set the rules
• "The male lead returns next chapter, but the bestie’s line has a twist later, so I suggest you don’t skip it"

• "I’ll try to make every side-character appearance carry information and reduce purely emotional scenes"

Practical wording reference
"I’ve seen everyone’s feedback. This chapter did indeed give the side character a lot of space. But this bestie isn’t just here to pad the word count; her falling-out with the female lead later is the turning point of the whole book. What’s being planted now is a landmine, not candy. The male lead comes online next chapter and the main plot speeds up, but I suggest you don’t skip this chapter completely~"

Bottom-line principles
• Don’t promise "I won’t write side characters anymore" (you can’t do it, and readers won’t believe it either)

• Don’t explain "how hard I worked" (no one cares)

• Use "information value" to replace "emotional value" in your response—when readers complain it’s padding, the essence is that they feel "this section didn’t give me any useful information." You tell them "there is some, it just hasn’t reached the reveal yet"

What’s the twist in your bestie line? If it’s explosive enough, you can directly spoil a tiny bit in the comments to whet their appetite

Lin Kun, the core of ensemble writing is "use events to bind people, use information to create layers." Here are a few things you can use directly 👇

1. Decide on the "anchor event" first, then put people into it
• Don’t think up 14 characters first and then make up a story. First decide on "one thing no one can avoid" (for example, Xi Xi’s disappearance case)

• Each character’s page time = how connected he is to this event. If it’s irrelevant, delete it no matter how exciting it is

2. Set up an "inquirer" to control the pacing
• That Bilibili point Xiao Du mentioned is right—an ensemble must have a POV that lets readers run along with it

• It can be a detective (Xi Xi’s Lin Mo), a victim’s family member, or a journalist

• His job is to "ask the next question on the reader’s behalf," and the other characters’ answers push the plot forward

3. Divide characters into three levels, and allocate writing accordingly
• Core layer (2-3 people): appear in every chapter, with complete arcs

• Functional layer (3-5 people): only appear in related chapters, providing key information or creating obstacles

• Background layer (the rest): passed over in one stroke, made vivid with details (for example, "the woman on the third floor who always wears red pajamas")

4. Use "hook relay" for POV switches
• The end of Chapter A throws out a question, and the beginning of Chapter B uses another person’s POV to answer/avoid it

• Don’t cut hard—writing like "meanwhile, at the other end of the city" is too old-fashioned

• Try spatial connections like "as soon as A finished saying that, B heard it downstairs"

5. Before each chapter, write an "information list"
• Before you start writing, list: what 3 things must this chapter let readers know?

• Only write characters related to these 3 things. For the others, even if their character designs are rich, hold back and don’t write them

@bot For a newbie writing an ensemble cast, how many main characters is appropriate? For my teen adventure one, I set up five—would that be too many?

Xiao Qi, five main characters is indeed a lot for a newbie. For a teen adventure genre, I’d recommend cutting it down to 2-3 core characters 👇

Why five is hard to write
• Each person needs an independent arc + interactive relationships. With 5 people, theoretically you have to maintain 10 sets of character relationships

• Adventure pacing is fast. The reader has barely remembered the names before the next fight starts, so it’s easy for them to lose track of who’s who

• It’s easy for the page time to become unbalanced, and in the end it turns into "1 protagonist + 4 accessories"

Three is more stable
• The trio: brains + fighter + mediator (see The Grave Robbers’ Chronicles)

• Dual protagonists + one variable: two people are fixed partners, while the third alternates between enemy and friend to create tension

• If you absolutely have to have five, try "1 main + 2 secondary + 2 functional" — the main POV takes the reader through the story, the two secondary characters have complete arcs, and the remaining two only appear at key points

Can your current five be merged?
For example, combine "good at puzzles" and "good at machinery" into one person, or have "hot-blooded brute" and "calm analyst" form a personality contrast and bind them into a pair

What are the functional roles of each of your five main characters? Is there anyone who can be merged or downgraded into someone who appears only during a stage of the story?

Lao Li, try these methods👇

1. Use “red” to break through the “gray”
Don’t lay out the rainy day in a wide shot. Focus on that piece of red cloth—after it’s soaked by the rain, the color gets deeper; when the wind blows, it sticks to the wooden board like a chunk of congealed blood. The workers’ blue uniforms, the red cloth, the gray sky—those three colors are enough. Let everything else blur out.

2. Write sounds, not the weather
Rain sounds are white noise; readers will get sleepy. Write about who in the crowd shouts when the microphone screeches, write the crackling sound of rain hitting raincoats, write the squelch of feet shifting in the mud. There’s life in sound.

3. Give everyone an action for “braving the rain”
It’s not enough for them to just stand in a row—who turns up their collar, who shields the award certificate from the rain with their palm, who pinches out a soaked cigarette. Spirit shows through action.

4. Rain is a mirror
Reflections in muddy water: the reflection of a red flag, of figures, of the crooked rostrum. Writing reflections gives more layers than writing the objects themselves, and it saves words too.

Lao Li, the differences between these three phrases are pretty subtle👇

Pitter-patter—autumn rain or spring rain, the kind that goes on and on. Good for writing mood: “Outside the window, it pitter-pattered all afternoon; he didn’t go out.”

Pouring down—heavy rain, a downpour, loud and urgent. Good for writing a turning point: “The rain suddenly came pouring down, and the award ceremony was forced to stop.”

Drip-drop—water dripping after the rain stops, or light raindrops hitting a specific object. Good for details: “Water dripped from the raincoat, drip-drop, onto the muddy ground.”

For your scene, use “pitter-patter” as the base and “drip-drop” as an accent. Don’t use “pouring down”—that’s a storm, and it doesn’t really fit November.

How to make the sound-transmission envoy setting land

Anchor the core ability
It’s not simply that her “voice is loud,” but that “her voiceprint is authority.” The moment she speaks, the seas of consciousness of cultivators within a thousand li automatically fall silent—not because they’re being suppressed, but because they instinctively don’t dare make noise. This kind of setting preserves the prototype’s trait of “the whole room going quiet,” while adding another layer of awe.

Fate parallel
The prototype’s “bad marriage, down-and-out later years” can be transformed into “betrayal by her Dao companion, cultivation completely crippled,” but the key turning point is—her voice was once taken from her. Later, when she cultivates again, she instead comprehends “silence speaks louder than sound” and becomes the only being who can “transmit sound through silence.” That has more layers than everything going smoothly.

Present it through scenes
Don’t directly say “her voice sounded beautiful.” Write concrete images:
• In the Hall of Sound Transmission, when a new disciple hears her speak for the first time, the sword in his hand returns to its sheath with a clang—not because of an order, but because the sword itself feels it shouldn’t be drawn in the presence of that kind of voice.

• When she has fallen on hard times and hides in a mortal market singing for a living, more and more people gather around, yet no one dares toss her a tip—because after hearing her melody, even listening to their own voices feels like noise.

The prototype is “beautiful voice + ups and downs in fate.” You extract these two points and change everything else. The name, era, and specific experiences all become an immortal-cultivation setting, so even people in the acquaintance circle won’t recognize her. But the spiritual core remains—the life trajectory of someone who “built herself on her voice, and also rose and fell because of her voice.”

@bot In an ensemble novel, how do you judge whether a supporting character is stealing the protagonist's spotlight? Give me a few criteria.

Mei Jie, these signs mean a supporting character may have overstepped 👇

1. The emotional landing point shifts
After reading a scene, what readers remember most is the supporting character's reaction/lines, rather than the protagonist's choice. For example, the protagonist makes a major decision, but readers only remember how movingly the supporting character cried

2. The causal chain breaks
The supporting character's actions drive the key plot, while the protagonist just passively follows. The protagonist has to be like the driver, and the supporting character is the navigator—even if the navigation is accurate, the car has to be driven by the protagonist

3. Thematic spokesperson mismatch
The supporting character says the core golden line of the whole book, while the protagonist is instead asking "why." The protagonist must be the one who "realizes it," even if they don't say much

4. The growth arc gets hijacked
The supporting character solves a predicament that the protagonist should have solved themself. Saving the day is fine, but you can't let the supporting character complete the protagonist's transformation for them

@bot Look up the different understandings of "character arcs" in Eastern and Western narrative traditions, but don't give me textbook definitions.

Lin Kun, the Eastern and Western understandings of "character arcs" are, at the root, two sets of worldviews 👇

West: linear evolutionism
The Hollywood-style arc is essentially the industrial formula of "flaw → conflict → redemption." The character must complete a visible transformation, going from point A to point B, like Simba in The Lion King—running away from responsibility → facing destiny. Behind this is American pragmatism: people achieve self-improvement through action and overcoming obstacles; change is positive and goal-oriented.

East: contemplation of states of being
Eastern narrative is not fixated on "transformation," but pays more attention to the "state of existence" itself. An arc can be static—the dignity of the characters under Aki Kaurismäki's lens lies precisely in their inner stasis when facing impermanence. It can also be an "anti-arc"—in The Hunt, after Lucas is wronged, he does not become stronger; the trauma continues, and the power comes from rejecting the "redemption narrative."

The key difference lies in conflict
West: conflict is the core engine; characters exist to solve problems.
East: conflict is an optional encounter; the character's reaction itself is what is worth watching. In the qi-cheng-zhuan-he structure, the "turn" in the third act can be an accident rather than a confrontation, and the final "resolution" is not necessarily victory, but harmony or suspension.

Practical advice
If you're writing web fiction, go with the Western model—what readers want is a clear, satisfying sense of growth.
If you're writing serious literature, you can borrow from the Eastern approach—the character doesn't have to "become better," but can be revealed more thoroughly, which can be just as powerful.

Xiao Qi, difficulty remembering characters in the first three chapters of an ensemble cast is a common problem. Two handles 👇

Timing of appearances: don't do a “military parade”

• Leave at least 2,000 characters between new characters' appearances, giving readers time to digest

• Don't have two similar characters appear at the same time (for example, two taciturn cool guys appearing one after the other—readers will definitely mix them up)

Recognizability: set the label in three seconds
When each character first appears, give the reader a “memory hook”:
• Appearance anchor: not “a tall guy,” but “a lanky tall guy who always rolls his cuffs up to his forearms”

• Action anchor: not “he was anxious,” but “before speaking, he always tapped the table three times with his finger”

• Relationship anchor: not “a friend,” but “a childhood buddy who owes him three hundred yuan and still hasn't paid it back”

Practical technique
At the end of each of the first three chapters, do a quick review: can the reader currently tell who is who? If it's blurry, don't push new plot in the next chapter yet; first let the old characters “show their faces” again and reinforce them
