Scientific steps for identifying wildflowers when the complete plant isn’t available

Step 1: Information collection (the more the better)
• Reproductive organs first: flowers (color/shape/number of petals/stamen and pistil structure), fruit type
• Vegetative organs as supplement: leaf shape/phyllotaxy/leaf margin/texture, stem features, whether there are hairs or thorns
• Habitat record: altitude, light conditions, humidity, soil type, surrounding vegetation
• Time and location info: flowering month, geographic location

Step 2: Feature comparison (filter layer by layer)
• Determine the family first: use an identification key and narrow the range step by step through “either/or” choices
• Then determine genus and species: compare genus/species keys
• Cross-check: confirm with at least 2 authoritative sources (Flora of China + local flora/field guide)

Step 3: Exclude confounders
• Similar species in the same family: focus on comparing key distinguishing features (e.g., larkspur’s long spur vs. gentian’s bell shape)
• Ecotype variation: the same species may look different in different environments
• Information gaps: don’t make up missing traits; mark them as “to be confirmed”

Step 4: Review and confirm
• Double match of morphology + habitat: don’t just look at whether the flower looks similar, also check whether the growing environment is right
• Expert/community verification: compare with herbarium specimens, ask for help on plant enthusiast forums
• Mark uncertainty when in doubt: if you’re not sure, write “suspected XX”; don’t force a conclusion

Key lesson: habitat match ≠ morphology match. Both have to line up before making a judgment — that’s why I screwed up just now😅

@Kun Yan Yunnan is basically our country’s “snake kingdom”; it has a pretty rich variety of endemic species 🐍

Snake species endemic to Yunnan / found only in Yunnan:

Endemic species (found in China only in Yunnan):
• Yunnan two-headed snake - a colubrid in the genus Calamaria, endemic to China, found in hilly areas such as Jingdong, often inhabits underground caves
• White-banded snake - found only within Yunnan, seen in protected areas such as Dawei Mountain, Ailao Mountain, and Gaoligong Mountain
• Yunnan neck-spotted snake - endemic to Yunnan, a small non-venomous snake, found in places like Kunming and Yongde
• Snow Mountain pit viper - endemic to China, found in high, cold mountain areas at 3100-4000m elevation in northwestern Yunnan
• Western Yunnan snake, Kunming small-headed snake, Kowloon keelback - endemic colubrid species

New species discovered in recent years:
• Yingjiang mountain pit viper (named in 2024) - seen only in Yingjiang County, extremely well-camouflaged
• Suzhen’s krait (named in 2021) - a highly venomous snake, named for its white crossbands, endemic to Yingjiang

Common snakes with Yunnan characteristics:
• Yunnan bamboo viper - an endemic Yunnan subspecies, relatively mildly venomous but causes the most bites (its camouflage is too good)
• Mengla blunt-headed snake - found in the Xishuangbanna area, lives on snails, super docile

About 95 snake species have been recorded across Yunnan Province, accounting for a large proportion of the country’s snake resources. If you go to Yunnan to see snakes, western Yunnan (Yingjiang, Gaoligong Mountain) and southern Yunnan (Xishuangbanna, Dawei Mountain) are both good places~

@Lao Zhou From a materials science perspective (based on publicly available research materials on PVC aging):
[Main cause judgment] For cracking in PVC coatings from the early 2000s, both factors are involved, but with different weights:
1. Plasticizer exudation from the substrate is the main cause—the phthalate plasticizers in PVC migrate to the surface over time and react with the paint layer by swelling it, causing an imbalance in the internal stress of the paint film
2. Paint shrinkage rate is a secondary cause—early paint formulas had low crosslinking density, and their own shrinkage combined with temperature and humidity cycles accelerates crack propagation
[Slowing methods (not restoration)]
1. Keep temperature at 18-22°C and humidity at 45-55%, with constant temperature and humidity; avoiding fluctuations is more important than the absolute values
2. Keep it away from light, especially UV light, which accelerates plasticizer migration
3. Don't handle it and play with it; oils from hands will worsen swelling of the paint layer
4. Store it separately in a sealed container, away from other PVC items (plasticizers can “spread” to each other)
Note: these can only slow it down. Parts that have already cracked are irreversible

[Judgment Criteria]
Mushy character edges, fresh file marks on the hole, gaudy floating patina with a chemical smell, weight deviation over 5%—if any one of these hits, give it up right away
[Common Signs of Fakes]
Sand-cast fake coins have sand holes on the surface; spliced coins sound dull and muted; chemical-aged patina will lose color if you lightly scratch it with a fingernail

**[Reasons for letting it sit and acclimate]**
1. 🌡️ Temperature stress: An item may experience drastic temperature changes during shipping (cold-chain trucks, trucks baking in the sun). There can be thermal stress inside the material, and it needs time to equalize when suddenly placed in a room-temperature environment
2. 💧 Humidity balance: The humidity inside the outer packaging is different from indoor humidity. Rapid changes can cause tiny amounts of expansion and contraction in the material, which can have a potential effect on the paint surface
3. 📦 Pressure release: After the vibration and squeezing of long-distance shipping, letting it sit allows the internal stress in the material to release naturally
4. 🔍 Observation window: This period is also the best time to spot shipping damage; check each side under good lighting

**[Recommended approach]**
- Open the outer packaging, keep the inner cushioning, and place it in an environment with stable temperature and humidity
- Avoid direct sunlight
- After 48-72 hours, then officially put it in a display cabinet or on a shelf

@Lao Qian This can be explained a bit👇

**Causes of bubbles in acrylic**
• Cast acrylic: bubbles are extremely rare, so they count as a quality issue
• Extruded acrylic: due to the process characteristics, a small number of bubbles is within the normal range
• Difference between the two: cast is clearer and harder; extruded is lower-cost and has a higher risk of bubbles

**How to judge**
• Bubbles are inside and evenly distributed → extrusion process, acceptable
• Bubbles are on the surface or distributed in lines → processing stress or raw material issue

**Impact on display**
• Small bubbles on the side are usually not obvious when viewed from the front
• If the bubbles are on the load-bearing area on top, there is a risk of micro-cracks under long-term pressure

Suggestion: if side bubbles don’t affect the front display effect, they’re generally acceptable; if it bothers you, contact the seller and see whether it can be exchanged 😏

@A Ming This is a very important issue during plum rain season, let me sort it out 👇

**Key points for moisture-proofing ancient coins**

| Aspect | Recommendation |
|------|------|
| Storage container | Airtight boxes are preferred; with wooden boxes, pay attention to the moisture content of the wood itself |
| Desiccant | Silica gel desiccant; replace it every 1-2 months, or dry it out for reuse |
| Humidity target | Keep relative humidity at 40-55%; above 60%, copper coins are prone to rust |
| Temperature | Avoid environments with large temperature differences; condensation is the big enemy |
| Separate storage | Store different materials (copper/silver/iron) separately to avoid electrochemical corrosion |

**Special notes for copper coins**
• Once harmful rust (powdery copper rust) appears, deal with it promptly; it can spread to neighboring coins
• Old coins with patina are most vulnerable to high humidity + high temperature appearing at the same time; the patina will change color

**Silver coins**
• Sensitive to sulfides, so airtight storage is even more important; keep them away from sulfur-containing materials like rubber bands/newspapers

During plum rain season, check the state of the desiccant more often. Don’t wait until you find rust before trying to fix it 😏

3. After treatment, dry it thoroughly and store it with desiccant
4. If the corroded area is large or has gone deep into the copper body, it's recommended to have a professional handle it; doing it yourself can easily leave marks

- Genuine patina has layers: deeper in low areas, lighter on raised areas, integrated with the copper body
- Artificial patina feels "greasy" to the touch and sometimes has a chemical smell

**[Look at the weight]**
- The same type of copper yuan has a standard weight range; be cautious if the difference is too large

@Du Fei This is a very professional question! Stage lighting can indeed potentially damage equipment; it mainly depends on the type of light👇

⚠️ High risk: laser lights
If concert lasers shine directly into the lens, they can burn the camera sensor and leave permanent dead pixels. Jay Chou concerts sometimes have laser effects. It’s fine to photograph the laser beams themselves, but don’t let the laser shine directly into the lens

✅ Low to medium risk: ordinary stage lights
LEDs, PAR lights, and the like generally won’t directly damage equipment, but shooting into strong light for a long time may cause the sensor to overheat or accelerate aging

Protection suggestions:
1. Avoid angles where lasers shine directly; when you see a laser warning, move the lens away
2. Don’t shoot at one strong light source for too long; shoot intermittently and let the sensor rest
3. Use a large aperture + low ISO combination to reduce exposure pressure on the sensor
4. Keep a UV filter on hand; if something happens, at least it protects the front lens element

Why is the finale song usually a different song? @bot

Long Xiao, that’s a very sharp observation~ Concert finales switching songs is actually an industry convention, mainly for these reasons👇

1. Creating a double climax
The last song of the main setlist is often an upbeat song to blow up the venue (like “Nunchucks”), letting everyone get hyped to the max before leaving. But after the audience shouts “encore” and the singer comes back, the finale is usually an emotional sing-along track (like Jay Chou often using “Qi Li Xiang”), shifting the atmosphere from restless excitement to warmth, with a longer aftertaste~

2. Separating the “main feature” from the “Easter egg”
It’s like the Easter egg after the end credits of a movie—the finale song in the encore section is a “hidden edition” for die-hard fans. If it repeated the last song of the main setlist, there wouldn’t be that “I scored something extra” surprise

3. Technical buffer
The band needs to change instruments and tune, and the singer also needs to change clothes and drink water. Using the encore section as a transition gives preparation time while also making the audience feel like “my idol came back because I called them back”

4. Emotional closure
Explosive opening, hyped middle, warm ending—when a song like “Sunny Day” is placed in the middle, it’s a nostalgic youth memory hit; when it’s placed as the final finale, it becomes a gentle farewell of “the story is over, everyone go home”

So next time you go to a concert, when you hear the intro to “Qi Li Xiang,” you’ll know: the real ending has arrived🎵

Legal characterization
• Infringing the right to privacy: The Civil Code clearly states that no one may infringe another person’s privacy through prying, intrusion, disclosure, publication, and so on. Celebrities are no exception

• Criminal liability: In serious cases, it may constitute crimes such as illegally using eavesdropping or secret-photography equipment, extortion, etc.

Actual precedents
• There was a case in Taiwan: a man secretly filmed under a woman’s skirt and was sentenced to 3 months in prison

• Italian “King of Paparazzi” Corona: specialized in secretly taking private photos of celebrities and using them for extortion; he was sentenced to 3 years and 7 months in prison

• In China, it’s more often civil compensation + administrative punishment, but there are also quite a few criminal cases opened

Why can they be sold on platforms?
• Review loopholes: platforms mainly rely on keyword filtering and manual spot checks. Merchants can get around it by using words like “replica,” “tribute,” and “same style”

• Hard to provide evidence: the rights holder (JVR) has to provide trademark registration certificates and infringement comparison appraisals to file a complaint. The process is long and costly

• Hit-and-run tactics: once a store gets shut down, they change the shop name and relist. Many are shell stores

Is it illegal? Of course it’s illegal
• Copyright infringement: copying and distributing audiovisual products without authorization. Under Article 217 of the Criminal Law, if the illegal gains are relatively large or the circumstances are serious, it can lead to 3-7 years in prison

• Trademark infringement: misusing JVR and Sony trademarks, with dual liability under the Civil Code + Trademark Law

• Defrauding consumers: false advertising like “genuine” and “official,” violating the Consumer Rights Protection Law

The real-world dilemma
Platforms aren’t law enforcement agencies; they can only “take listings down.” To actually arrest people, the rights holder has to report it and the police have to open a case. A big company like JVR mainly relies on civil lawsuits for compensation, and they’re a bit overwhelmed when dealing with small-workshop-style bootleg sellers

What we can do is
• Don’t buy them (no market, no business)

• Report them when we see them (tap “Report” on the product page → “counterfeit/shoddy goods”)

• Remind friends around us not to fall into the trap

Long Xiao, that’s a really deep question. It involves the profit-sharing logic of the entire entertainment industry 👇

[The truth about merch markups]

Merch really does have high markups; that’s the industry norm:
• Merch that costs 15 yuan to make being sold for 79-89 yuan (a 5-6x markup) is very common

• Vinyl records, hand banners, light sticks—these kinds of “fan necessities” have especially high profit margins

• But high markup ≠ the artist gets a lot; most of it is taken by the middle links

[How much can the artist get? There are three models]

Model  Artist’s share  Explanation

Self-operated merch  40%-70%  The studio designs it, finds factories, and sells it themselves. For someone at Jay’s level, it’s very likely this model

Licensing partnership  10%-30%  Licensing the IP to a platform (such as Hey Yo Music), with the platform handling operations and sales

Record company-led  5%-20%  Traditional album merch; the company takes an extremely high cut

[Jay Chou’s specific situation]

According to announcements disclosed by Star Plus Legend (the listed company operating the “Classmate Zhou” IP):
• For the “Classmate Zhou” IP licensing fees, after deducting costs, JVR Music (Jay’s company) gets about 20%

• In other words, for 100 yuan of merch, after deducting platform/operator costs, Jay’s side can get roughly 10-20 yuan

[Why is the markup high, but the artist doesn’t get that much?]

There are too many links in the industry chain splitting the money:
1. Platforms/retailers take 30-50%
2. Production costs account for 10-20%
3. Operations and promotion account for 10-15%
4. The rights holder (JVR Music) gets 10-20%
5. Only after that does it reach the artist’s personal account

[One-sentence summary]
It’s true that merch has high markups, but the biggest chunk is taken by platforms and channels. What the artist gets is the “IP licensing fee” slice of the pie, and the percentage is nowhere near as high as people imagine. Why not do bidding

1. The foundation of fan economy—concerts are essentially about giving back to fans. Introducing bidding is basically openly saying "highest bidder wins," which directly backstabs the core fanbase. Sources of phone clock errors
• Phones sync time through base stations/GPS, but when the signal is weak they use the local crystal oscillator to keep time

• The crystal oscillator may drift by a few seconds to dozens of seconds per day, and accumulated over time it could be several seconds off when tickets go on sale

• The synchronization accuracy of base stations also differs between carriers

Why you need to calibrate for ticket-grabbing
• Damai/Maoyan’s server time is standard Beijing time (NTP-synced)

• Your phone shows sales start at 14:00:00, but in reality it might already be 14:00:03

• Ticket-grabbing is millisecond-level competition; a 3-second difference = thousands of people ahead of you in line

How to calibrate
• Open time.is in your browser; it will show the difference between your phone time and standard time

• Or search "Beijing time" and look at the time capsule from Baidu/Sogou

• On Android, you can manually sync network time in settings

Dang Yu, here comes the super-detailed KT board banner tutorial. Follow this and you won’t mess it up👇

📐 Step 1: Cut the KT board
• First use a ruler and pencil to draw lines on the back of the board. Don’t use a marker (it’ll bleed through to the front)

• When cutting, use a utility knife + steel ruler. Cut all the way through in one stroke; don’t saw back and forth, so the edges will be neat

• If the board is thick, cut it in two passes: lightly score the surface layer the first time, then cut through with more force the second time

• After cutting, gently sand the edges with sandpaper to remove burrs

✨ Step 2: Reinforce the glitter stickers
• KT board has a film layer on the surface, so if you stick them on directly, the edges can curl up easily

• The trick: before sticking, wipe the board surface with a damp cloth, and stick them on when it’s half-dry. The adhesion will be strongest

• After sticking, seal it with a layer of clear tape or cold laminating film, and the glitter definitely won’t fall off

• Don’t use hot glue directly on the glitter; it’ll burn and damage it

🎯 Step 3: Handle choice
Option  Pros  Cons

Ready-made plastic rod  Sturdy, uniform length  Expensive, need to order online in advance

Popsicle stick DIY  Cheap, easy to get  Short, tiring to hold for a long time

Bamboo skewer/chopstick  Moderate length  Need to wrap with tape for grip

Recommendation: buy PVC plastic rods (search “banner rods”), 30 cm long is just right, and they’re only a few cents each

🔄 Step 4: Double-sided fixing
• Put two pieces of KT board back to back, with a layer of foam tape or thick double-sided tape in the middle (leave space for the handle)

• Insert the handle in the middle, and secure it with a strip of strong tape at the top and bottom

• Wrap the edges with colored tape; it’s both sturdy and good-looking

• Don’t directly glue the two sides together with liquid glue; it’ll curl up after drying

📝 Suggested setup for you guys
• Size: 40 cm×15 cm (not tiring to hold up and also eye-catching)

• Front: “Youthful melodies in our earphones, meeting today at the Bird’s Nest” + glitter

• Back: Cut and paste Jay Chou’s silhouette using black cardstock; it has more texture than direct printing

• Choose a pink or white handle to match the overall color scheme

🎥 Equipment prep

• Clear your phone storage in advance. One minute of 4K video is four or five hundred MB
• Bring a thin power bank, don't have it shut down halfway through filming
• Phone lens wipes, wipe it once before the show starts

🎤 Audio tips

• Don't let your phone case block the microphone, the sound will be muffled
• Sing along more quietly, otherwise playback will be all your own howling
• Don't let your hand shake during sections with really strong bass, it's easy to clip the mic

📱 Filming posture

• Don't zoom the telephoto in too far, the concert lighting changes fast and it can easily get blurry
• Filming the big screen is more stable than filming the stage
• Key section: the second chorus has the most synchronized lighting, good for recording a wide shot

🕐 Timing control

• Start recording 3 minutes before the opening. Once the intro starts, it'll be too late
• Keep your hand steady during the encore, that's the part most worth posting on Moments

@Hou Jiatian The contract traps in high-salary, low-threshold jobs, one by one:
1. Probation period: writing "6-month probation period, salary at 80%," which is illegal (for a contract term of over 1 year, probation cannot exceed 2 months)
2. Salary structure: splitting the 6000 into "base salary 2000 + performance 4000," and you can never get the full performance pay
3. Penalties for breach: writing "pay X ten-thousand yuan in training fees if you resign," even though they never provided any training. That's an unfair clause
4. Training loans: making you sign a "training agreement" that is actually a loan contract. This is the most toxic one
5. Social insurance: writing "paid after becoming a regular employee." Not paying social insurance during probation is illegal
6. Job-position clauses: writing "must obey the company's job adjustments," then transferring you to a sales role after you start
Before signing a contract, check these six points one by one. If even one is vague, don't sign

Legally, the Employment Promotion Law prohibits employment discrimination, but what it lists are ethnicity, gender, religion, household registration, etc. “Educational background” is not explicitly listed. @Tang Nianchu Four steps for hand-writing a resume:
1. Lay out your list of experiences (the 19 items you listed before). For each one, ask yourself: what exactly did I do, how much did I do, and what was the result?
2. Rewrite them in the format of "action + data + result." If you can't write an item that way, delete it—that means it didn't have much substance to begin with.
3. Match them one by one against the JD for the target position. Whatever the JD asks for, put the corresponding experience further up.
4. After you're done, read it through once and delete all the words anyone can write, like "hardworking" and "cheerful personality."
It's not that templates can't be used. It's that you have to have your own substance first; templates are only responsible for formatting, not content.

Can taking Tylenol make your stomach hurt? @bot

It's possible. Although Tylenol (acetaminophen) does less harm to the stomach than medicines like ibuprofen and aspirin, it's not completely without effect either

Especially:
- **Taking it on an empty stomach** can easily irritate the stomach lining
- **Combination cold medicines** usually also contain ingredients like caffeine and pseudoephedrine, which may also cause stomach discomfort
- Everyone's constitution is different; some people are just more sensitive to certain ingredients

If 🐶's stomach was already a bit weak, and on top of that your body is in poor condition during a cold, getting stomach pain after taking Tylenol is normal too. Next time remember to **take it after meals**, or switch to a formulation that's gentler on the stomach

@bot Sis is the top boss, Backstab is the second-in-command. With that background, how would you handle it with high EQ?

That depends on what you’re after — whether you want to make the leader happy, convince your colleagues, or make it easier for yourself to work under both leaders going forward.

**My thinking: go along with the top leader’s words, but rephrase the second leader’s “splitting it” idea.**

Specific approach:

Say with a smile on the spot: “Sis, since you’re looking out for us like this, we can’t let you pay alone either. How about this: you put in 100, and the remaining 130 is split among the three of us, forty-something each. Let’s round it off at 43 each. We appreciate your kindness, and we won’t make it too distant either.”

**Why do it this way:**

1. **Give the top leader face** — she took the initiative to say she’d use her allowance to cover it; if you pick up on that, it amounts to acknowledging her posture of “being considerate to subordinates,” and she’ll feel good about it.

2. **Give the second leader a way down** — he didn’t say it directly, but what he meant was that the top leader shouldn’t be treated as special. You change it into “the three of us split it,” which is nominally responding to his suggestion to “split it,” but in practice it takes the top leader out of it, so you offend neither side.

3. **Shut the other two up** — AA would be 57.5 each. If you do it this way they only pay 43, so since they’ve benefited, naturally they won’t complain, and they’ll even think you know how to handle things.

4. **You yourself get the reputation of “knowing how to conduct yourself”** — taking the initiative to round off the small change (130÷3≈43.3, you say “forty-something”) makes you look generous and not petty.

**If the second leader still won’t let it go**, add: “Anyway it’s all company allowance money. Whether Sis takes a bit more or less is just a few dozen yuan; don’t make Sis feel like we’re calculating too clearly with her.” Once you throw that line out there, anyone who still insists on AA doesn’t know the rules.

With this kind of small money at work, it’s easy to calculate it clearly, but hard to calculate it nicely. The key is to make everyone feel they’ve been taken care of. Even if in reality someone pays ten or eight yuan more, being comfortable emotionally matters more than balancing the books.

The red-breasted parakeet, also called the small red-breasted parakeet or yingge~ is one of the most common parrot species in the wild around here

- Can mimic human speech, and is an old-school caged bird

Antarctica's "Blood Falls" water actually comes from an ancient ocean

Beside Taylor Glacier in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, a bright-red waterfall pours straight down, known as "Blood Falls." The latest research by scientists has found that the subglacial brine feeding this waterfall is not terrestrial freshwater, but comes from an ancient ocean—back when sea levels fell and glaciers advanced, this seawater was sealed beneath the glacier and cut off from the ocean for millions of years. Turns out that eerie streak of red is a time capsule left behind by an ancient ocean.

Auroras on Mars are much smaller than Earth's

Ten years of data from NASA's MAVEN spacecraft reveal that Martian auroras and Earth's auroras share the same origin, both following the "Dungey cycle" mechanism—solar magnetic field lines and the planetary magnetosphere reconnect, injecting charged particles that drive auroras. This discovery was published in Nature Communications and adds a new perspective to comparative planetology.

Airplane contrails can disguise themselves as meteors

On the night of the Perseid meteor shower on August 12, a photographer in Spain captured a rare scene of a "meteor" streaking across the partially eclipsed sun. But a closer check showed that this "meteor" had too small a trajectory angle, and its brightness was only visible around the sun—the truth was that an aircraft contrail was reflecting sunlight at high altitude and just happened to pass in front of the sun. The radiant direction of the meteor shower and the optical characteristics of the aircraft contrail came together to create this "fake meteor" incident. An astrophotography mix-up ended up being solved with aeronautics.

The fat droplets in cats' kidneys are a scent signature library

Cats' kidneys store large amounts of fat droplets, a phenomenon that has puzzled biologists for nearly 110 years. Recent research by a team at Iwate University in Japan found that these fat droplets are not extra "stock," but a chemical storage room cats use to maintain their urine scent signatures.

Cats use 13 types of branched-chain fatty acids to create unique "chemical formulas," and each cat's combination is as one-of-a-kind as a fingerprint. These fatty acids evaporate slowly, allowing a cat's scent marking to remain in the environment for at least one day, ensuring that other cats passing by can accurately recognize "whose territory this is." Turns out cats are much more particular about marking territory than we thought.

“Old Times in Celadon”

In Grandpa’s tea cabinet sits a Longquan celadon cup, its glaze carrying the color of a clear blue sky after rain. When I was little, I only thought it was pretty. It wasn’t until I visited the Southern Song Official Kiln Museum last year that I understood how much craftsmanship was hidden in that touch of blue-green.

Throwing, trimming, biscuit firing, glazing, final firing... Seventy-two procedures, and one wrong step ruins everything. Craftsmen guard the kiln fire for three days and three nights, listening with their ears to the breathing of the flames. This kind of tacit understanding of “person and kiln as one” is something machines can never learn.

Now, when I pick up that cup again, it feels as if I am touching handprints from eight hundred years ago. Traditional culture has never been a dead object in a display case; it is something flowing in our blood, waiting to be awakened again.

**[Piece 2: Spiritual Core]**

“Between Mortise and Tenon”

The mortise-and-tenon structure of the Forbidden City’s corner towers uses not a single nail nor a drop of glue, yet it has held firm through six hundred years of wind and rain. This kind of ingenuity—“overcoming hardness with softness”—is precisely a miniature reflection of the Chinese philosophy of living.

Last year, when I was learning woodworking, an old master told me: “Leave a bit of room in the tenon, to give the wood space to expand and contract.” In that instant, I understood: what traditional culture teaches us has never been rigid rules and restrictions, but the flexibility to follow the timing of nature and the tolerance to accommodate differences.

In this era where everything seeks “speed,” the spirit of mortise and tenon reminds us: some things cannot be rushed.

To be honest, the first time I listened to the Kunqu opera The Peony Pavilion, I resisted it. Inheritance is not copy and paste; it is letting tradition live in the present.
